grupos.html:
1Definition and criteria

PPH (operational definition): blood loss ≥300 mL with any abnormal hemodynamic sign (HR>100, shock index>1, SBP<100, DBP<60), or blood loss ≥500 mL — whichever occurs first, within 24 h postpartum. Enhanced surveillance during the first 2 h.

Massive hemorrhage: loss/replacement of 50% of blood volume in 3 h, OR ≥150 mL/min, OR ≥1.5 mL/kg/20 min, OR ≥4 units in 24 h.

Activation rule: meet the PPH criterion (≥300 mL with any abnormal sign, or ≥500 mL) or any sign of shock → initiate MOTIVE and ACTIVATE CODE RED. Maternal decompensation signs carry more weight than blood loss volume.

Important: Vélez grades shock severity; it does not define hemorrhage. For activation, use WHO 2025: 300 mL with any abnormal sign is already postpartum hemorrhage, even if Vélez classifies it as compensated (500-1000 mL).

3Flowchart — Golden Hour

Active management of the 3rd/4th stage (6 steps, WHO 2025):

  • 1. Drying / initial assessment
  • 2. Uterotonic (oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV, or carbetocin 100 µg if cold chain is unavailable, or misoprostol 400-600 µg orally)
  • 3. Delayed cord clamping 1-3 min + skin-to-skin contact
  • 4. Controlled cord traction + countertraction
  • 5. Verify intact placenta + contracted uterus without massage
  • 6. Monitoring every 15 min for 2 h

60 minLevel III and conditions?

Resuscitation targets: normal mental status, capillary refill <3 s, SBP>90, SpO2≥95%, shock index<0.9, T°>35°C, lactate<2 mmol/L, fibrinogen>200 mg/dL.

Most deaths from postpartum hemorrhage occur in the first 2-3 h, and WHO calls for treatment to begin within 15 min of diagnosis. The survival figures are from the MSPBS guideline; peer-reviewed literature supports the urgency of the first hour, not those exact percentages.

CaVeSal® Obstetric Alert (EAPO 2025 + MAMÁ Score): the same vital signs are assessed using both scales, and the worse color takes precedence (MAMÁ Score ≥5 or any 3 = red; 2-4 = yellow; 0-1 = green). It adds what EAPO does not measure (oxygen therapy, urine output via catheter, graded level of consciousness), while EAPO adds what the MAMÁ Score does not measure (bleeding, proteinuria, headache, seizures, abdominal pain). Example: SpO₂ 96 % with a mask → green on EAPO for oxygen saturation, MAMÁ Score 3 = red. MAMÁ Score values are in Code Yellow, card 8. Obstetric early warning scales have a median sensitivity of 89 % for severe morbidity (Umar 2019).

4Medications

TXA: 1 g IV over 10 min (1 mL/min), second dose of 1 g if bleeding continues at 30 min or recurs within 24 h. DO NOT use more than 3 h after birth. It is treatment for established PPH; WHO 2025 does not recommend routine prophylaxis (see fact sheet 24).

Heat-stable carbetocin: ONLY for prevention when the cold chain fails — NOT for treatment of established uterine atony.

4 Ts (causes): Tone 70% (atony), Trauma 20% (lacerations), Tissue 10% (retained products), Thrombin 1% (coagulopathy).

E-MOTIVE: Early detection, uterine Massage, Oxytocics, Tranexamic acid, IV fluids, physical Examination and escalation.

24Tranexamic acid: from WOMAN to the present

Key message: TXA is treatment for diagnosed postpartum hemorrhage, given as soon as possible and always within 3 h of birth. The sooner it is given, the greater the benefit: most deaths from PPH occur within the first 2-3 h. It is not used for routine prophylaxis (WHO 2025, recommendations 14 and 15, new).

Administration: 1 g (ampoule 100 mg/mL, 10 mL) IV at 1 mL/min, i.e., over 10 min. Avoid rapid bolus: it may cause hypotension. A second dose of 1 g if bleeding continues at 30 min or recurs within 24 h of the first dose.

Safety: IV route only; never intrathecal or epidural (documented wrong-route error causing seizures and death). No trial showed an increase in thromboembolic events.

Beyond 3 h: no benefit and the estimate points toward harm; the WHO does not recommend it after this time.

54T's, maneuvers and escalation Level 0-3

Tone (70%) — atony: oxytocin 5 U IV over 3 min + infusion 30 U/500 cc at 125 cc/h, methylergonovine, TXA, uterine massage, bimanual compression, balloon.

Trauma (20%) — lacerations: inspect the birth canal, repair, TXA.

Tissue (10%) — retained tissue: inspect the uterine cavity, remove retained tissue/placenta, TXA.

Thrombin (1%) — coagulopathy: coagulation tests, manual clot formation test in a tube for 7 min, correct with plasma/cryoprecipitate/platelets.

Control maneuvers: bimanual compression, external aortic compression, manual removal of the placenta, uterine inversion maneuver, hydrostatic balloon (Bakri), non-pneumatic anti-shock garment.

Escalation of response: Level 0 = E-MOTIVE (early detection); Level 1 = TXA + bimanual uterine compression; Level 2 = 2nd-line pharmacologic agents + intrauterine balloon + transfusion; Level 3 = surgery (B-Lynch, Hayman, Cho sutures; O'Leary, Posadas, Tsirulnikov or hypogastric artery ligations; hysterectomy). The Zea technique (vaginal clamping of the uterine arteries) serves as a bridge, and arterial embolization is an option in the stable patient.

19Perineal tears — classification and repair (RCOG GTG 29)

Sultan classification (RCOG 2015)
GradeStructures involved
1Perineal skin and/or vaginal mucosa

  • If uncertain between 3a and 3b, classify as 3b (higher grade). A rectal buttonhole tear with an intact sphincter is not grade 4: repair it and document it separately.
  • Systematic examination with digital rectal examination for every tear before repair.
  • Grades 3-4: repair in the operating room under regional or general anesthesia, with good lighting and an assistant; if there is active bleeding, vaginal packing while transferring the patient.
  • Full-thickness EAS tear: overlap or end-to-end technique; 3a / partial tear: end-to-end. IAS: separate end-to-end repair. Avoid figure-of-eight (hemostatic) sutures, which cause ischemia.
  • Digital rectal examination at the end (to rule out transfixing sutures).
  • Postoperative care: broad-spectrum antibiotics, laxatives; avoid suppositories and enemas; follow-up with pelvic floor physiotherapy (6-12 weeks).
  • Grades 1-2: continuous layered repair with rapidly absorbing polyglactin 910.

6Placental abruption with fetal death — mode of delivery and amniotomy

Essential prerequisite: the mother must be hemodynamically stable (no shock or cardiovascular instability). If the mother is unstable → immediate cesarean delivery, regardless of whether the fetus is alive or dead (WHO).

Amniotomy in this context: perform as early as possible (not delayed) — unlike the general rule of delayed amniotomy in the physiological partograph. Objectives: (1) reduce intrauterine pressure (decompress the retroplacental hematoma and potentially halt progressive separation), and (2) allow internal monitoring if vaginal birth is attempted.

Guideline recommendations for fetal death + placental abruption (stable mother)
SourceRecommendation
WHOVaginal delivery (induction with misoprostol) if the mother is stable; cesarean delivery only in the event of maternal hemodynamic instability, regardless of fetal status.
RCOG Green-top No. 63Attempt vaginal delivery if the maternal condition is stable, with induction of labor. Cesarean delivery only for a maternal indication (uncontrolled hemorrhage, failed induction).
MSF GuidelinesUrgent uterine evacuation (vaginal delivery or cesarean delivery) regardless of gestational age; cesarean delivery becomes imperative if labor progresses very slowly, even in the event of fetal demise.
PubMed (J Obstet Gynaecol Res, PMID 28370793)Case series of 16 patients: vaginal delivery was attempted in 15 and achieved in 14 (93.3%). Feasible and safe following fetal demise due to placental abruption, regardless of gestational age, parity, cervical maturity, or duration of labor, when intensive medical resources are available.

Why vaginal delivery is preferred in this scenario: severe placental abruption with fetal demise is frequently associated with consumptive disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)—cesarean delivery in a coagulopathic patient increases the risk of intraoperative hemorrhage due to atony/coagulopathy and peripartum hysterectomy. Vaginal delivery avoids a surgical wound in the presence of a coagulation disorder.

Management protocol:

  1. Maternal stabilization: two large-bore IV lines (16-18G), Ringer's lactate, consider type and crossmatch, fibrinogen/PT/aPTT/platelet count. Activate the massive obstetric hemorrhage protocol if bleeding is heavy.
  2. Early amniotomy to decompress the uterus and allow internal monitoring.
  3. Labor induction: oral or vaginal misoprostol (WHO recommendation for fetal demise/anomaly in the 3rd trimester) + oxytocin if needed.
  4. Monitor progress: if labor progresses very slowly despite induction, cesarean delivery becomes imperative even in the event of fetal demise. There is no fixed time limit as long as maternal-fetal monitoring shows no progression of the placental abruption.
  5. Correction of coagulopathy if cesarean delivery is required: thrombocytopenia <50,000/µL or hypofibrinogenemia <100-200 mg/dL with cryoprecipitate/platelets/fresh frozen plasma before or during surgery.
  6. Postpartum: monitor for PPH and residual coagulopathy; emotional support and bereavement care.

Absolute contraindications to vaginal delivery: uncontrolled hemorrhage, placental abruption with maternal hemodynamic instability, suspected uterine rupture, classic obstetric indication for cesarean delivery (placenta previa, vasa previa).

General note on amniotomy (WHO): amniotomy alone is not recommended as the sole method of labor induction (moderate-quality evidence, weak recommendation)—it is considered only when prostaglandins and oxytocin are unavailable. This is the only documented exception for an emergency maternal hemorrhagic indication.

7Prevention of Postpartum Hemorrhage — a three-moment framework

Conceptual framework (Pregnancy → Childbirth → Postpartum): PPH results from accumulated factors across 6 categories—social determinants, maternal conditions/diseases, pregnancy factors, childbirth factors, placental factors, and health system factors (antenatal and intrapartum). The pathway to morbidity and mortality progresses as follows: normal/complicated birth → PPH → severe PPH → death/complications—with a specific intervention possible at each stage: preventive measures → early diagnosis → first-response treatment → treatment of refractory cases → post-PPH supportive care.

8Antenatal prevention

Identification and appropriate management of gestational anemia, including the use of intravenous iron when indicated (moderate-to-severe anemia, intolerance or lack of response to oral iron, or advanced gestational age with little time to correct anemia orally). Correcting anemia antenatally reduces morbidity and mortality associated with blood loss during childbirth.

9Intrapartum prevention

Perineal protection during the second stage to reduce trauma and facilitate spontaneous birth, according to the woman's preferences and available options: perineal massage, warm compresses, manual perineal support.

🚫 Avoid routine episiotomy—reserve it for specific indications, not as a routine practice.

Sources: UNFPA / Universidad de Antioquia (Grupo Nacer) — Framework for reducing PPH morbidity and mortality · WHO Consolidated Guidelines for prevention, diagnosis, treatment of PPH (Geneva, 2025) · WHO recommendations for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage.

12Variant B — WHO 2025 protocol (no fixed round table, 200mg/dL threshold)

Fibrinogen replacement threshold: <2 g/L (=200 mg/dL), target ≥ 2g/L.

Typically 3-4g of fibrinogen ≈ 8-10 units of cryoprecipitate.

13Other protocol elements

Cell salvage (intraoperative recovery of autologous blood): an option at centers with the technical capacity.

PBM (Patient Blood Management): a patient blood optimization strategy — minimize blood loss, optimize hematopoiesis, tolerate anemia when safe.

Postpartum iron: recommended by WHO 2025 when significant postpartum anemia is present.

Crystalloids over colloids (Recommendation 28): isotonic crystalloids are recommended over colloids for IV fluid resuscitation in PPH; this applies to the 500 mL boluses of warmed crystalloids in the first 20-minute flowchart. Reaffirmed by FIGO 2022 as part of the PPH care bundle.

Controlled cord traction (Du, Ye & Zheng 2014): meta-analysis of 30,532 patients; reduces manual removal of the placenta (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.58-0.84) with no difference in severe PPH (RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.88-1.01).

Sustained uterine massage: not routinely recommended after prophylactic oxytocin (Chen et al., ACOG 2013); monitor uterine tone.

Non-pneumatic anti-shock garment (NASG): a temporizing measure while transfer is underway or definitive treatment is being prepared (FIGO 2022, Escobar, Nassar, Theron et al.).

  • Bakri: success rate 79.5-85.9% in systematic reviews; in a meta-analysis of 28 studies, 82% with balloon alone (95% CI 78-86%) and 95% with additional procedures. Lower success after cesarean delivery (69-78%) than after vaginal birth (90%).
  • Sutures: no technique demonstrated clear superiority; efficacy ~75% after failure of medical treatment and ~80% as second-line treatment after failed vascular ligation; risk of synechiae 5-10%.
  • Combined balloon + suture: success rate >91.7% in refractory PPH; avoids hysterectomy in up to 75% of cases that would otherwise require it.
  • Condom/Foley balloon (improvised): WHO 2021 recommends its use only where other treatments, including immediate surgery, are already available. Assembly: 16-18 Foley catheter with the distal tip cut off, inserted into a condom, secured with silk about 5 fingers from the end (without obstructing the lumen); fill with 500 cc of 0.9% normal saline, with vaginal packing to prevent expulsion. In a comparative study of 12 patients (6 per group), the improvised balloon achieved 100% success (6/6), with no complications or associated surgeries, comparable to the SOS Bakri balloon, although time to hemostasis was slightly longer (6.8 vs. 4.6 min, not statistically significant). Source: Jiménez L, Veroes J, Vera M, Colmenares M, Di Muro J, Márquez D. Rev Obstet Ginecol Venez. 2020;80(3):227-235.

Comparative reference; the surgical step-by-step is beyond the scope of a quick-reference guide. Included in the Code Red Level 2-3 escalation — in our setting (Paraguay), where Bakri/Ellavi are not always available, the improvised balloon is the usual and clinically equivalent option.

18“Diamond of Death”: why calcium should be corrected during massive transfusion

Evolution of the classic lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy) with a fourth vertex: hypocalcemia. All four components reinforce one another: each worsens the other three.

  • Hypothermia ↔ Hypocalcemia ↔ Acidosis ↔ Coagulopathy.
  • This is the pathophysiologic framework behind the practical recommendation to replace calcium IV during massive transfusion (see protocol, subcards 10-13).
  • In PPH, low ionized calcium is associated with greater bleeding severity (Epstein et al., Br J Anaesth 2021).

20Blood volume, allowable blood loss, and quantification of bleeding

  • Estimated blood volume: 100 mL/kg in healthy pregnancy; 70 mL/kg in obesity or volume contraction (severe preeclampsia).
  • Maximum allowable blood loss: (initial Hb − minimum Hb) × blood volume ÷ [(initial Hb + minimum Hb) × 0.5]. Usual minimum Hb 7 g/dL.
  • Quantify, do not estimate by eye: 1 g = 1 mL. Wet weight − dry weight (pads, gauze, drapes) + suction volume − amniotic fluid − irrigation.
  • Separate amniotic fluid before placental delivery (change the canister or record the volume).
  • Express blood loss as a % of blood volume and compare it with the Vélez shock classification (subcard 2).

fichas.texto: PPH (operational definition): blood loss ≥300 mL with any abnormal hemodynamic sign (HR>100, shock index>1, SBP<100, DBP<60), or blood loss ≥500 mL — whichever occurs first, within 24 h postpartum. Enhanced surveillance during the first 2 h. Massive hemorrhage: loss/replacement of 50% of blood volume in 3 h, OR ≥150 mL/min, OR ≥1.5 mL/kg/20 min, OR ≥4 units in 24 h. Activation rule: meet the PPH criterion (≥300 mL with any abnormal sign, or ≥500 mL) or any sign of shock → initiate MOTIVE and ACTIVATE CODE RED. Maternal decompensation signs carry more weight than blood loss volume. Definition Criterion Status WHO/FIGO/ICM 2025 (rec. 22) ≥300 mL measured + HR >100, SI >1, SBP <100, or DBP <60; or ≥500 mL measured. All modes of delivery, within 24 h, enhanced surveillance during the first 2 h Current — used by the calculator reVITALize / ACOG PB 183 (2017) ≥1000 mL cumulative, or blood loss with signs or symptoms of hypovolemia, within 24 h (any mode of delivery) Variant Classic (WHO 2012 and traditional texts) ≥500 mL in vaginal delivery; ≥1000 mL in cesarean delivery No longer current The WHO 2025 applies the same criterion to cesarean delivery and warns against normalizing greater blood loss with this route. Always measure objectively (calibrated drape or weighing). Source: WHO/FIGO/ICM, Consolidated guidelines on PPH, 2025. Before and now — why it is no longer 500 or 1000 mL Before (classic definition, no longer current) Now (WHO/FIGO/ICM 2025) Definition ≥500 mL in vaginal delivery; ≥1000 mL in cesarean delivery ≥300 mL with any abnormal sign, or ≥500 mL, for all modes of delivery Activation Code Red with >1000 mL and/or signs of shock When criteria are met: initiate MOTIVE and activate Code Red Measurement Visual estimation, which underestimates blood loss Objective measurement: calibrated drape or weighing What matters more Volume The sign of maternal decompensation (HR >100, SI >1, SBP <100, DBP <60) Why it changed: with high thresholds and visual estimation, diagnosis was delayed. Objective measurement and action at the first sign of decompensation allow treatment to begin earlier. For cesarean delivery, the WHO advises against normalizing greater blood loss. Source: WHO/FIGO/ICM 2025, recommendation 22 and observations. Shock index (HR/SBP): >0.9 marker of severity; ≥1.4 urgent need for intervention; ≥1.7 high probability of an adverse outcome.

fichas.texto: For every patient on admission and at each assessment. EAPO is not a score: each parameter has a color and a single red activates the obstetric emergency, which is then directed to the code according to the cause (hemorrhage → Code Red · hypertension → HDP · infection → Code Yellow — Sepsis · cardiac arrest → Obstetric Code Blue). EAPO MSPBS 2025/2022: parameters by color Parameter Red Yellow Green RR (breaths/min) ≥22 · ≤11 20-21 12-19 SpO₂ (%) <95 — 95-100 Temperature (°C) ≥39 · ≤35 38 36-37 HR (bpm) ≥100 · ≤59 — 60-99 SBP (mmHg) ≥160 · ≤70 140-159* · 71-99 100-139 DBP (mmHg) ≥110 · 51-59 90-109 60-89 Neurological Only responds to pain · unconscious Disoriented Alert Appearance Pale · cyanotic · jaundiced Diaphoretic Normal Urine output No urine output in 6 h or >30 mL/h — Yes Proteinuria (dipstick) +++ or more — + / ++ Genital bleeding Heavy Spotting Absent Purulent discharge · headache with visual or auditory disturbance · seizures Yes — No Abdominal pain With peritoneal irritation Without irritation No * Note: the 2025 sheet is used, and gaps are supplemented with the 2022 version (the 2025 sheet does not include the SBP 140-159 row). EAPO variants from MSPBS (cited, not used in the calculation) Cutoff 2025 sheet (calculator) Code Red Guide, 2nd ed. 2022 RR red / yellow ≥22 / 20-21 ≥25 / 20-24 Temperature red / yellow ≥39 / 38 ≥40 / 38-39 SBP 140-159 No row Yellow Monitoring frequency by color Color EAPO (MSPBS) MAMÁ Score (Ecuador MSP) Red Every 5-10 min ≥5 or any 3: every 30 min Yellow Every 20-30 min 2-4: every 1 h Green Every 1-2 h 0-1: every 4 h Golden hour and survival by intervention (hemorrhage) Time Phase Data Minute 0 Activation Stabilize and decide 1-20 min Resuscitation and diagnosis The compensatory response lasts about 20-30 min 20 min without compensatory action Stabilization Survival 60 % 40-60 min DIC is assumed Survival <20 % >60 min Advanced management High probability of DIC Most deaths from postpartum hemorrhage occur in the first 2-3 h, and WHO calls for treatment to begin within 15 min of diagnosis. The survival figures are from the MSPBS guideline; peer-reviewed literature supports the urgency of the first hour, not those exact percentages. CaVeSal® Obstetric Alert (EAPO 2025 + MAMÁ Score): the same vital signs are assessed using both scales, and the worse color takes precedence (MAMÁ Score ≥5 or any 3 = red; 2-4 = yellow; 0-1 = green). It adds what EAPO does not measure (oxygen therapy, urine output via catheter, graded level of consciousness), while EAPO adds what the MAMÁ Score does not measure (bleeding, proteinuria, headache, seizures, abdominal pain). Example: SpO₂ 96 % with a mask → green on EAPO for oxygen saturation, MAMÁ Score 3 = red. MAMÁ Score values are in Code Yellow, card 8. Obstetric early warning scales have a median sensitivity of 89 % for severe morbidity (Umar 2019). CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS Paraguay, DSSR. Heat-stable carbetocin: ONLY for prevention when the cold chain fails — NOT for treatment of established uterine atony. 4 Ts (causes): Tone 70% (atony), Trauma 20% (lacerations), Tissue 10% (retained products), Thrombin 1% (coagulopathy). fichas.titulo: Tranexamic acid: from WOMAN to the present
fichas.texto: Key message: TXA is treatment for diagnosed postpartum hemorrhage, given as soon as possible and always within 3 h of birth. The sooner it is given, the greater the benefit: most deaths from PPH occur within the first 2-3 h. It is not used for routine prophylaxis (WHO 2025, recommendations 14 and 15, new). Trials of tranexamic acid in postpartum hemorrhage Trial Population Primary outcome What changed WOMAN 2017 20,060 women with established PPH, 21 countries Death from bleeding 1.5 % vs 1.9 % (RR 0.81; CI 0.65-1.00). Within 3 h: 1.2 % vs 1.7 % (RR 0.69; CI 0.52-0.91). No reduction in hysterectomy. No increase in thrombosis TXA becomes standard treatment when given early TRAAP 2018 4,079, vaginal birth, prophylaxis PPH ≥500 mL 8.1 % vs 9.8 % (RR 0.83; CI 0.68-1.01), not significant Does not support routine prophylaxis for vaginal birth TRAAP2 2021 4,551, cesarean, prophylaxis Calculated blood loss >1000 mL or transfusion 26.7% vs 31.6% (adjusted RR 0.84; CI 0.75-0.94); no differences in secondary clinical outcomes Less measured blood loss, no clear clinical benefit MFMU 2023 11,000 cesarean deliveries, 31 hospitals in the US Death or transfusion 3.6% vs 4.3% (adjusted RR 0.89; CI 0.74-1.07) Does not support prophylaxis at cesarean delivery WOMAN-2 2024 15,068 women with moderate or severe anemia, vaginal birth Clinical PPH 7.0% vs 6.6% (RR 1.05; CI 0.94-1.19). No thromboembolic events Prophylaxis does not prevent PPH even in women with anemia IPD meta-analysis 2024 54,404 women, 5 trials Life-threatening bleeding 0.65% vs 0.85% (OR 0.77; CI 0.63-0.93), with no increase in thrombosis Small and safe benefit; still does not change the WHO recommendation Administration: 1 g (ampoule 100 mg/mL, 10 mL) IV at 1 mL/min, i.e., over 10 min. Avoid rapid bolus: it may cause hypotension. A second dose of 1 g if bleeding continues at 30 min or recurs within 24 h of the first dose. Safety: IV route only; never intrathecal or epidural (documented wrong-route error causing seizures and death). No trial showed an increase in thromboembolic events. Beyond 3 h: no benefit and the estimate points toward harm; the WHO does not recommend it after this time.

fichas.texto: Tone (70%) — atony: oxytocin 5 U IV over 3 min + infusion 30 U/500 cc at 125 cc/h, methylergonovine, TXA, uterine massage, bimanual compression, balloon. Trauma (20%) — lacerations: inspect the birth canal, repair, TXA. Tissue (10%) — retained tissue: inspect the uterine cavity, remove retained tissue/placenta, TXA. Thrombin (1%) — coagulopathy: coagulation tests, manual clot formation test in a tube for 7 min, correct with plasma/cryoprecipitate/platelets. Control maneuvers: bimanual compression, external aortic compression, manual removal of the placenta, uterine inversion maneuver, hydrostatic balloon (Bakri), non-pneumatic anti-shock garment. Escalation of response: Level 0 = E-MOTIVE (early detection); Level 1 = TXA + bimanual uterine compression; Level 2 = 2nd-line pharmacologic agents + intrauterine balloon + transfusion; Level 3 = surgery (B-Lynch, Hayman, Cho sutures; O'Leary, Posadas, Tsirulnikov or hypogastric artery ligations; hysterectomy). The Zea technique (vaginal clamping of the uterine arteries) serves as a bridge, and arterial embolization is an option in the stable patient.

fichas.titulo: Perineal tears — classification and repair (RCOG GTG 29)
fichas.texto: Sultan classification (RCOG 2015) Grade Structures involved 1 Perineal skin and/or vaginal mucosa 2 Perineal muscles, without involving the anal sphincter 3a <50% of the external anal sphincter (EAS) thickness 3b >50% of the EAS thickness 3c EAS and internal anal sphincter (IAS) 4 Anal sphincter (EAS + IAS) and anorectal mucosa If uncertain between 3a and 3b, classify as 3b (higher grade). A rectal buttonhole tear with an intact sphincter is not grade 4: repair it and document it separately. Systematic examination with digital rectal examination for every tear before repair. Grades 3-4: repair in the operating room under regional or general anesthesia, with good lighting and an assistant; if there is active bleeding, vaginal packing while transferring the patient. Full-thickness EAS tear: overlap or end-to-end technique; 3a / partial tear: end-to-end. IAS: separate end-to-end repair. Avoid figure-of-eight (hemostatic) sutures, which cause ischemia. Digital rectal examination at the end (to rule out transfixing sutures). Postoperative care: broad-spectrum antibiotics, laxatives; avoid suppositories and enemas; follow-up with pelvic floor physiotherapy (6-12 weeks). Grades 1-2: continuous layered repair with rapidly absorbing polyglactin 910. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 29 (2015) · Sultan AH. fichas.titulo: Placental abruption with fetal death — mode of delivery and amniotomy
fichas.texto: Essential prerequisite: the mother must be hemodynamically stable (no shock or cardiovascular instability). If the mother is unstable → immediate cesarean delivery, regardless of whether the fetus is alive or dead (WHO). Amniotomy in this context: perform as early as possible (not delayed) — unlike the general rule of delayed amniotomy in the physiological partograph. Objectives: (1) reduce intrauterine pressure (decompress the retroplacental hematoma and potentially halt progressive separation), and (2) allow internal monitoring if vaginal birth is attempted. Guideline recommendations for fetal death + placental abruption (stable mother) Source Recommendation WHO Vaginal delivery (induction with misoprostol) if the mother is stable; cesarean delivery only in the event of maternal hemodynamic instability, regardless of fetal status. RCOG Green-top No. 63 Attempt vaginal delivery if the maternal condition is stable, with induction of labor. Cesarean delivery only for a maternal indication (uncontrolled hemorrhage, failed induction). MSF Guidelines Urgent uterine evacuation (vaginal delivery or cesarean delivery) regardless of gestational age; cesarean delivery becomes imperative if labor progresses very slowly, even in the event of fetal demise. PubMed (J Obstet Gynaecol Res, PMID 28370793) Case series of 16 patients: vaginal delivery was attempted in 15 and achieved in 14 (93.3%). Feasible and safe following fetal demise due to placental abruption, regardless of gestational age, parity, cervical maturity, or duration of labor, when intensive medical resources are available. Why vaginal delivery is preferred in this scenario: severe placental abruption with fetal demise is frequently associated with consumptive disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)—cesarean delivery in a coagulopathic patient increases the risk of intraoperative hemorrhage due to atony/coagulopathy and peripartum hysterectomy. Vaginal delivery avoids a surgical wound in the presence of a coagulation disorder. Management protocol: Maternal stabilization: two large-bore IV lines (16-18G), Ringer's lactate, consider type and crossmatch, fibrinogen/PT/aPTT/platelet count. Activate the massive obstetric hemorrhage protocol if bleeding is heavy. Early amniotomy to decompress the uterus and allow internal monitoring. Labor induction: oral or vaginal misoprostol (WHO recommendation for fetal demise/anomaly in the 3rd trimester) + oxytocin if needed. Monitor progress: if labor progresses very slowly despite induction, cesarean delivery becomes imperative even in the event of fetal demise. There is no fixed time limit as long as maternal-fetal monitoring shows no progression of the placental abruption. Correction of coagulopathy if cesarean delivery is required: thrombocytopenia <50,000/µL or hypofibrinogenemia <100-200 mg/dL with cryoprecipitate/platelets/fresh frozen plasma before or during surgery. Postpartum: monitor for PPH and residual coagulopathy; emotional support and bereavement care. Absolute contraindications to vaginal delivery: uncontrolled hemorrhage, placental abruption with maternal hemodynamic instability, suspected uterine rupture, classic obstetric indication for cesarean delivery (placenta previa, vasa previa). General note on amniotomy (WHO): amniotomy alone is not recommended as the sole method of labor induction (moderate-quality evidence, weak recommendation)—it is considered only when prostaglandins and oxytocin are unavailable. This is the only documented exception for an emergency maternal hemorrhagic indication.

fichas.titulo: Prevention of Postpartum Hemorrhage — a three-moment framework
fichas.texto: Conceptual framework (Pregnancy → Childbirth → Postpartum): PPH results from accumulated factors across 6 categories—social determinants, maternal conditions/diseases, pregnancy factors, childbirth factors, placental factors, and health system factors (antenatal and intrapartum). The pathway to morbidity and mortality progresses as follows: normal/complicated birth → PPH → severe PPH → death/complications—with a specific intervention possible at each stage: preventive measures → early diagnosis → first-response treatment → treatment of refractory cases → post-PPH supportive care.

fichas.texto: Identification and appropriate management of gestational anemia, including the use of intravenous iron when indicated (moderate-to-severe anemia, intolerance or lack of response to oral iron, or advanced gestational age with little time to correct anemia orally). Correcting anemia antenatally reduces morbidity and mortality associated with blood loss during childbirth.

fichas.titulo: Variant B — WHO 2025 protocol (no fixed round table, 200mg/dL threshold)
fichas.texto: Fibrinogen replacement threshold: <2 g/L (=200 mg/dL), target ≥ 2g/L. Typically 3-4g of fibrinogen ≈ 8-10 units of cryoprecipitate. No fixed round table — guided by ongoing clinical and laboratory assessment (unlike the rigid round-based Pacheco 2013 protocol). After the 2nd round/reassessment: administer tranexamic acid (TXA) 1g IV if not already administered.

fichas.titulo: Quantification of blood loss: calibrated drape and visual chart
fichas.texto: Operational recommendation: use a calibrated blood collection drape when available (an objective method recognized by WHO 2025); otherwise, use the visual equivalency chart. The chart supplements, but does not replace, objective measurement. Volumetric equivalents by pad/surface (Bose et al., BJOG 2006) Item Estimated volume Stained sanitary pad 30 mL Saturated sanitary pad 100 mL Soaked 10×10 cm gauze 60 mL Incontinence brief 250 mL 45×45 cm gauze pad 350 mL Full kidney dish (basin) 500 mL Spill on floor, 100 cm diameter 1000 mL PPH confined to the bed 1500 mL PPH with spill on the floor 2000 mL CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: WHO 2025 · Bose et al., BJOG 2006. Calibrated drape (BRASSS-V drape): simple, low-cost, accurate, and objective; usable in a wide range of settings, with a hygienic surface for childbirth. In its trial, visual estimation underestimated actual blood loss by 33% compared with the calibrated drape (correlation with spectrophotometry 0.92).

fichas.titulo: Drugs and fluids in PPH: differences that matter (WHO 2025)
fichas.texto: Misoprostol: dose and route vary by indication Indication Dose and route WHO 2025 recommendation Prevention of PPH 400 or 600 µg ORAL Recommendation 7.3 — for all births Treatment of PPH (2nd line) 800 µg SUBLINGUAL Recommendation 25 — if IV oxytocin is unavailable or bleeding does not respond (with IV ergometrine or an oxytocin+ergometrine combination) CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: WHO 2025 (PPH) · FIGO 2022 · Zheng 2014 · Chen et al. 2013. Crystalloids over colloids (Recommendation 28): isotonic crystalloids are recommended over colloids for IV fluid resuscitation in PPH; this applies to the 500 mL boluses of warmed crystalloids in the first 20-minute flowchart. Reaffirmed by FIGO 2022 as part of the PPH care bundle. Controlled cord traction (Du, Ye & Zheng 2014): meta-analysis of 30,532 patients; reduces manual removal of the placenta (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.58-0.84) with no difference in severe PPH (RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.88-1.01). Sustained uterine massage: not routinely recommended after prophylactic oxytocin (Chen et al., ACOG 2013); monitor uterine tone. Non-pneumatic anti-shock garment (NASG): a temporizing measure while transfer is underway or definitive treatment is being prepared (FIGO 2022, Escobar, Nassar, Theron et al.).

fichas.titulo: Balloon tamponade and uterine compression sutures
fichas.texto: Intrauterine balloon tamponade devices (same principle: hydrostatic pressure) Device Characteristic Bakri Obstetric-specific design; up to 500 mL Ellavi Less expensive; similar design to Bakri Condom + Foley/Nelaton catheter Low-cost adaptation for resource-limited settings Rusch catheter Adapted hydrostatic balloon Sengstaken-Blakemore Double balloon (gastric + esophageal); designed for esophageal varices and adapted for uterine tamponade Uterine compression sutures Technique Particularity B-Lynch Classic, “suspender” suture; requires open hysterotomy Hayman Simplified modification; does not require hysterotomy (uterus closed) Pereira Multiple transverse and vertical sutures; closed uterus Ho-Cho Multiple square sutures; particularly indicated for placenta accreta Uterine sandwich Simultaneous intrauterine balloon + external compression suture (B-Lynch + Bakri) Devascularization and vascular control Technique Particularity Zea (vaginal) Vaginal clamping of the uterine arteries with ring forceps in the lateral parametrium of the cervix; bridging measure while preparing the operating room or addressing the cause. Also useful before evacuating a cervical ectopic pregnancy O'Leary Bilateral ligation of the uterine arteries via laparotomy; first-line conservative surgical option Posadas Selective devascularization: posterior ligation of the uterine arteries and internal tubal arteries, without opening the broad ligament; 96.4% success in 750 cases Tsirulnikov Triple stepwise ligation: round ligaments, utero-ovarian ligaments, and uterine arteries Hypogastric arteries Internal iliac artery ligation; more complex (ureteral and venous risk), reserved for failure of the preceding procedures Arterial embolization Interventional radiology in a hemodynamically stable patient; fertility-preserving CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: INPer — Zea technique · IMSS Clinical Practice Guideline 162 · Ginecol Obstet Méx — Posadas technique · Series of 750 cases. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: WHO 2021 · MSPBS Code Red 2022. Bakri: success rate 79.5-85.9% in systematic reviews; in a meta-analysis of 28 studies, 82% with balloon alone (95% CI 78-86%) and 95% with additional procedures. Lower success after cesarean delivery (69-78%) than after vaginal birth (90%). Sutures: no technique demonstrated clear superiority; efficacy ~75% after failure of medical treatment and ~80% as second-line treatment after failed vascular ligation; risk of synechiae 5-10%. Combined balloon + suture: success rate >91.7% in refractory PPH; avoids hysterectomy in up to 75% of cases that would otherwise require it. Condom/Foley balloon (improvised): WHO 2021 recommends its use only where other treatments, including immediate surgery, are already available. Assembly: 16-18 Foley catheter with the distal tip cut off, inserted into a condom, secured with silk about 5 fingers from the end (without obstructing the lumen); fill with 500 cc of 0.9% normal saline, with vaginal packing to prevent expulsion. In a comparative study of 12 patients (6 per group), the improvised balloon achieved 100% success (6/6), with no complications or associated surgeries, comparable to the SOS Bakri balloon, although time to hemostasis was slightly longer (6.8 vs. 4.6 min, not statistically significant). Source: Jiménez L, Veroes J, Vera M, Colmenares M, Di Muro J, Márquez D. Rev Obstet Ginecol Venez. 2020;80(3):227-235. Comparative reference; the surgical step-by-step is beyond the scope of a quick-reference guide. Included in the Code Red Level 2-3 escalation — in our setting (Paraguay), where Bakri/Ellavi are not always available, the improvised balloon is the usual and clinically equivalent option.

fichas.titulo: “Diamond of Death”: why calcium should be corrected during massive transfusion
fichas.texto: Evolution of the classic lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy) with a fourth vertex: hypocalcemia. All four components reinforce one another: each worsens the other three. Hypothermia ↔ Hypocalcemia ↔ Acidosis ↔ Coagulopathy. This is the pathophysiologic framework behind the practical recommendation to replace calcium IV during massive transfusion (see protocol, subcards 10-13). In PPH, low ionized calcium is associated with greater bleeding severity (Epstein et al., Br J Anaesth 2021).

fichas.titulo: Blood volume, allowable blood loss, and quantification of bleeding
fichas.texto: Estimated blood volume: 100 mL/kg in healthy pregnancy; 70 mL/kg in obesity or volume contraction (severe preeclampsia). Maximum allowable blood loss: (initial Hb − minimum Hb) × blood volume ÷ [(initial Hb + minimum Hb) × 0.5]. Usual minimum Hb 7 g/dL. Quantify, do not estimate by eye: 1 g = 1 mL. Wet weight − dry weight (pads, gauze, drapes) + suction volume − amniotic fluid − irrigation. Separate amniotic fluid before placental delivery (change the canister or record the volume). Express blood loss as a % of blood volume and compare it with the Vélez shock classification (subcard 2). Methods for estimating blood volume Method Use 100 / 70 mL/kg (SOGC 431) Used by the calculator “Rule of 30”: 100 mL/kg SA Health PPH 30–60% increase over nonpregnant blood volume Williams Obstetrics (Pritchard) Nonlinear formula by BMI (obese women have fewer mL/kg) Lancaster University, nonlinear proposal Nadler (height and weight, nonpregnant) Nadler, PubMed 30252333 CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: SOGC Guideline No. 431 (J Obstet Gynaecol Can 2022) · ACOG Committee Opinion No. 794 (2019).

grupos.titulo: HDP Code — Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
grupos.bajada: Severe preeclampsia, hypertensive emergency, and eclampsia.
grupos.html:
1Definition and criteria

Pregnancy >20 weeks + 2 BP readings 15 min apart if severe (≥160/110) or 4 h apart if mild (140-159/90-109) + evidence of end-organ damage (clinical: headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, pulmonary edema; laboratory: AST/ALT≥70, LDH≥600, platelets<100,000, bilirubin≥1.2) OR proteinuria (≥300 mg/24h, protein/creatinine ratio≥0.3, albumin/creatinine ratio≥0.8, dipstick≥2+) OR angiogenic tests sFlt1/PlGF>38.

Proteinuria is NOT required for the diagnosis of severe preeclampsia.

Prevention: calcium 1-2 g/day in all pregnant patients; aspirin 150 mg/day based on risk factors (1 high-risk factor or 2 moderate-risk factors).

2Classification and team

Code activation: SBP>160 or DBP>110 or eclamptic seizures.

Team: Coordinator, Assistant, Circulating Nurse.

Post-target monitoring: every 10 min for the 1st hour, every 15 min for the 2nd hour, every 30 min for the 3rd hour, every hour from the 4th hour for an additional 4 h.

Sustained severe-range BP for >15 min = life-threatening emergency.

3Flowchart — SSSAO / stepwise algorithm

SSSAO mnemonic: Support, Safety, magnesium sulfate (loading dose 4-6 g IV, maintenance 1-2 g/h until 24 h postpartum), Antihypertensives (reduce by 20-25% over 24-48 h, target 135/85 per NICE), Obstetric management (fetal maturation at 24-34 weeks, fetal well-being, delivery: non-severe PE at 37 weeks, severe PE at 34 weeks).

Stepwise hypertensive emergency algorithm: IV labetalol 20→40 mg / oral nifedipine 10→20→20 mg / IV hydralazine 10 mg, reassessing every 10-20 min.

Fluid management: no bolus, total 80 mL/h or 1 mL/kg/h, max 125 mL/h.

Eclampsia: seizure control with a 4-6 g IV MgSO4 bolus (or 2 g IV if already receiving it), maintenance 2 g/h, second 2 g IV bolus if seizures recur. Intubate if: unconscious after seizure, status epilepticus, aspiration, hypoxia. Continue MgSO4 for at least 24 h postpartum or from the last seizure.

4Medications

All patients with severe PE receive MgSO4; mode of delivery is determined by obstetric factors, NOT automatic cesarean delivery.

5Expanded classification and additional severity criteria (ACOG PB 222 / FIGO / ISSHP)

Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia: new-onset proteinuria, or sudden loss of blood pressure control, or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks of gestation in a patient with hypertension predating pregnancy.

Additional severity criterion — Progressive renal insufficiency: serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling of baseline creatinine (not previously included alongside LDH/bilirubin — added as an independent laboratory criterion).

Urine output — alternative weight-based threshold: <0.5 mL/kg/h, as an alternative to the absolute threshold of <30 mL/h already used for MgSO4 toxicity monitoring.

6Chronic/oral maintenance antihypertensives (outside the acute crisis)

DrugDoseMaximum dose
Oral labetalol100-400mg every 8-12h2,400mg/day
Methyldopa250-500mg PO every 6-8h2g/day
Extended-release nifedipine20-60mg PO every 12-24h120mg/day
🚫 Contraindicated in pregnancy: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct renin inhibitors — teratogenicity, fetal renal failure.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG PB 222 (2020) · NICE NG133 · FIGO 2019 · ISSHP 2021.

7Aspirin prophylaxis — variations in initiation window (2 approaches)

SourceDoseInitiation window
FIGO 2019 / USPSTF150mg/nightWeeks 11-14⁺⁶ to 36
ACOG PB 222 (2020)100-150mg/dayWeeks 12-16 to 36

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: FIGO 2019 · USPSTF 2021 · ACOG PB 222.

High-risk indications (warrant initiation of aspirin): history of preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, type 1 or 2 diabetes, kidney disease, SLE/APS, multiple pregnancy.

Calcium: 1.5-2.0g/day in populations with low dietary calcium intake (<800mg/day) — same FIGO caveat used in Prevention (subcard 1).

8Additional safety notes

  • Nifedipine in hypertensive crisis: swallow with water; DO NOT administer sublingually.
  • MgSO4 antidote: Calcium gluconate 10% 1g (10mL) slow IV. Two administration-rate options: 3-5 min (MSPBS/CaVeSal regimen) or 10 min (ACOG/WHO).
  • Monitoring for MgSO4 toxicity: discontinue if RR <12 breaths/min; some guidelines use <12-16 breaths/min (CaVeSal regimen) and others <12-14 breaths/min (ACOG). Patellar reflex present and urine output ≥30 mL/h in all regimens.

9MgSO4 regimens — Pritchard · Zuspan · IM

The Calculator uses the Pritchard/MSPBS regimen by default. The Zuspan IV regimen is the intravenous alternative and is preferred for neuroprotection; the University of Antioquia uses a larger dilution volume with the same total dose.

RegimenLoading doseMaintenance
Pritchard / MSPBS14 g total: 10 g IM (5 g = 10 cc in each buttock) + 4 g IV (8 cc + 12 cc of NS in a 20 cc syringe, over 20 min)IV 1-2 g/h in a 100 cc Volutrol, or IM 5 g every 4 h, for 24 h
Zuspan (IV)4 g IV over 20-30 min1-2 g/h IV for 24 h (preeclampsia); for neuroprotection, until delivery or for 12 h
University of AntioquiaSame total dose with a larger dilution volume (see source protocol)

IM maintenance — how to administer (clarification to prevent underdosing): each dose is 5 g PER SCHEDULED DOSE (10 cc total). Option 1 (official text): 10 cc in one buttock, alternating buttocks at each scheduled dose. Option 2 (administration variant proposed by CaVeSal®): 5 cc (2.5 g) in each buttock at the same scheduled dose, repeated at the next scheduled dose (every 4 h). The frequent error is to administer a TOTAL of 5 cc per scheduled dose (2.5 g): the full dose is 10 cc (5 g).

Typical sequence of toxicity: 1st, decreased urine output (<30 mL/h, risk of accumulation); 2nd, loss of the patellar reflex; 3rd, respiratory depression (RR <12-16 breaths/min). Rescue: calcium gluconate 10%, 1 g (10 cc) slow IV over 3-5 min, in the event of respiratory depression or instability (this is not gram-for-gram neutralization). The regimen may be repeated (repeat regimen) according to clinical course.

9HELLP syndrome: ACOG, Tennessee, and Mississippi criteria

Comparison of the 3 diagnostic systems
SystemPlateletsTransaminasesHemolysis / LDHUse
ACOG PB 222 (2020)<100.000/µLAST and ALT >2 times the upper limit of normalLDH ≥600 U/LClinical diagnosis; no subdivision by class
Tennessee (Sibai)<100.000/µLAST ≥70 U/LLDH ≥600 U/L (or bilirubin >1.2 mg/dL with abnormal smear: schistocytes)Complete HELLP = 3 criteria; partial = 1-2 criteria
Mississippi — Class 1 (severe)≤50.000/µLAST or ALT ≥70 U/LLDH ≥600 U/LHigher risk of DIC and hemorrhage
Mississippi — Class 2 (moderate)>50.000 a ≤100.000/µLAST or ALT ≥70 U/LLDH ≥600 U/LIntermediate risk
Mississippi — Class 3 (mild)>100.000 a ≤150.000/µLAST or ALT ≥40 U/LLDH ≥600 U/LDetects early forms not included in ACOG/Tennessee

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (2020) · tabla Tennessee vs Mississippi (PMC2654858) · Clin Liver Dis 2019 (PMC6448736) · StatPearls, HELLP Syndrome.

  • ACOG management: because of its morbidity and mortality, many authors recommend delivery in HELLP syndrome regardless of gestational age, after maternal stabilization. ACOG considers the evidence insufficient to use corticosteroids to attenuate the disease (they are used for fetal lung maturation according to gestational age).
  • Neuraxial anesthesia (ACOG): acceptable with platelets ≥70,000/µL if the count is stable, there is no other coagulopathy, platelet function is normal, and the patient is not taking antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents (risk of epidural hematoma <0.2%).
  • Practical difference: ACOG sets the <100,000/µL cutoff for diagnosis; Mississippi subdivides by platelet nadir to grade bleeding risk and guide transfusion planning.

Correction of attribution: bilirubin >1.2 mg/dL and schistocytes belong to the Tennessee criteria (Sibai), not the diagnostic text of ACOG PB 222. In the Calculator the default criterion is Mississippi, with a selector for ACOG and Tennessee. Sources: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (2020) · tabla Tennessee vs Mississippi (PMC2654858) · Clin Liver Dis 2019 (PMC6448736) · StatPearls, HELLP Syndrome.

10sFlt-1/PlGF ratio: diagnostic and prognostic thresholds

Interpretation (Roche Elecsys assay; cutoffs depend on the platform)
Ratio<34 weeks≥34 weeksInterpretation
≤38Rules outRules outRules out PE in the following week (NPV >99%)
38-85 / 38-11038-8538-110Intermediate zone: repeat in 1-2 weeks
>85 / >110>85>110High suspicion or diagnostic support for PE
>655 / >201>655>201Extreme angiogenic imbalance: high probability of delivery within 48 h

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Verlohren S et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2012;206(1):58.e1-8 (cited in PMC11012921) · Villalaín C et al. J Am Heart Assoc 2020;9:e015548 (ratio >655) · Sá CPN et al. Rev Bras Ginecol Obstet 2020;42(11).

  • Spanish cohort, J Am Heart Assoc 2020 (237 pregnancies with a ratio >655, 20-37 weeks): median time to delivery was 4 days with established PE and 7 days without PE at the time of testing; 60.5% were still pregnant at 48 h with PE (compared with 29.4% in the original series, in which clinicians were blinded to the result). High frequency of FGR (85-90% at delivery) and severe features.
  • Some authors propose >1000 as a better predictor of adverse perinatal outcome (Stolz et al.).
  • The ratio quantifies the biological severity of placental and systemic disease; it does not replace clinical assessment when deciding timing of delivery.

The Calculator replicates the logic of the CaVeSal prenatal calculator (≤38 / 85 or 110 depending on GA / >655). Sources: Verlohren S et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2012;206(1):58.e1-8 (cited in PMC11012921) · Villalaín C et al. J Am Heart Assoc 2020;9:e015548 (ratio >655) · Sá CPN et al. Rev Bras Ginecol Obstet 2020;42(11).

11Maternal ophthalmic artery (OA) Doppler

Key index: systolic peak ratio PSV2/PSV1 (peak ratio). In normal pregnancy it is usually <0.6; in PE, the second peak approaches or exceeds the first.

PSV2/PSV1 ratioInterpretation
>0,65Cutoff for predicting PE (Kalafat 2018 meta-analysis; AUC 0.67 for early-onset PE)
<0,70Normal (CaVeSal operational cutoff)
0,70-0,77Gray zone (CaVeSal operational cutoff)
≥0,78Severe vascular compromise (CaVeSal operational cutoff)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Kalafat E et al. UOG 2018;51(6):731-737 · Vaz de Melo PFM et al. BMC Pregnancy Childbirth 2023;23:343 · PMC12844109 review.

Vaz de Melo 2023 meta-analysis (8 studies, 1425 pregnant women): peak ratio and P2 have the best diagnostic performance (PR: sensitivity 84%, specificity 92%).

The 0.70 and 0.78 cutoffs come from the CaVeSal prenatal calculator and do not yet have a single verified primary reference; evidence for specifically predicting eclampsia is limited. Sources: Kalafat E et al. UOG 2018;51(6):731-737 · Vaz de Melo PFM et al. BMC Pregnancy Childbirth 2023;23:343 · PMC12844109 review.

12sFlt-1/PlGF vs ophthalmic artery Doppler in established severe preeclampsia

Complementary tools, not competitors
CharacteristicsFlt-1/PlGF ratioOphthalmic artery Doppler
NatureBiochemical marker of antiangiogenesis and placental dysfunctionFunctional hemodynamic measurement of the maternal orbital/cerebral vascular territory
StrengthQuantifies systemic/multiorgan damage and the severity of placental diseaseReflects in real time the loss of maternal cerebral vascular autoregulation
Use in established diseaseHelps estimate the urgency of delivery (values >655 associated with delivery within days)Warning sign in the presence of neurovisual symptoms; supports monitoring of neurological risk
LimitationCutoffs depend on the platform; availability and costOperator-dependent; no universal cutoffs; limited evidence for eclampsia

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG PB 222 (2020) · FIGO 2019 · ISSHP 2021 · Kalafat E et al. UOG 2018.

In summary: the ratio quantifies overall biological severity; ophthalmic artery Doppler measures the immediate hemodynamic impact on the maternal cerebral microvasculature. Neither replaces clinical criteria for severe features (BP, symptoms, laboratory findings).

13Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) — thresholds and variants

Formula: MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3.

Variant A — CaVeSal prenatal calculator logic (used by the Calculator)
ConditionLevelManagementSource cited
MAP ≥105 (any GA)High — warning signSuspected gestational hypertension/preeclampsia, especially >20 weeks. Assess proteinuria, sFlt-1/PlGF, liver and renal function. Close monitoring.WHO / NICE / ISUOG

MAP ≤90No alert——
Variant B — predictive performance (Cnossen et al., BMJ 2008; 34 studies, 60,599 women)
Population / measureCutoffSens.Spec.LR+LR−
Low risk — 2nd-trimester MAP (AUC 0.76)≥90 mmHg62%82%3,50,46
High risk — DBP at 13-20 weeks≥75 mmHg——2,80,39

MAP predicts PE better than SBP, DBP, or their increase, but alone has modest predictive value: it is used within combined models. In FMF first-trimester screening, MAP is included as MoM in the algorithm along with uterine artery PI and PlGF, not as an absolute cutoff. fichas.texto: Pregnancy >20 weeks + 2 BP readings 15 min apart if severe (≥160/110) or 4 h apart if mild (140-159/90-109) + evidence of end-organ damage (clinical: headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, pulmonary edema; laboratory: AST/ALT≥70, LDH≥600, platelets<100,000, bilirubin≥1.2) OR proteinuria (≥300 mg/24h, protein/creatinine ratio≥0.3, albumin/creatinine ratio≥0.8, dipstick≥2+) OR angiogenic tests sFlt1/PlGF>38. Proteinuria is NOT required for the diagnosis of severe preeclampsia. Prevention: calcium 1-2 g/day in all pregnant patients; aspirin 150 mg/day based on risk factors (1 high-risk factor or 2 moderate-risk factors).

Post-target monitoring: every 10 min for the 1st hour, every 15 min for the 2nd hour, every 30 min for the 3rd hour, every hour from the 4th hour for an additional 4 h. fichas.texto: SSSAO mnemonic: Support, Safety, magnesium sulfate (loading dose 4-6 g IV, maintenance 1-2 g/h until 24 h postpartum), Antihypertensives (reduce by 20-25% over 24-48 h, target 135/85 per NICE), Obstetric management (fetal maturation at 24-34 weeks, fetal well-being, delivery: non-severe PE at 37 weeks, severe PE at 34 weeks). Stepwise hypertensive emergency algorithm: IV labetalol 20→40 mg / oral nifedipine 10→20→20 mg / IV hydralazine 10 mg, reassessing every 10-20 min. Fluid management: no bolus, total 80 mL/h or 1 mL/kg/h, max 125 mL/h. Eclampsia: seizure control with a 4-6 g IV MgSO4 bolus (or 2 g IV if already receiving it), maintenance 2 g/h, second 2 g IV bolus if seizures recur. Intubate if: unconscious after seizure, status epilepticus, aspiration, hypoxia. Continue MgSO4 for at least 24 h postpartum or from the last seizure.

fichas.texto: Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia: new-onset proteinuria, or sudden loss of blood pressure control, or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks of gestation in a patient with hypertension predating pregnancy. Additional severity criterion — Progressive renal insufficiency: serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling of baseline creatinine (not previously included alongside LDH/bilirubin — added as an independent laboratory criterion). Urine output — alternative weight-based threshold: <0.5 mL/kg/h, as an alternative to the absolute threshold of <30 mL/h already used for MgSO4 toxicity monitoring.

fichas.texto: Nifedipine in hypertensive crisis: swallow with water; DO NOT administer sublingually. MgSO4 antidote: Calcium gluconate 10% 1g (10mL) slow IV. Two administration-rate options: 3-5 min (MSPBS/CaVeSal regimen) or 10 min (ACOG/WHO). Monitoring for MgSO4 toxicity: discontinue if RR <12 breaths/min; some guidelines use <12-16 breaths/min (CaVeSal regimen) and others <12-14 breaths/min (ACOG). Patellar reflex present and urine output ≥30 mL/h in all regimens.

fichas.texto: The Calculator uses the Pritchard/MSPBS regimen by default. The Zuspan IV regimen is the intravenous alternative and is preferred for neuroprotection; the University of Antioquia uses a larger dilution volume with the same total dose. Regimen Loading dose Maintenance Pritchard / MSPBS 14 g total: 10 g IM (5 g = 10 cc in each buttock) + 4 g IV (8 cc + 12 cc of NS in a 20 cc syringe, over 20 min) IV 1-2 g/h in a 100 cc Volutrol, or IM 5 g every 4 h, for 24 h Zuspan (IV) 4 g IV over 20-30 min 1-2 g/h IV for 24 h (preeclampsia); for neuroprotection, until delivery or for 12 h University of Antioquia Same total dose with a larger dilution volume (see source protocol) IM maintenance — how to administer (clarification to prevent underdosing): each dose is 5 g PER SCHEDULED DOSE (10 cc total). Option 1 (official text): 10 cc in one buttock, alternating buttocks at each scheduled dose. Option 2 (administration variant proposed by CaVeSal®): 5 cc (2.5 g) in each buttock at the same scheduled dose, repeated at the next scheduled dose (every 4 h). The frequent error is to administer a TOTAL of 5 cc per scheduled dose (2.5 g): the full dose is 10 cc (5 g). Typical sequence of toxicity: 1st, decreased urine output (<30 mL/h, risk of accumulation); 2nd, loss of the patellar reflex; 3rd, respiratory depression (RR <12-16 breaths/min). Rescue: calcium gluconate 10%, 1 g (10 cc) slow IV over 3-5 min, in the event of respiratory depression or instability (this is not gram-for-gram neutralization). The regimen may be repeated (repeat regimen) according to clinical course. fichas.titulo: HELLP syndrome: ACOG, Tennessee, and Mississippi criteria
fichas.texto: Comparison of the 3 diagnostic systems System Platelets Transaminases Hemolysis / LDH Use ACOG PB 222 (2020) <100.000/µL AST and ALT >2 times the upper limit of normal LDH ≥600 U/L Clinical diagnosis; no subdivision by class Tennessee (Sibai) <100.000/µL AST ≥70 U/L LDH ≥600 U/L (or bilirubin >1.2 mg/dL with abnormal smear: schistocytes) Complete HELLP = 3 criteria; partial = 1-2 criteria Mississippi — Class 1 (severe) ≤50.000/µL AST or ALT ≥70 U/L LDH ≥600 U/L Higher risk of DIC and hemorrhage Mississippi — Class 2 (moderate) >50.000 a ≤100.000/µL AST or ALT ≥70 U/L LDH ≥600 U/L Intermediate risk Mississippi — Class 3 (mild) >100.000 a ≤150.000/µL AST or ALT ≥40 U/L LDH ≥600 U/L Detects early forms not included in ACOG/Tennessee CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (2020) · tabla Tennessee vs Mississippi (PMC2654858) · Clin Liver Dis 2019 (PMC6448736) · StatPearls, HELLP Syndrome. ACOG management: because of its morbidity and mortality, many authors recommend delivery in HELLP syndrome regardless of gestational age, after maternal stabilization. ACOG considers the evidence insufficient to use corticosteroids to attenuate the disease (they are used for fetal lung maturation according to gestational age). Neuraxial anesthesia (ACOG): acceptable with platelets ≥70,000/µL if the count is stable, there is no other coagulopathy, platelet function is normal, and the patient is not taking antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents (risk of epidural hematoma <0.2%). Practical difference: ACOG sets the <100,000/µL cutoff for diagnosis; Mississippi subdivides by platelet nadir to grade bleeding risk and guide transfusion planning. Correction of attribution: bilirubin >1.2 mg/dL and schistocytes belong to the Tennessee criteria (Sibai), not the diagnostic text of ACOG PB 222. In the Calculator the default criterion is Mississippi, with a selector for ACOG and Tennessee. fichas.titulo: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) — Swansea criteria
fichas.texto: Diagnosis: ≥6 of the 14 criteria in the absence of another cause to explain them. Swansea criteria (Ch'ng et al. 2002) # Criterion Cutoff 1 Vomiting — 2 Abdominal pain — 3 Polydipsia / polyuria — 4 Encephalopathy — 5 Elevated bilirubin >0.8 mg/dL (>14 µmol/L) 6 Hypoglycemia <72 mg/dL (<4 mmol/L) 7 Elevated uric acid >5.7 mg/dL (>340 µmol/L) 8 Leukocytosis >11.000/µL 9 Ascites or bright liver on ultrasound — 10 Elevated transaminases (AST/ALT) >42 IU/L 11 Elevated ammonia >47 µmol/L 12 Renal failure Creatinine >1.7 mg/dL (>150 µmol/L) 13 Coagulopathy PT >14 s or aPTT >34 s 14 Microvesicular steatosis on liver biopsy — CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Ch'ng CL et al. Gut 2002;51:876-80 · Knight M et al. Gut 2008;57:951-6 · StatPearls — Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy · PMC3503387. Validation (Knight 2008, UKOSS): PPV 85%, NPV 100%, sensitivity ≈100%, specificity 57% versus biopsy. Antithrombin III <65%: suggestive finding, not part of the 14 criteria. Management: maternal stabilization and immediate delivery, regardless of gestational age; ICU care (monitoring of glucose, coagulopathy, renal and liver function). Wording variant: some lists (Radiopaedia, NGO) write “urea >340 µmol/L” in criterion 7; the original article refers to urate (uric acid). Sources: Ch'ng CL et al. Gut 2002;51:876-80 · Knight M et al. Gut 2008;57:951-6 · StatPearls — Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy · PMC3503387.

fichas.titulo: Differential diagnosis: HELLP vs AFLP vs ICP
fichas.texto: Characteristic HELLP Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) Cholestasis (ICP) Timing >20 weeks / postpartum 3rd trimester (typically 30-38 weeks) 2nd-3rd trimester Key symptom Epigastric/RUQ pain, hypertension Nausea, vomiting, malaise, polydipsia Nocturnal palmoplantar pruritus Hypertension / proteinuria Usual Up to 50% No Platelets <100.000 (↓↓) Normal or ↓ (due to DIC) Normal Hemolysis / LDH LDH ≥600, schistocytes Mild or absent No Glucose Normal Hypoglycemia Normal Coagulation Normal except with DIC Prolonged PT/aPTT, fibrinogen ↓ Normal (PT ↑ only with vitamin K deficiency) Bilirubin Moderately ↑ ↑↑ Normal or mildly ↑ Ammonia / creatinine Creatinine may ↑ Ammonia and creatinine ↑ Normal Bile acids Normal May ↑ ↑ (specific marker) Management Delivery based on gestational age/severity Immediate delivery + ICU UDCA + delivery at 34-40 weeks based on TBA levels HELLP syndrome and AFLP overlap in up to 20-40% of cases (both may present with hypertension, thrombocytopenia, and elevated enzymes). Hypoglycemia, early coagulopathy, and elevated ammonia suggest AFLP. Sources: ACOG PB 222 · Knight 2008 · StatPearls · RCOG GTG 43.

fichas.titulo: MAP/HR index: hemodynamic phenotype in hypertension
fichas.texto: MAP ÷ HR approximates peripheral vascular resistance at the bedside, without echocardiography or noninvasive monitoring. MAP/HR Phenotype Suggested first-line approach >1,4 Hypodynamic: high resistance, normal or low cardiac output; more associated with FGR Calcium channel blocker (nifedipine) 1,1–1,4 Normodynamic Methyldopa <1,1 Hyperdynamic: high output, low resistance Labetalol or methyldopa Guides drug selection only for non-severe hypertension or maintenance therapy. Severe hypertension is treated immediately with the available drug. Some checklists use a single cutoff of 1.4 (≥1.4 hypodynamic). The calculator uses the three ranges from the systematic review. grupos.bajada: Early identification (OTAS), California criteria, and 1-hour bundle.
grupos.html:
1Definition and criteria

Definition (WHO 2017): "maternal sepsis is a life-threatening condition defined as organ dysfunction resulting from infection during pregnancy, childbirth, postabortion, or the postpartum period."

Suspected or confirmed infection + organ dysfunction = maternal sepsis. Sepsis-3 framework adapted to obstetrics: the focus shifts from the inflammatory response (SIRS) to organ dysfunction. WHO calls for two sets of criteria: early identification ("presumed maternal sepsis") to enable immediate action, and diagnostic confirmation for epidemiological purposes.

Prevention: handwashing, universal urine culture, clean birthing areas, sterile instruments, vector protection, disposal of contaminated materials, vaccination, education, STI screening/treatment.

Criteria for suspected sepsis (WHO GLOSS 2020; labeled "OTAS" in the reference handout, but not the OTAS triage scale): temperature>38°C or <35°C, SpO2<95%, SBP<90, HR>100, RR>25, altered mental status, uterine tenderness with suspected source.

2Classification — California Criteria

Suspected infection + 2 of 4: temp<36 or >38°C, HR>110, RR>24, WBC>15,000 or <4,000 or 10% bands = SEPSIS → start 1-2 L crystalloids + antibiotics + monitoring.

If MAP remains <65 after a 30 mL/kg bolus = SEPTIC SHOCK.

MSPBS, Code Red Guide, 2nd ed. 2022 (p. 76): septic shock = need for vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg with lactate ≥2 mmol/L (18 mg/dL) despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

This set (T, HR>110, RR>24, WBC with >10% bands) is the one used in the UdeA/UNFPA workshop, adapted from the CMQCC Toolkit. It is stricter than classic SIRS (HR>90, RR>20, WBC >12,000; see subcard 10). A slide from the same workshop states "MAP <60"; this is excluded because it lacks its own citation: the current cutoff is 65 (MSPBS + CMQCC + SOMANZ).

Adapted EAPO (MEOWS, reference from the handout): 7 parameters (temp, SBP, DBP, pulse, RR, SpO2, mental status, urine output). Score: 0=routine; 1-3=observation every 4h + notify charge nurse; ≥4 with a single "red 3" or total≥4="THINK SEPSIS" (observation every 4h + urgent notification); ≥6="THINK SEPSIS" (continuous monitoring + emergency notification).

Note: this reference EAPO-MEOWS differs from the official MSPBS EAPO used in the Full module — shown here only as an additional reference; do not confuse them.

3Flowchart — "Sepsis 4-5-3" Bundle (1st hour)

Take 4: cultures, laboratory tests for organ dysfunction + lactate, vital signs, imaging.

Give 5: O2 FiO2≥50%, crystalloids 20-30 mL/kg bolus + maintenance 1-2 mL/kg/h, broad-spectrum antibiotics, treatment of hyper/hypothermia, vasopressors if MAP<65 after bolus.

Consider 3: fetal well-being if >26 weeks, infection source control, thromboprophylaxis.

Targets: urine output>0.5 mL/kg/h or >30 mL/h, MAP ≥65 (MSPBS 2022; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021), PaO2>60 or SpO2>95%, Glasgow Coma Scale 15.

UdeA/UNFPA variant (slide "Therapeutic targets"): MAP >60 or SBP >85 mmHg, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h or >30 mL/h, SpO2 >95%, normal mental status.

Stabilize and refer: review at 3 h (diagnosis/treatment/labs, repeat lactate, reassess source) and at 6 h (review diagnosis/treatment, close monitoring; ideally transfer to a tertiary care center by 6 h).

4Medications — regimens by source

Urinary: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g q8h or gentamicin 3-5 mg/kg q24h.

Respiratory: ampicillin-sulbactam 3g q6h + clarithromycin 500mg q12h (+ oseltamivir if at risk for influenza).

Puerperal infection: clindamycin 900mg q8h + gentamicin 240mg q24h or amikacin 1g q24h; or ampicillin-sulbactam 3g q6h; or crystalline penicillin + metronidazole + gentamicin regimen.

Vasopressor: norepinephrine 0.05 µg/kg/min until MAP ≥65, via central line or 14-16G access. UdeA: dopamine 5 µg/kg/min via peripheral line as an alternative, only after volume repletion.

Sources: WHO GLOSS 2020; CMQCC Quality Improvement Toolkit 2022; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; WHO 2017 (WHO/RHR/17.02); MSPBS Paraguay, Code Red 2nd ed. 2021 (p. 76); University of Antioquia/UNFPA, Obstetric Emergencies Workshop — Maternal Sepsis.

DSI: general sepsis literature more commonly cites the rounded cutoff ≥2.0; 2.2 is used as the primary cutoff (Heras source), with this note on the variant most cited in the non-obstetric literature. VDI: the classic intensive care formula uses MAP in the denominator (VIS/MAP); the variant recorded here (DBP ÷ dose × HR) is specific to the Heras source.

Most useful individual criteria: HR >90 is almost always present (sensitivity 96 %) but has low specificity (45 %); by contrast, RR >30 and altered mental status are virtually absent in controls (specificity close to 100 %), although they are absent in more than half of sepsis cases.

Clinical interpretation: Use SIRS or maternal early warning criteria for screening; qSOFA to stratify severity; SOFA and lactate to confirm. The operational scores remain those in subcards 5-9.

Rounded values; confidence intervals and details by criterion are in the original article. Original definitions: Bone RC et al. Chest 1992;101:1644-55 · Singer M et al. JAMA 2016;315:801-10 · Mhyre JM et al. Obstet Gynecol 2014;124:782-6. The UdeA/UNFPA workshop cites this study for obstetric qSOFA (sensitivity 36-50 %, specificity 70-95 %).

11Causes, pathogens, mortality, and risk factors with ORs

  • Most common causes: chorioamnionitis 24.4%; endometritis 23.2%; pneumonia 11.0%.
  • Most common pathogens: E. coli 14.6%; other gram-negative bacilli 9.8%; group A Streptococcus 7.3%.
  • Mortality: 12.2% overall; 8.3% if antibiotics are started in <1 h versus 20% if >1 h.

Vasopressor: norepinephrine 0.05 µg/kg/min until MAP ≥65, via central line or 14-16G access. UdeA: dopamine 5 µg/kg/min via peripheral line as an alternative, only after volume repletion.

fichas.texto: Level Tool What it detects Rapid screening Shock Index (SI) = HR/SBP, cutoff ≥ 0.9 Initial alert for hemodynamic compromise Severity reinforcement Diastolic Shock Index (DSI) = HR/DBP, cutoff ≥ 2.2 Vasoplegia / poor prognosis — more sensitive than SI alone in septic shock Reinforcement, only if already receiving a vasopressor Vasoactive-Diastolic Index (VDI) = DBP ÷ (vasopressor dose × HR), risk if ≤ 6.7 Degree of vasopressor dependence — refractory shock CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MD Antonio Heras G. — Obstetric Coagulopathy and Sepsis Calculator · SOMANZ Sepsis Guidelines 2017 · MDCalc — Diastolic Shock Index. DSI: general sepsis literature more commonly cites the rounded cutoff ≥2.0; 2.2 is used as the primary cutoff (Heras source), with this note on the variant most cited in the non-obstetric literature. VDI: the classic intensive care formula uses MAP in the denominator (VIS/MAP); the variant recorded here (DBP ÷ dose × HR) is specific to the Heras source.

fichas.titulo: SIRS, qSOFA, and maternal early warning in pregnant women — diagnostic performance
fichas.texto: When is each tool activated? Tool Activated by Parameters SIRS (Bone 1992) ≥2 criteria T >38 or <36 °C · HR >90 · RR >20 or PaCO₂ <32 · leukocytes >12,000 or <4,000 qSOFA (Sepsis-3, Singer 2016) ≥2 criteria RR ≥22 · SBP ≤100 · altered mental status Maternal early warning criteria (Mhyre 2014) 1 criterion is sufficient SBP <90 or >160 · DBP >100 · HR <50 or >120 · RR <10 or >30 · SpO₂ <95 % on room air · urine output <35 mL/h for ≥2 h · agitation, confusion, or unresponsiveness · preeclampsia with persistent headache or dyspnea How well do they detect maternal sepsis? Tool Sens. Spec. Use SIRS ≥2 93 % 63 % Screen (many false alarms) Maternal early warning criteria (≥1) 82 % 87 % Intermediate qSOFA ≥2 50 % 95 % Severity (a negative result does not rule it out) CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Bauer ME et al. Risk Factors, Etiologies, and Screening Tools for Sepsis in Pregnant Women: A Multicenter Case-Control Study. Anesth Analg 2019;129(6):1613-1620 Most useful individual criteria: HR >90 is almost always present (sensitivity 96 %) but has low specificity (45 %); by contrast, RR >30 and altered mental status are virtually absent in controls (specificity close to 100 %), although they are absent in more than half of sepsis cases. Clinical interpretation: Use SIRS or maternal early warning criteria for screening; qSOFA to stratify severity; SOFA and lactate to confirm. The operational scores remain those in subcards 5-9. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Analysis based on Bauer ME et al. Anesth Analg 2019;129(6):1613-1620 (multicenter case-control study: 82 cases, 328 controls). Rounded values; confidence intervals and details by criterion are in the original article. Original definitions: Bone RC et al. Chest 1992;101:1644-55 · Singer M et al. JAMA 2016;315:801-10 · Mhyre JM et al. Obstet Gynecol 2014;124:782-6. The UdeA/UNFPA workshop cites this study for obstetric qSOFA (sensitivity 36-50 %, specificity 70-95 %).

fichas.titulo: Causes, pathogens, mortality, and risk factors with ORs
fichas.texto: Most common causes: chorioamnionitis 24.4%; endometritis 23.2%; pneumonia 11.0%. Most common pathogens: E. coli 14.6%; other gram-negative bacilli 9.8%; group A Streptococcus 7.3%. Mortality: 12.2% overall; 8.3% if antibiotics are started in <1 h versus 20% if >1 h. Factors associated with maternal sepsis (approximate crude OR) Group Factor and magnitude of association Childbirth and puerperium Cesarean delivery during labor ~21 · cesarean delivery before labor ~16 · fetal demise ~15 · retained products of conception ~13 · PROM >24 h ~9 · preterm delivery ~6 · multiple pregnancy ~6 · antenatal corticosteroids ~5 · GBS positive ~2 · nulliparity ~2 Chronic disease Liver disease ~15 · heart failure ~10 · chronic kidney disease ~10 Other BMI ≥40 ~4 · smoking ~3 · African American or Asian ethnicity ~4 (US population) CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Bauer ME et al., Anesth Analg 2019;129(6):1613-1620 · WHO Statement on Maternal Sepsis (WHO/RHR/17.02)Delivery variables exclude cases of sepsis prior to delivery (reverse causality). fichas.texto: Gibbs criteria: fever + ≥2 of the following Criterion Cutoff Maternal fever (mandatory) ≥37.8 °C (Gibbs 1982); many guidelines use ≥38.0 °C Maternal tachycardia >100 bpm Fetal tachycardia >160 bpm Uterine pain / tenderness — Foul-smelling / purulent amniotic fluid or discharge — Maternal leukocytosis >15,000/mm³ (without recent corticosteroids) The current designation «Triple I» (NICHD 2015, ACOG CO 712) is detailed in the PROM tab, subcard 8. grupos.titulo: Obstetric Code Blue — CPR / Maternal Cardiac Arrest
grupos.bajada: Causes of maternal collapse, CABD sequence and perimortem cesarean delivery. Different icon from HDP to avoid confusion.
grupos.html:
1Causes of maternal collapse

Mnemonic (Knapp C & Bhatia K, Br J Hosp Med 2022): Accidents/anesthetic complications/asthma; Bleeding (hemorrhages); Cardiovascular; Drugs/medications (magnesium sulfate); Embolic (amniotic fluid, pulmonary); Fever (sepsis, septic shock); General (6Ts and 6Hs); Hypertension (HDP, HELLP).

“Perpetuates cardiac arrest” — 6Hs: Hypoxia, hypo-/hyperkalemia, H+ acidosis, hypothermia, hypovolemia, hypoglycemia.

6Ts: Cardiac tamponade, pulmonary thrombosis, coronary thrombosis, tablets/toxins, pneumothorax, trauma.

2CABD sequence and airway

Unresponsive/unconscious patient → activate Obstetric Code Blue → check pulse for 10 seconds → if no pulse, initiate CABD (Circulation: compressions; Airway: open; Breathing: positive-pressure ventilation; Defibrillate if shockable rhythm).

Chest compressions 30:2, ventilations every 2 min or 5 cycles → aortocaval decompression (left uterine displacement) → open the airway → epinephrine 1mg IV every 3-5 min.

Modifications in pregnancy: deeper chest compressions, left uterine displacement, early endotracheal intubation + cricoid pressure.

Airway: O2 100% at 15L/min → intubation attempt 1 and 2 → if unsuccessful, supraglottic airway device attempt 1 and 2 → if unsuccessful, bag-mask ventilation → if ineffective, cricothyrotomy. 8-10 ventilations/min, monitor CO2, minimize time without compressions, 6.0-7.0mm tube.

3Rhythm and flowchart

VF/pulseless VT: initial shock 150J biphasic or 360J monophasic + 2 min CPR (30:2); if there is no response, another shock + amiodarone 300mg IV (150mg additional if VT persists).

Asystole/PEA: continue compressions and ventilation, verification protocol.

Epinephrine 1mg IV every 3-5 min: for a nonshockable rhythm, administer immediately once IV access is obtained; for a shockable rhythm, after the 2nd shock.

4-minute rule: preparation for hysterotomy begins when cardiac arrest is recognized. If there is no return of spontaneous circulation by minute 4, initiate resuscitative hysterotomy (perimortem cesarean delivery) on site, without transferring the patient or stopping CPR, to achieve delivery by minute 5 → alert the neonatal team if GA>24 weeks. Timer on the calculator, Obstetric Code Blue.

Minute 0Unresponsive → activate code
Minutes 0-4CABD + aortocaval decompression + prepare for hysterotomy
Minute 4Initiate hysterotomy
Minute 5Birth

4Perimortem cesarean delivery and MgSO4 toxicity

Perimortem cesarean delivery: <20 weeks NO; 20-24 weeks depending on suspected aortocaval compression; >24 weeks ALWAYS.

Magnesium sulfate toxicity: calcium gluconate 10% 30mL, or calcium chloride 10% 10mL (1g).

5Maternal collapse: sepsis vs PE vs amniotic fluid embolism (POCUS + ROTEM)

Septic shockMassive PEAmniotic fluid embolism
ContextProgressive onset; fever or source; sudden collapse is rareSudden dyspnea, chest pain; VTE risk factorsLabor, cesarean delivery or first 30 min postpartum
POCUS: heartHyperdynamic LV (or late septic cardiomyopathy)Dilated RV (RV/LV >1), “D-shaped” septum, McConnell sign; sometimes intracardiac thrombusDilated and hypokinetic RV, “D-shaped” septum, small LV; then biventricular failure
POCUS: IVC / veins / lungSmall, collapsible IVC; look for a source (consolidation, collections)Dilated IVC; deep vein thrombosis on lower-extremity compression ultrasoundDilated IVC; pulmonary edema possible
Coagulation / ROTEMLate coagulopathy; SIC score ≥4 (ISTH 2025)No inherent consumptive coagulopathyEarly and disproportionate coagulopathy: very low FIBTEM, possible hyperfibrinolysis (high EXTEM ML)
Key actionAntibiotics within the first hour, guided crystalloid fluids, norepinephrineAnticoagulation; thrombolysis if cardiac arrest or shockHigh-quality CPR, avoid fluid overload, RV support, early massive transfusion, tranexamic acid
  • A dilated RV does not distinguish PE from AFE. Severe early coagulopathy points to AFE; its absence points to PE.
  • No laboratory test confirms AFE: it is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.

Practice the three cases in the simulator: Septic shock · Massive PE · Amniotic fluid embolism.

grupos.html:
1General measures and mandatory anticoagulation

For all patients (pregnancy, labor or postpartum): adequate hydration and early ambulation.

Mandatory anticoagulation (regardless of the risk scale) if there is: active venous thromboembolic disease (DVT, PE, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis), high-risk cardiac conditions (arrhythmias, prosthetic valves, cardiomyopathy with reduced LVEF, intracardiac thrombi, pulmonary hypertension), or known thrombophilia.

24-level scale (traffic light)

Risk level, activation threshold and color
LevelActivated byExamples of factors
Very high1 factorVery high-risk inherited thrombophilia, recurrent VTE
High1 factorMorbid obesity (BMI>40), APS, single prior VTE
Moderate2 or more factorsObesity (BMI 30-39), preeclampsia, cesarean delivery, multiple pregnancy
Low3-5 factors (non-pharmacological) / 6+ (+pharmacological from week 28)Age>35, overweight, smoking, chronic hypertension

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Grillo-Ardila CF et al. Rev Colomb Obstet Ginecol 2017;68(4):285-304 (rounded values; confidence intervals in the original).

Rule: the most severe level applies when at least one factor is present (factors are not added across levels).

3Weight-based LMWH doses (prophylactic)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Grillo-Ardila CF et al. Rev Colomb Obstet Ginecol 2017 · MSPBS.

Weight >170 kg — two alternatives: not included in the Colombian CPG table (specialist assessment) · enoxaparin 0.6 mg/kg/day according to the MSPBS Thromboprophylaxis draft (corrected, unpublished version). In the absence of LMWH: unfractionated heparin.

4Contraindications to LMWH

Known bleeding disorder (hemophilia, von Willebrand disease, acquired coagulopathies), active antepartum or postpartum bleeding, risk factors for major obstetric hemorrhage (e.g., placenta previa), thrombocytopenia (<75,000/µL), recent cerebrovascular event (within the last 4 weeks), severe renal disease (GFR<30 mL/min/1.73m²).

Fondaparinux, dabigatran and rivaroxaban are not approved for use during pregnancy. Warfarin and heparins are safe during breastfeeding.

5Epidemiology and relative risk by period (RDI)

Incidence of VTE during pregnancy/postpartum: 0.76-1.72 per 1000 (4× the risk in the general population). Accounts for 14.9% of global maternal mortality.
