9GRADE recommendations — non-pharmacological measures

  • LMWH: strong recommendation in favor, low-quality evidence — no preference for a specific type.
  • Unfractionated heparin: alternative when LMWH is not feasible (strong recommendation in favor).
  • Fondaparinux: consider only if heparins are contraindicated (good practice point).
  • Antiplatelet agents: weak recommendation against use for VTE prevention (very low-quality evidence).
  • Intermittent pneumatic compression + pharmacological prophylaxis: weak recommendation against — no clear additional benefit and more bleeding.
  • Regional anesthesia preferred over general anesthesia: weak recommendation in favor, associated with lower VTE risk (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.55-0.79 for DVT).
  • Graduated compression stockings: reduce DVT OR 0.33 (0.26-0.41), proximal DVT OR 0.26, PE OR 0.38 — strong recommendation in favor, very low-quality evidence.
  • Hydration: “avoid dehydration” is a weak recommendation in favor, with very low-quality evidence. Vigorous hydration/hemodilution increased the risk of postoperative DVT in a controlled trial (RR 4.50, 95% CI 1.06-19.11) — never recommend “aggressive hydration” as a thromboprophylaxis measure.

10Perianesthetic timing and postpartum restart

Last dose before the procedure: 12h before induction/cesarean (prophylactic dose); 24h before if very high risk and receiving anticoagulation doses (therapeutic).

Postpartum restart: 12h after delivery/cesarean if not contraindicated (non-pharmacological measures in the meantime). In patients at high risk of postpartum hemorrhage: non-pharmacological measures only until the bleeding risk is minimal.

Source (traffic-light system, subcards 1-10): Grillo-Ardila CF, Mogollón-Mariño AC, Amaya-Guío J, Molano-Franco D, Correa LP. Guía de práctica clínica para la prevención de eventos tromboembólicos venosos durante la gestación, el parto o el puerperio. Rev Colomb Obstet Ginecol. 2017;68(4):285-304. DOI: 10.18597/rcog.3084.

Diagnosis of VTE, APS, and care protocol

Physiology, DVT, PE (adapted YEARS algorithm), APS, MSPBS screening, and 15-step protocol.

1Physiology of coagulation in pregnancy

VTE risk: pregnancy ×10 vs nonpregnant individuals; postpartum period (6 weeks) ×5, peak in the first week; cesarean delivery ×4 vs vaginal delivery.

ChangeFactors
↑ ProcoagulantsFibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, X, von Willebrand factor, PAI-1, and PAI-2
↓ AnticoagulantsProtein S
No significant changesFactors II, V, IX, protein C, antithrombin III

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Grillo-Ardila CF et al. Rev Colomb Obstet Ginecol 2017;68(4):285-304 (rounded values; confidence intervals in the original).

Anatomic predilection: left lower extremity and proximal iliofemoral veins (May-Thurner phenomenon: compression of the left iliac vein by the right iliac artery, combined with compression of the inferior vena cava by the gravid uterus).

2Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)

Clinical presentation: pain along the course of the vein, unilateral edema, increased local temperature, difference in limb circumference, superficial collateral circulation.

Test of choice: venous Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities (loss of compressibility or absence of flow). If negative and suspicion persists (especially for iliac vein thrombosis): repeat at 3 and 7 days or consider MRI.

Management: confirmed DVT → therapeutic-dose LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 h).

3Pulmonary embolism (PE) — YEARS algorithm adapted for pregnancy

Clinical presentation: sudden or progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis, tachypnea, tachycardia, cyanosis, syncope.

If leg symptoms are present: Doppler ultrasound first; if DVT is confirmed → anticoagulate without further testing.

YEARS criteria: signs of DVT · hemoptysis · PE as the most likely diagnosis
YEARS criteriaD-dimerManagement
0<1000 ng/mL (1.0 µg/mL)PE ruled out; do not anticoagulate
0≥1000 ng/mLCT pulmonary angiography
≥1<500 ng/mL (0.5 µg/mL)PE ruled out
≥1≥500 ng/mLPulmonary CT angiography (or V/Q scan)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: van der Pol LM et al. NEJM 2019;380:1139-49 (Artemis) · Medicina Fetal Barcelona (2021).

The D-dimer cutoff differs by branch (1000 vs 500 ng/mL); it is not simplified to a single value. This algorithm avoided CT pulmonary angiography in 32-65% of pregnant patients, depending on trimester. Source: van der Pol LM et al. NEJM 2019;380:1139-49 (Artemis) · Medicina Fetal Barcelona (2021).

4Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) and thrombophilias

Indication for testing: Personal history of VTE or adverse obstetric history (≥3 miscarriages <10 weeks, fetal death ≥10 weeks with a morphologically normal fetus, severe FGR <34 weeks, severe preeclampsia <34 weeks).

Hereditary: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C, protein S, or antithrombin III deficiency, factor XII mutation. Acquired/mixed: hyperhomocysteinemia, APS.

APS criteria
TypeCriterion
Clinical (≥1)≥1 documented vascular thrombosis or ≥1 criterion for obstetric morbidity
Laboratory (2 tests 12 weeks apart)Lupus anticoagulant · anticardiolipin IgG/IgM >40 GPL/MPL · anti-β2-glycoprotein I IgG/IgM

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Medicina Fetal Barcelona 2021 · ACOG PB 196 and 197 (2018) · RCOG GTG 37a.

Treatment during pregnancy: Aspirin 100 mg/night from preconception or diagnosis until week 36 + prophylactic LMWH from ultrasound confirmation of fetal heartbeat until delivery. Postpartum: aspirin + prophylactic LMWH for 42 days.

Do not confuse with aspirin 150 mg/night for preeclampsia prevention (HDP tab): these are different indications and doses. Sources: Medicina Fetal Barcelona 2021 · ACOG PB 196 and 197 (2018) · RCOG GTG 37a.

5Risk screening — MSPBS draft

  • Normal risk (1/6000): no antepartum thromboprophylaxis, except if hospitalized with ≥4 of: BMI >30 kg/m², age ≥35 years, smoking, preeclampsia, multiple pregnancy, significant varicose veins.
  • High risk (>3/1000): rule out APS and thrombophilias; multidisciplinary management.
  • COVID-19: thromboprophylaxis if hospitalized for moderate, severe, or critical illness; continue for 14 days after discharge (moderate) or 1 month (severe/critical).
  • Postpartum: according to the postpartum score (previous section); continue during hospitalization and decide with hematology whether to continue.

Source: MSPBS draft «Thromboembolism and pregnancy. Thromboprophylaxis» (corrected, unpublished version).

6Protocol for suspected VTE — 15 steps (MSPBS draft)

  1. Triage: identity, gestational age/postpartum status, reason for presentation, and warning signs (sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tachypnea, cyanosis, syncope, tachycardia, painful and swollen lower limb).
  2. Assess hemodynamic stability; if there is severe compromise or suspected PE: oxygen, monitoring, and transfer to a higher level of care with referral form and perinatal record.
  3. Complete the perinatal medical history, with emphasis on thromboembolic risk factors.
  4. Clear information and emotional support throughout the process.
  5. Vital signs: BP, HR, RR, temperature, SpO₂.
  6. Determine gestational age or postpartum day (LMP, delivery date, perinatal record).
  7. Obstetric assessment: fundal height, FHR, uterine activity, fetal movements.
  8. Focused history: symptoms, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, cough/hemoptysis, leg pain/swelling, personal or family history of VTE/thrombophilia, immobilization, surgery, cesarean delivery, trauma, obesity.
  9. Focused physical examination: respiratory and cardiovascular systems, and lower extremities (unilateral edema, pain, warmth, difference in circumference, collateral veins).
  10. Studies as available: venous duplex ultrasound, ECG, blood gas analysis, chest radiograph with abdominal shielding, CT pulmonary angiography or V/Q scan.
  11. Presumptive or confirmed diagnosis of DVT/PE.
  12. Weight-adjusted LMWH (subcard 3 of block 1), unless contraindicated.
  13. Additional measures: early mobilization, compression stockings >20 mmHg, intermittent pneumatic compression (if LMWH is contraindicated, cesarean delivery/high risk, prior VTE, travel >4 h).
  14. Education for the patient and family: adherence, warning signs, seek immediate care if symptoms worsen.
  15. Detailed documentation in the medical record and follow-up scheduling.

Sources: Medicina Fetal Barcelona — Tromboembolismo venoso (2021) · RCOG Green-top 37a (2015) · ACOG Practice Bulletins 196 and 197 (2018) · ASH 2018 · van der Pol LM et al. NEJM 2019 · MSPBS Paraguay draft “Tromboembolismo y embarazo. Tromboprofilaxis” (corrected version).

fichas.texto: Clinical presentation: pain along the course of the vein, unilateral edema, increased local temperature, difference in limb circumference, superficial collateral circulation. Test of choice: venous Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities (loss of compressibility or absence of flow). If negative and suspicion persists (especially for iliac vein thrombosis): repeat at 3 and 7 days or consider MRI. Management: confirmed DVT → therapeutic-dose LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 h).

fichas.titulo: Pulmonary embolism (PE) — YEARS algorithm adapted for pregnancy
fichas.texto: Clinical presentation: sudden or progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis, tachypnea, tachycardia, cyanosis, syncope. If leg symptoms are present: Doppler ultrasound first; if DVT is confirmed → anticoagulate without further testing. YEARS criteria: signs of DVT · hemoptysis · PE as the most likely diagnosis YEARS criteria D-dimer Management 0 <1000 ng/mL (1.0 µg/mL) PE ruled out; do not anticoagulate 0 ≥1000 ng/mL CT pulmonary angiography ≥1 <500 ng/mL (0.5 µg/mL) PE ruled out ≥1 ≥500 ng/mL Pulmonary CT angiography (or V/Q scan) CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: van der Pol LM et al. NEJM 2019;380:1139-49 (Artemis) · Medicina Fetal Barcelona (2021). The D-dimer cutoff differs by branch (1000 vs 500 ng/mL); it is not simplified to a single value. This algorithm avoided CT pulmonary angiography in 32-65% of pregnant patients, depending on trimester. Source: van der Pol LM et al. NEJM 2019;380:1139-49 (Artemis) · Medicina Fetal Barcelona (2021).

fichas.texto: Indication for testing: Personal history of VTE or adverse obstetric history (≥3 miscarriages <10 weeks, fetal death ≥10 weeks with a morphologically normal fetus, severe FGR <34 weeks, severe preeclampsia <34 weeks). Hereditary: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C, protein S, or antithrombin III deficiency, factor XII mutation. Acquired/mixed: hyperhomocysteinemia, APS. APS criteria Type Criterion Clinical (≥1) ≥1 documented vascular thrombosis or ≥1 criterion for obstetric morbidity Laboratory (2 tests 12 weeks apart) Lupus anticoagulant · anticardiolipin IgG/IgM >40 GPL/MPL · anti-β2-glycoprotein I IgG/IgM CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Medicina Fetal Barcelona 2021 · ACOG PB 196 and 197 (2018) · RCOG GTG 37a. Treatment during pregnancy: Aspirin 100 mg/night from preconception or diagnosis until week 36 + prophylactic LMWH from ultrasound confirmation of fetal heartbeat until delivery. Postpartum: aspirin + prophylactic LMWH for 42 days. Do not confuse with aspirin 150 mg/night for preeclampsia prevention (HDP tab): these are different indications and doses. Sources: Medicina Fetal Barcelona 2021 · ACOG PB 196 and 197 (2018) · RCOG GTG 37a.

fichas.texto: Normal risk (1/6000): no antepartum thromboprophylaxis, except if hospitalized with ≥4 of: BMI >30 kg/m², age ≥35 years, smoking, preeclampsia, multiple pregnancy, significant varicose veins. High risk (>3/1000): rule out APS and thrombophilias; multidisciplinary management. COVID-19: thromboprophylaxis if hospitalized for moderate, severe, or critical illness; continue for 14 days after discharge (moderate) or 1 month (severe/critical). Postpartum: according to the postpartum score (previous section); continue during hospitalization and decide with hematology whether to continue. Source: MSPBS draft «Thromboembolism and pregnancy. Thromboprophylaxis» (corrected, unpublished version).

fichas.titulo: Protocol for suspected VTE — 15 steps (MSPBS draft)
fichas.texto: Triage: identity, gestational age/postpartum status, reason for presentation, and warning signs (sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tachypnea, cyanosis, syncope, tachycardia, painful and swollen lower limb). Assess hemodynamic stability; if there is severe compromise or suspected PE: oxygen, monitoring, and transfer to a higher level of care with referral form and perinatal record. Complete the perinatal medical history, with emphasis on thromboembolic risk factors. Clear information and emotional support throughout the process. Vital signs: BP, HR, RR, temperature, SpO₂. Determine gestational age or postpartum day (LMP, delivery date, perinatal record). Obstetric assessment: fundal height, FHR, uterine activity, fetal movements. Focused history: symptoms, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, cough/hemoptysis, leg pain/swelling, personal or family history of VTE/thrombophilia, immobilization, surgery, cesarean delivery, trauma, obesity. Focused physical examination: respiratory and cardiovascular systems, and lower extremities (unilateral edema, pain, warmth, difference in circumference, collateral veins). Studies as available: venous duplex ultrasound, ECG, blood gas analysis, chest radiograph with abdominal shielding, CT pulmonary angiography or V/Q scan. Presumptive or confirmed diagnosis of DVT/PE. Weight-adjusted LMWH (subcard 3 of block 1), unless contraindicated. Additional measures: early mobilization, compression stockings >20 mmHg, intermittent pneumatic compression (if LMWH is contraindicated, cesarean delivery/high risk, prior VTE, travel >4 h). Education for the patient and family: adherence, warning signs, seek immediate care if symptoms worsen. Detailed documentation in the medical record and follow-up scheduling.

grupos.bajada: Obstetric emergency: stepwise management in less than 60 seconds, HELPERR mnemonic, and complications.
grupos.html:
1General framework for dystocia (3 Ps)

Risk factors for dystocic labor — maternal: maternal age <18 or >35 years, multiparity/nulliparity, non-gynecoid pelvis, concomitant uterine injury, congenital pelvic defects, maternal history of dystocia, prior cesarean delivery, post-term pregnancy, prior stillbirth, prolonged or instrumented labor, induction with prostaglandins, weight gain >12kg, height <155cm. Fetal: weight >4000g, non-cephalic presentation.

Causes of dystocia by component
PMain causes
PowerInadequate uterine contractions; insufficient pushing effort (maternal exhaustion, sensory and motor effects of epidural anesthesia)
PassengerAbnormal fetal head position (occiput posterior, deep transverse arrest, asynclitism); fetal abnormalities (hydrocephalus, cervical or sacral masses)
PelvisPelvic narrowing–uterine dysfunction: the most common cause of dystocia. Cephalopelvic disproportion, pelvic deformities, cervical stenosis

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Valenti EA, Andina E, Rey A, et al. Clinical practice guidelines: Shoulder dystocia. Rev Hosp Mat Inf Ramón Sardá 2007;26(1):37-41 · Magnin G, Pierre F. Distocia de hombros. EMC Ginecología-Obstetricia 1999;5-067-A-10 · Romero Gutiérrez G, Ríos López JC, Cortés Salim P, Ponce Ponce de León AL. Risk factors associated with dystocic labor. Ginecol Obstet Mex 2007;75(9):533-8.

2Definition, magnitude, and incidence

Definition: inability of one or both shoulders to pass through the pelvic inlet. It is the obstetric condition most strongly associated with birth trauma (20-50%). Obstetric emergency.

Mechanism: the biparietal diameter exceeds the diameter of the pelvic inlet; pressure at the level of the pubic symphysis from endogenous forces 4-9 times greater than exogenous forces.

Incidence by estimated fetal weight
Fetal weightIncidence
2500-4000 g0.3-1%
4000-4500 g5-7%

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Valenti EA, Andina E, Rey A, et al. Clinical practice guidelines: Shoulder dystocia. Rev Hosp Mat Inf Ramón Sardá 2007;26(1):37-41 · Magnin G, Pierre F. Distocia de hombros. EMC Ginecología-Obstetricia 1999;5-067-A-10 · Romero Gutiérrez G, Ríos López JC, Cortés Salim P, Ponce Ponce de León AL. Risk factors associated with dystocic labor. Ginecol Obstet Mex 2007;75(9):533-8.

⚠️ 50% of cases occur in fetuses with normal weight — macrosomia alone is not predictive; the team must be prepared for every delivery.

3Specific risk factors

CategoryFactors
Maternal statusObesity, multiparity, advanced maternal age, diabetes
Current pregnancyMacrosomia, diabetes, excessive weight gain, post-term pregnancy, pelvic narrowing
Obstetric historyMacrosomia, history of shoulder dystocia, history of gestational diabetes
LaborArtificial induction, prolonged second stage, midpelvic forceps

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Valenti EA, Andina E, Rey A, et al. Clinical practice guidelines: Shoulder dystocia. Rev Hosp Mat Inf Ramón Sardá 2007;26(1):37-41 · Magnin G, Pierre F. Distocia de hombros. EMC Ginecología-Obstetricia 1999;5-067-A-10 · Romero Gutiérrez G, Ríos López JC, Cortés Salim P, Ponce Ponce de León AL. Risk factors associated with dystocic labor. Ginecol Obstet Mex 2007;75(9):533-8.

4Initial management — first 60 seconds

Turtle sign: retraction of the fetal head toward the perineum after delivery — diagnostic sign.

🚫 NO TRACTION
🚫 NO FUNDAL PRESSURE (increases risk of brachial plexus injury/uterine rupture)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Valenti EA, Andina E, Rey A, et al. Clinical practice guidelines: Shoulder dystocia. Rev Hosp Mat Inf Ramón Sardá 2007;26(1):37-41 · Magnin G, Pierre F. Distocia de hombros. EMC Ginecología-Obstetricia 1999;5-067-A-10 · Romero Gutiérrez G, Ríos López JC, Cortés Salim P, Ponce Ponce de León AL. Risk factors associated with dystocic labor. Ginecol Obstet Mex 2007;75(9):533-8.

  • Act in less than 60 seconds.
  • Wide prophylactic episiotomy.
  • McRoberts maneuver (see subcard 6).
  • Call for help: obstetrician, pediatrician, anesthesiologist.

5HELPERR mnemonic (30-60 sec per step)

LetterAction (English)Associated maneuver
HCall for HelpAsk for help
EEvaluate for EpisiotomyEvaluate episiotomy
LLegsMcRoberts maneuver
PSuprapubic PressureSuprapubic pressure
EEnterInternal maneuvers — Rubin, Woods
RRemove the Posterior ArmPosterior arm delivery
RRoll the PatientRotate the Patient — Gaskin Maneuver

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Valenti EA, Andina E, Rey A, et al. Clinical practice guidelines: Shoulder dystocia. Rev Hosp Mat Inf Ramón Sardá 2007;26(1):37-41 · Magnin G, Pierre F. Distocia de hombros. EMC Ginecología-Obstetricia 1999;5-067-A-10 · Romero Gutiérrez G, Ríos López JC, Cortés Salim P, Ponce Ponce de León AL. Risk factors associated with dystocic labor. Ginecol Obstet Mex 2007;75(9):533-8.

6Stepwise maneuvers — first-line

External maneuvers, without additional anesthesia.

ManeuverReported effectiveness
McRoberts (hyperflexion and hyperabduction of the maternal hips)Resolves 90% of cases
Suprapubic pressure (on the anterior shoulder, in an oblique direction)Resolves 40-80% of cases
Discontinue oxytocin infusionConcurrent measure, not a physical maneuver

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Valenti EA, Andina E, Rey A, et al. Clinical practice guidelines: Shoulder dystocia. Rev Hosp Mat Inf Ramón Sardá 2007;26(1):37-41 · Magnin G, Pierre F. Distocia de hombros. EMC Ginecología-Obstetricia 1999;5-067-A-10 · Romero Gutiérrez G, Ríos López JC, Cortés Salim P, Ponce Ponce de León AL. Risk factors associated with dystocic labor. Ginecol Obstet Mex 2007;75(9):533-8.

7Stepwise maneuvers — second-line

Internal fetal manipulation, requires regional anesthesia.

  • Woods maneuver ("corkscrew" — screw-like rotation of the posterior shoulder, 180°, to an anterior position).
  • Rubin maneuver (rotation of the more accessible shoulder toward the oblique diameter, adducting the shoulders).
  • Jacquemier maneuver (delivery of the posterior shoulder: the posterior arm is moved backward, the forearm is flexed over the arm, the hand is grasped, and the posterior shoulder is disengaged).
  • Posterior axillary traction.
  • Gaskin maneuver (maternal position on all fours — changes pelvic geometry without direct fetal manipulation).

8Last-resort maneuvers

Greater fetal morbidity and mortality — use only if the above maneuvers fail.

  • Deliberate clavicular fracture (reduces the biacromial diameter).
  • Zavanelli maneuver (cephalic replacement and emergency cesarean delivery).
  • Abdominal rescue (hysterotomy with disimpaction of the shoulder from the abdomen, followed by assisted vaginal delivery).
  • Symphysiotomy (surgical division of the pubic symphysis).

If all the above fail: downward traction on the head + moderate suprapubic pressure, under general anesthesia.

9Documentation and fetal complications

Document (medicolegal): explanation to the patient, severity/complexity, procedures and possible sequelae, maneuvers and timing.

Fetal complications
Brachial plexus injury~16.7% (1 in 6 cases)
Clavicle or humerus fracture—
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with neurologic damage—
Erb palsy (C5-C6 roots)~50% of brachial plexus palsies — deltoids, biceps, supraspinatus/infraspinatus, brachioradialis
Klumpke palsy (C8-T1 roots)~40% of brachial plexus palsies — intrinsic hand muscles, flexors and extensors

Ginecol Obstet Mex 2007;75(9):533-8.

10Maternal complications

Postpartum hemorrhage11%
Fourth-degree perineal tears3.8%
Endometritis—
Uterine rupture—

Ginecol Obstet Mex 2007;75(9):533-8.

Assistance with Breech Presentation at Birth — Maneuvers

Epidemiology, types of presentation, ACOG criteria for vaginal delivery, and sequence of maneuvers (MSF/PMC).

1Epidemiology and risk factors

Incidence: 3-4% of births. The frequency increases at lower gestational ages (more common in preterm infants).

Risk factors: prematurity, uterine relaxation/multiparity, pelvic tumor, pelvic narrowing, hydramnios, oligohydramnios, hydrocephalus and anencephaly, history of prior breech delivery, uterine anomalies.

2Types of breech presentation

EnglishSpanishDescription
Frank BreechFrank breechHips flexed, knees extended — legs extended upward alongside the trunk
Complete BreechComplete breechHips and knees flexed — "squatting" position
Footling BreechFootling breech / feet firstOne or both feet below the buttocks as the presenting part

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Williams Obstetrics (Breech Delivery) · ACOG CO 745 (2018) · MSF — Breech presentation.

Only frank or complete breech presentations are candidates for vaginal delivery (see subcard 4); footling breech is excluded.

3Risks to the mother and fetus

MotherFetus
Higher incidence of complications and infectionUmbilical cord prolapse
Uterine ruptureFemoral, clavicular, and humeral fractures
Tears at various levelsBrachial plexus stretch injury
Uterine atony—

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Williams Obstetrics (Breech Delivery) · ACOG CO 745 (2018) · MSF — Breech presentation.

4ACOG criteria for attempted vaginal delivery

All criteria must be met — failure to meet any one indicates cesarean delivery:

  • Estimated fetal weight <3,500 g.
  • Biparietal diameter <96 mm (range 90-100mm, Williams Obstetrics citing Giuliani 2002 and Roman 2008 — not a specific ACOG cutoff).
  • Clinically adequate pelvis.
  • Frank or complete breech (footling breech excluded).
  • Flexed fetal head.
  • Absence of fetal anomalies.
  • No contraindications to vaginal delivery.
  • Absence of concomitant pathology.

This checklist is available as a binary (yes/no) mini-calculator in the Calculator mode.

5Guiding principle — "hands-off"

General management of breech labor, not a specific maneuver: the infant should be delivered by maternal pushing, supported only by the bony parts (hips and sacrum), without traction, without pulling on the legs, without touching the infant until the scapulae appear (to avoid triggering the respiratory reflex before the head is delivered).

⏱️ Once the umbilicus is out: complete delivery within a maximum of 3 minutes (risk of cord compression). Ensure the back does not rotate to a posterior position.

6Maneuvers in order of use

#ManeuverWhen used
1PinardBreech / incomplete footling breech — bring down the legs
2LovsetRetained shoulders / arms extended above — bring down the arms
3BrachtEntrapped head after releasing the arms — first-line option
4Mauriceau-Smellie-VeitEntrapped head if Bracht fails
5SuzorRetained shoulders if Lovset fails
6Forceps for the aftercoming headEntrapped head if Bracht and Mauriceau fail (experienced operator)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Williams Obstetrics (Breech Delivery) · ACOG CO 745 (2018) · MSF — Breech presentation.

7Detailed technique for each maneuver

Pinard: insert two fingers into the vagina and “hook” the leg from medial to lateral just above the knee; flex at the hip and abduct to release the foot. Repeat with the other leg if the breech is complete.

Lovset: place the thumbs over the sacrum, grasp the hips, and rotate 90°; release the anterior arm; counter-rotate 180° and release the posterior arm.

Bracht: hold the hips and lift with both hands toward the maternal abdomen without traction; the neck pivots over the symphysis. An assistant applies suprapubic pressure.

Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit (modified): kneel at a 45° downward angle; support the infant on the hand and forearm; place the index and middle fingers on the maxilla (NOT inside the mouth — risk of mandibular fracture); place the other hand on either side of the neck; lower the head, bringing the subocciput beneath the symphysis; use a sweeping motion, bringing the back toward the maternal abdomen. Apply suprapubic pressure along the pelvic axis.

Suzor: rotate the back 90°; pull downward; insert one hand along the back to locate the anterior arm; place the thumb in the axilla and the middle finger along the arm; lower the anterior arm; lift by the feet to release the posterior shoulder.

8Complete operational sequence

  1. Verify the criteria for vaginal delivery (subcard 4) — if not met, cesarean delivery.
  2. Confirm the type of presentation (subcard 2) — frank/complete breech are candidates; footling breech is highly unfavorable.
  3. Delivery: hands off — allow descent with maternal pushing.
  4. Legs (if not delivered spontaneously): Pinard.
  5. Arms: Lovset (or Suzor if it fails).
  6. Head: Bracht → if unsuccessful, Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit → if unsuccessful, forceps for the aftercoming head.
  7. Timer: from delivery of the umbilicus, a maximum of 3 minutes to deliver the head.
  8. Document maneuvers and times (medicolegal).

Source: Vizcaíno A. “Parto Pélvico.” SlideShare (18/01/10) · ACOG Committee Opinion No. 265/340/745 (qualitative position, no BPD cutoff) · Williams Obstetrics 24th/25th ed. — Breech Delivery (Giuliani 2002; Roman 2008) · MSF Guidelines — Breech presentation · PMC — Footling Breech Delivery.

fichas.texto: Internal fetal manipulation, requires regional anesthesia. Woods maneuver ("corkscrew" — screw-like rotation of the posterior shoulder, 180°, to an anterior position). Rubin maneuver (rotation of the more accessible shoulder toward the oblique diameter, adducting the shoulders). Jacquemier maneuver (delivery of the posterior shoulder: the posterior arm is moved backward, the forearm is flexed over the arm, the hand is grasped, and the posterior shoulder is disengaged). Posterior axillary traction. Gaskin maneuver (maternal position on all fours — changes pelvic geometry without direct fetal manipulation).

fichas.texto: General management of breech labor, not a specific maneuver: the infant should be delivered by maternal pushing, supported only by the bony parts (hips and sacrum), without traction, without pulling on the legs, without touching the infant until the scapulae appear (to avoid triggering the respiratory reflex before the head is delivered). ⏱️ Once the umbilicus is out: complete delivery within a maximum of 3 minutes (risk of cord compression). Ensure the back does not rotate to a posterior position.

fichas.texto: Pinard: insert two fingers into the vagina and “hook” the leg from medial to lateral just above the knee; flex at the hip and abduct to release the foot. Repeat with the other leg if the breech is complete. Lovset: place the thumbs over the sacrum, grasp the hips, and rotate 90°; release the anterior arm; counter-rotate 180° and release the posterior arm. Bracht: hold the hips and lift with both hands toward the maternal abdomen without traction; the neck pivots over the symphysis. An assistant applies suprapubic pressure. Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit (modified): kneel at a 45° downward angle; support the infant on the hand and forearm; place the index and middle fingers on the maxilla (NOT inside the mouth — risk of mandibular fracture); place the other hand on either side of the neck; lower the head, bringing the subocciput beneath the symphysis; use a sweeping motion, bringing the back toward the maternal abdomen. Apply suprapubic pressure along the pelvic axis. Suzor: rotate the back 90°; pull downward; insert one hand along the back to locate the anterior arm; place the thumb in the axilla and the middle finger along the arm; lower the anterior arm; lift by the feet to release the posterior shoulder.

Confirm the type of presentation (subcard 2) — frank/complete breech are candidates; footling breech is highly unfavorable. Delivery: hands off — allow descent with maternal pushing. Legs (if not delivered spontaneously): Pinard. Arms: Lovset (or Suzor if it fails). Head: Bracht → if unsuccessful, Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit → if unsuccessful, forceps for the aftercoming head. Timer: from delivery of the umbilicus, a maximum of 3 minutes to deliver the head. Document maneuvers and times (medicolegal).

grupos.bajada: Diagnosis, management by gestational age, latency antibiotic regimens, and criteria for immediate delivery.
grupos.html:
1Diagnosis

Clinical: clear fluid leaking from the vagina — reliability >90% if visualized at the external cervical os on speculum examination.

Confirmatory tests:

  • Fern test.
  • Nitrazine test (pH>6.5 turns blue).
  • Commercial biomarkers (PAMG-1/AmniSure, IGFBP-1/Actim PROM).
  • Measurement of urea and creatinine in vaginal secretions — urea 94%/82% and creatinine 98%/90% (sensitivity/specificity, Alao 2023); low cost, useful in resource-limited settings. See comparative table in subcard 7.

Diagnostic amniocentesis (gold standard in equivocal cases): ultrasound-guided instillation of indigo carmine, vaginal tampon, confirmation of staining at 20-30 min.

Methylene blue CONTRAINDICATED for intra-amniotic use — teratogenic; causes neonatal jejunal/ileal atresia, severe hyperbilirubinemia, fetal methemoglobinemia, and hemolysis. Safe alternatives: indigo carmine or fluorescein.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Alao AI et al. Arch Gynecol Obstet 2023;307(2):447-452.

Microbiological analysis of amniotic fluid: Gram stain, culture (aerobes/anaerobes/Mycoplasma/Ureaplasma), amniotic fluid glucose (<14 mg/dL suggests intra-amniotic infection), leukocyte count.

2Management by gestational age

Gestational ageManagement
Previable (<22-24 wk)Expectant management as an outpatient/inpatient; counseling on the risk of pulmonary hypoplasia, deformities, and stillbirth. No corticosteroids, tocolysis, or routine antibiotics.
Preterm, remote from term (24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷ wk)Expectant inpatient management; complete course of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone/dexamethasone); magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if delivery is imminent and GA<32 wk; mandatory latency antibiotic prophylaxis; tocolysis contraindicated or limited to 48h to complete corticosteroid treatment (if no infection).
Late preterm (34⁰/⁷-36⁶/⁷ wk)ACOG/FIGO recommendation: delivery/induction at diagnosis. Exception: expectant management until 37 weeks only if there are no signs of infection + close monitoring.
At term (≥37⁰/⁷ wk)Induction (oxytocin or misoprostol if the cervix is unfavorable) within 12-24h to reduce the risk of intrauterine infection.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG · FIGO.

3Latency antibiotic regimens (24-34 wk)

Standard ACOG/NICHD regimen (7 days):

  • Days 1-2 IV: Ampicillin 2g q6h + erythromycin 250mg q6h (or azithromycin 1g PO as a single dose).
  • Days 3-7 PO: Amoxicillin 250mg q8h + erythromycin base 333mg q8h (MSPBS 2018 uses amoxicillin 500mg; see card 17).

Alternative regimen (with azithromycin, widely used):

  • Ampicillin 2g IV q6h x48h → amoxicillin 250mg PO q8h x5 days + azithromycin 1g PO as a single dose at admission (ACOG: an appropriate substitute for erythromycin).
Avoid amoxicillin + clavulanic acid — risk of neonatal necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC).

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG.

4Criteria for immediate delivery

Contraindicate expectant management at any gestational age:

  • Clinical chorioamnionitis / confirmed intra-amniotic infection (Gibbs criteria).
  • Placental abruption.
  • Acute fetal compromise (non-reassuring FHR / abnormal biophysical profile).
  • Established labor.
  • Fetal death.

5Fetal lung maturation and neuroprotection (submodule shared with TPL)

These therapies are shared with the Threatened Preterm Labor (TPL) module — same regimen, same table of recommendations by guideline:

Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation (3 recommendations)
GuidelineGA window
ACOG24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷ weeks (consider “late preterm” 34⁰/⁷-36⁶/⁷ if no prior course was given)
FIGO/WHO24⁰/⁷-34⁶/⁷ weeks (in settings with adequate neonatal care capacity)
NICEOffer 24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷; consider 34⁰/⁷-35⁶/⁷

Regimens: Betamethasone 12mg IM every 24h (2 doses total); Dexamethasone 6mg IM every 12h (4 doses total). Rescue dose: a single dose or repeat course if >14 days since the initial course, GA<34 weeks, and imminent risk of delivery within 7 days.

Fetal neuroprotection with MgSO4 (3 recommendations)
GuidelineGA cutoff
ACOG<32⁰/⁷ weeks
NICE<30⁰/⁷ weeks; consider 30⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷
FIGO/WHO<32⁰/⁷ weeks (some consensus statements extend to <34 weeks if delivery is imminent)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG · FIGO · WHO · NICE.

Regimen: loading dose 4g IV over 20-30min; maintenance 1g/h IV until delivery or for a total of 24h; antidote: Calcium Gluconate 10% 1g IV.

In the Calculator, the single cutoff used is that of MSPBS Paraguay (corticosteroids: 24⁰/⁷ to 34⁰/⁷ weeks, not from 34¹/⁷ onward · MgSO4: less than 32 weeks); ACOG/FIGO/NICE variations are listed in this guide — see Calculator Mode.

6Definitions and subtypes of rupture

  • PROM: rupture of membranes occurring at least 2 hours before the onset of labor, regardless of GA (FASGO 2018 consensus).
  • Latency period: time between rupture and onset of labor; inversely proportional to GA (longer when rupture occurs earlier).
Subtypes by site of rupture (widely used teaching terminology in Spanish-language obstetric education)
SubtypeCharacteristic
High rupture of membranesRupture above the internal cervical os; scant or intermittent fluid leakage.
Low rupture of membranesRupture near the internal cervical os; frank fluid leakage.
False rupture of membranesRupture of only one membrane (amniochorion) with persistence of the other; difficult to diagnose, with confirmatory tests that may yield false-negative results.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: FASGO. 2018 Obstetrics Consensus: Premature rupture of membranes.

These subtypes are not included in the 2018 FASGO Consensus and are presented without specific attribution to that source.

7Diagnostic performance of confirmatory tests

Sensitivity and specificity by method
MethodSensitivitySpecificityNote
Nitrazine (pH >6.5)90-97%16-70%Low specificity: false positives with blood, semen, and bacterial vaginosis.
Crystallization (Fern test)55-98%30-88%Wide range; depends on the operator.
PAMG-1 (AmniSure)98-99%98-100%Considered the best commercial biomarker (reference standard in SOGOCEP/FLASOG); some studies report sensitivity of 95.7-97.3%.
IGFBP-1 (Actim PROM)74-97%74-97%Commercial alternative to PAMG-1; individual studies show ~89-90% sensitivity and ~83-87% specificity.
Vaginal urea (cutoff 1.25 mg/dL)94%82%Low cost; useful in resource-limited settings (Alao 2023).
Vaginal creatinine (cutoff 0.23 mg/dL)98%90%Low cost; useful in resource-limited settings (Alao 2023).

8Triple I (clinical chorioamnionitis): criteria for suspected infection

“Triple I” (Intrauterine Inflammation, Infection or both) is the modern term proposed by the 2015 NICHD workshop and adopted by ACOG/SMFM; it replaces “clinical chorioamnionitis” (classic Gibbs 1982 criteria: fever ≥37.8 °C + ≥2 signs; many guidelines use ≥38.0 °C).

Definition in ACOG Committee Opinion 712 (2017)
CategoryCriterion

Isolated maternal feverTemperature 38.0-38.9 °C without other factors, whether persistent or not.
Management of Triple I: broad-spectrum antibiotics, delivery, and maternal resuscitation. In PROM, monitoring uses the same obstetric qSOFA (SBP <90, RR ≥25, altered mental status) used in the sepsis module; ≥2 points = high risk of deterioration.

9Risk stratification for multidrug-resistant bacteria (MDR)

Patient at risk of MDR = 1 major criterion or 2 or more minor criteria (comorbidities count as one criterion).

  • Major criterion: previous infection or colonization with MDR bacteria.
  • Minor criterion 1: comorbidity (CKD, pregestational diabetes, heart disease, COPD) or immunosuppression (neutropenia, transplant, corticosteroids >20 mg/day of prednisone or equivalent for >2 weeks, immunosuppressants/cytotoxic agents, HIV with CD4 <200, primary immunodeficiencies).
  • Minor criterion 2: indwelling urinary catheter.
  • Minor criterion 3: hospital admission in the previous 3 months, regardless of duration.
  • Minor criterion 4: systemic antibiotic (oral or IV) in the previous 3 months, regardless of duration (common in recurrent UTIs).
  • Minor criterion 5: origin from an endemic area (Latin America, the Caribbean, Asia, non-EU Mediterranean) and <6 months in the country, or >6 months in the country but travel to or visits from family from that country in the previous 6 months.

10Erythromycin vs azithromycin: meta-analysis

Seaman et al., AJOG 2022 (5 studies, 1289 patients):

  • Latency: no difference (6.6 vs 6.7 days; mean difference 0.07 days, 95% CI −0.45 to 0.60).
  • Clinical chorioamnionitis: OR 0.53 (95% CI 0.39-0.71) with azithromycin; median prevalence 14% vs 25% with erythromycin (approximately 47% relative reduction).

Azithromycin is not intended to achieve longer latency: it aims for equal efficacy with better tolerability and less chorioamnionitis (FLASOG 2026 pearl). Source: Seaman AN et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2022;226(6):794-801.

13Regional context: outpatient management vs continuous hospitalization

Conditional golden rule: without active remote monitoring (continuous temperature sensor, outpatient CTG with remote transmission) or emergency access to a hospital within <15 min, continuous hospitalization is the only standard that safeguards the mother and fetus and provides medico-legal safety.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: RCOG · ACOG · NICE.

Outpatient management should only be considered if all these requirements are met:

  • Patient at low risk of infection, strictly selected.
  • Guaranteed maternal adherence and stable connectivity.
  • 24/7 monitoring by a specialized team.
  • Immediate access to obstetric and neonatal ICU care.
  • Response in <15 min to a critical alarm.

Recommendation to use regional clinical judgment, consistent with RCOG #73, ACOG, and NICE NG25 (inpatient expectant management by default).

Minor criterion 1: comorbidity (CKD, pregestational diabetes, heart disease, COPD) or immunosuppression (neutropenia, transplant, corticosteroids >20 mg/day of prednisone or equivalent for >2 weeks, immunosuppressants/cytotoxic agents, HIV with CD4 <200, primary immunodeficiencies). Minor criterion 2: indwelling urinary catheter. Minor criterion 3: hospital admission in the previous 3 months, regardless of duration. Minor criterion 4: systemic antibiotic (oral or IV) in the previous 3 months, regardless of duration (common in recurrent UTIs). Minor criterion 5: origin from an endemic area (Latin America, the Caribbean, Asia, non-EU Mediterranean) and <6 months in the country, or >6 months in the country but travel to or visits from family from that country in the previous 6 months. Antibiotic regimen if at risk of MDR (Medicina Fetal Barcelona, 2025) Situation Regimen Initial Ampicillin 2 g q/6 h IV + Ertapenem 1 g q/24 h IV + Clarithromycin 500 mg q/12 h PO De-escalation (negative rectal MDR screening swab) Ampicillin 2 g q/6 h IV + Ceftriaxone 1 g q/12 h IV + Clarithromycin 500 mg q/12 h PO (or other options susceptible according to the antibiogram) Penicillin/beta-lactam allergy Teicoplanin 600 mg q/12 h IV (2 initial doses, then q/24 h) + Aztreonam 1 g q/8 h IV + Clarithromycin 500 mg q/12 h PO CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Medicina Fetal Barcelona protocol, preterm and term PROM (09/2025). In the absence of suspected multidrug-resistant bacteria, the standard regimen in subcard 3 is maintained. Source: Medicina Fetal Barcelona protocol, preterm and term PROM (09/2025).

fichas.titulo: Decision tree: immediate delivery vs expectant management
fichas.texto: Confirmed preterm PROM ▼ Is there any criterion for immediate delivery? ▼ YES — deliver immediately Triple I / clinical chorioamnionitis · placental abruption · acute fetal compromise · cord prolapse · active labor · active maternal bleeding NO — expectant management according to gestational age ▼ Inpatient admission, monitoring (subcard 12), corticosteroids, latency antibiotics, and magnesium sulfate according to GA Gestational age category for expectant management Previable (<24 wk) Counseling (pulmonary hypoplasia, deformities, fetal demise). No routine corticosteroids, tocolysis, or antibiotics. 24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷ wk Inpatient expectant management; corticosteroids, latency antibiotics, magnesium sulfate if <32 wk and delivery is imminent. 34⁰/⁷-36⁶/⁷ wk Delivery at diagnosis (ACOG/FIGO); expectant management until 37 wk only in the absence of infection and with close monitoring. ≥37 wk Induction within 12-24 h. fichas.titulo: Regional context: outpatient management vs continuous hospitalization
fichas.texto: Conditional golden rule: without active remote monitoring (continuous temperature sensor, outpatient CTG with remote transmission) or emergency access to a hospital within <15 min, continuous hospitalization is the only standard that safeguards the mother and fetus and provides medico-legal safety. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: RCOG · ACOG · NICE. Outpatient management should only be considered if all these requirements are met: Patient at low risk of infection, strictly selected. Guaranteed maternal adherence and stable connectivity. 24/7 monitoring by a specialized team. Immediate access to obstetric and neonatal ICU care. Response in <15 min to a critical alarm. Recommendation to use regional clinical judgment, consistent with RCOG #73, ACOG, and NICE NG25 (inpatient expectant management by default).

fichas.texto: GA Management Antibiotics Less than 24 weeks (previable) Expectant management; decision made jointly with the parents. No group B streptococcus prophylaxis, corticosteroids, tocolysis, or MgSO4 before viability Consider from 20⁰/⁷ weeks 24⁰/⁷ a 33⁶/⁷ Inpatient expectant management (or refer to a Level III facility); IV crystalloids; CBC and CRP every 48 h; temperature monitoring. Corticosteroids at 24-34 weeks; MgSO4 if <32 weeks and delivery is likely within 24 h; tocolysis only to complete corticosteroid administration or for 48 h. Deliver if contractions, infection, or fetal compromise persist One of: ampicillin 2 g IV, then 1 g every 4 h · amoxicillin 500 mg PO every 8 h · clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 h (allergy) · erythromycin 250 mg PO every 6 h · amoxicillin + sulbactam 1.5 g every 8 h; 7 days or until delivery + azithromycin 1 g PO once 34⁰/⁷ a 36⁶/⁷ Consider delivery by the most appropriate route Same options. Alternative if available: ampicillin 1-2 g IV every 6 h + erythromycin 500 mg PO every 6 h (48 h), then amoxicillin 500 mg PO every 6 h + erythromycin 500 mg PO every 8 h (5 days) 37⁰/⁷ or more Deliver by the most appropriate route according to cervical status Group B streptococcus positive: ampicillin 2 g IV q4 h until delivery. More than 18 h without infection: penicillin G 5 M IU, then 2.5 M q4 h, or ampicillin 2 g, then 1 g q4 h Chorioamnionitis (any GA) Delivery regardless of GA; notify neonatology Ampicillin 2 g IV q6 h + gentamicin 2 mg/kg, then 1.5 mg/kg q8 h (or 5 mg/kg q24 h); for cesarean delivery, add metronidazole 500 mg q8 h or clindamycin 900 mg q8 h; until 48 h without signs Difference from ACOG PB 217 (2020): amoxicillin 250 mg q8 h + erythromycin 333 mg q8 h during the oral phase, and no latency antibiotics from 34⁰/⁷ onward (only Group B streptococcus prophylaxis). fichas.titulo: Corticosteroids after 34 weeks: benefit versus harm
fichas.texto: CaVeSal® approach: antenatal corticosteroids are suggested from 24⁰/⁷ to 34⁰/⁷ (MSPBS), in the absence of chorioamnionitis. Other guidelines extend the limit: ACOG through 36⁶/⁷ and NICE to consider through 35⁶/⁷. Study Design Outcome ALPS (NEJM 2016) Randomized trial, 34⁰/⁷-36⁵/⁷ Benefit: composite respiratory outcome 11.6% vs 14.4% (RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.66-0.97). Harm: neonatal hypoglycemia 24.0% vs 15.0% (RR 1.60; 1.37-1.87) ALPS follow-up (JAMA 2024) 949 children, median age 7 years No difference in cognitive impairment (17.1% vs 18.5%; adjusted RR 0.94; 0.73-1.22) Ninan (JAMA Pediatr 2022) Observational cohort, more than 1.25 million children Among late preterm and term infants exposed: more neurocognitive visits (HR 1.12) and mental or behavioral disorders in infants born at term (HR 1.47). Low certainty: does not prove causality Aviram (Arch Dis Child Fetal Neonatal Ed 2022) Population-based retrospective cohort (Ontario), 25,668 infants born at 34⁰/⁷ to 36⁶/⁷; 2,689 exposed to corticosteroids before 34⁰/⁷ At 5 years: higher suspicion of neurocognitive disorder (adjusted HR 1.12; 95% CI 1.05-1.20) and more audiometric assessments (adjusted HR 1.20) and vision assessments (adjusted HR 1.06). Observational: does not prove causality Cutoff variations Guideline Limit Conditions MSPBS 2018 (calculator) 24⁰/⁷-34⁰/⁷ No chorioamnionitis NICE NG25 Consider through 35⁶/⁷ Risk of preterm birth ACOG CO 713 Up to 36⁶/⁷ Delivery likely within 7 days, no prior course, no chorioamnionitis; caution in pregestational diabetes European guideline on perinatal care 2023 34⁰/⁷-34⁶/⁷ only in selected cases; 35⁰/⁷-36⁶/⁷ only in trials At 35-36⁶/⁷, reduces transient tachypnea, with no effect on RDS and more hypoglycemia If corticosteroids are given after 34 weeks: neonatal glucose monitoring. Chorioamnionitis: ALPS showed no increase in chorioamnionitis or sepsis, and neither did a meta-analysis (RR 0.86) (WAPM, J Perinat Med 2022). The citation "Li G et al. Lancet Neurol 2022;21:948-962" (>16,000 women) does not exist in PubMed or Lancet Neurology; the title corresponds to Aviram 2022, whose data are shown above. grupos.bajada: Diagnosis, tocolysis, and shared fetal lung maturation/neuroprotection submodule (see also PROM tab).
grupos.html:
1Diagnosis and clinical criteria

Definition: regular uterine activity (≥4 contractions/20min or ≥8/60min) + cervical changes, between 22⁰/⁷ and 36⁶/⁷ weeks.

Transvaginal cervical ultrasound (TVUS):

  • Cervical length (CL) >30mm → high negative predictive value (rules out active preterm labor).
  • CL <25mm (or <20mm) → short cervix / elevated risk.

Biomarkers if CL 20-30mm: fetal fibronectin (fFN) or PAMG-1 (PartoSure) — if negative, avoids unnecessary tocolysis.

2Tocolysis — complete regimens

Objective: delay delivery 48-72h to complete fetal lung maturation, provide neuroprotection, and transfer to a Level III center. Use: weeks 22/24 to 33⁶/⁷.

DrugRegimenMaintenance schedule
Nifedipine (1st-line ACOG/FIGO)Loading dose 10-20mg orally every 20min (max 40mg in 1st hour); maintenance 10-20mg orally every 6-8h for 48h.c/6-8h
Atosiban (NICE/RCOG first line)6.75mg IV bolus over 1min; infusion 300mcg/min for 3h, then 100mcg/min until 48h are completed.Continuous infusion (0-3h / 3-48h phases)
Indomethacin (preferred before week 32)50-100mg rectal/oral initial dose, then 25-50mg orally every 6h for a maximum of 48h.c/6h
Isoxsuprine (beta-agonist)100 mg (10 ampoules of 10 mg) in 500 cc of 5% dextrose or normal saline; start at 10 drops/min (100 mcg/min), increase by 10 drops every 15 min up to 40 drops/min (400 mcg/min); 12 h (max 24 h).Continuous infusion; monitor HR/BP with each adjustment
⚠️ Nifedipine + MgSO4: DO NOT combine — risk of severe hypotension/cardiovascular collapse.
⚠️ Indomethacin: DO NOT use after week 32 — premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, oligohydramnios.

Progesterone (prevention, not acute tocolysis): micronized vaginal progesterone 200 mg/day, started between 16-24 weeks and continued until at least 34 weeks, for a short cervix (≤25 mm) or history of preterm birth (NICE NG25 · SOGC 398).

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG · FIGO · NICE · RCOG.

3Tocolysis hours timer (concept — calculation in Calculator Mode)

The Calculator includes a single timer, reusable for all 3 drugs, with an internal cadence parameterized according to the active drug:

  • Manual trigger: starts when “tocolysis initiated” is selected — not assumed automatically.
  • Active alerts at dose milestones: alert at each hour corresponding to the next maintenance dose for the drug (see table above).
  • Pause/stop button: preserves the accumulated time (e.g., “tocolysis stopped at 18h 40min”) without resetting to zero.
  • End of window: alert at 48h (or 72h) — “tocolysis target reached; reassess continuation/transfer.”
  • Joint display with the uterine activity record (contractions/20-60min) to assess clinical response.

7Rescue course, benefits and long-term risks of corticosteroids

  • Do not repeat routinely. Single rescue course if risk of delivery recurs, the previous course was >14 days ago, and gestational age is <34 weeks (risk of delivery within 7 days).
  • Benefits: reduces neonatal RDS by 34%, neonatal mortality by 31%, intraventricular hemorrhage by 46%, and necrotizing enterocolitis by 54%.
  • Betamethasone vs dexamethasone (ASTEROID, Crowther 2019): no difference in the primary outcome (death or neurodevelopmental disability at 2 years: 33% vs 32%; RR 0.97). With dexamethasone: fewer cesarean deliveries (43% vs 52%; RR 0.84) and less hypertension at 2 years (32% vs 41%; RR 0.78). Intraventricular hemorrhage did not differ (RR 1.09; p=0.72).

Survival and cerebral palsy in low birthweight infants: implications for perinatal care. Paediatr Perinat Epidemiol 1992;6:298-310 · Moster D et al. NEJM 2008;359(3):262-273.

Prevalence of cerebral palsy: 2-2.5/1000 live births, inversely proportional to gestational age. Prematurity accounts for 75% of perinatal deaths and 50% of neurological abnormalities (excluding malformations).

Justifies prioritizing neuroprotection at the earliest gestational ages. Citation chain: Petrini 2009 (J Pediatr; HR 3.39 at 34-36 weeks), Stanley 1992 (Paediatr Perinat Epidemiol), Moster 2008 (NEJM; RR 78.9 at 23-27 weeks). The 8× value has no specific primary reference identified.

Drug Regimen Maintenance schedule Nifedipine (1st-line ACOG/FIGO) Loading dose 10-20mg orally every 20min (max 40mg in 1st hour); maintenance 10-20mg orally every 6-8h for 48h. c/6-8h Atosiban (NICE/RCOG first line) 6.75mg IV bolus over 1min; infusion 300mcg/min for 3h, then 100mcg/min until 48h are completed. fichas.titulo: Rescue course, benefits and long-term risks of corticosteroids
fichas.texto: Do not repeat routinely. Single rescue course if risk of delivery recurs, the previous course was >14 days ago, and gestational age is <34 weeks (risk of delivery within 7 days). Benefits: reduces neonatal RDS by 34%, neonatal mortality by 31%, intraventricular hemorrhage by 46%, and necrotizing enterocolitis by 54%. Betamethasone vs dexamethasone (ASTEROID, Crowther 2019): no difference in the primary outcome (death or neurodevelopmental disability at 2 years: 33% vs 32%; RR 0.97). With dexamethasone: fewer cesarean deliveries (43% vs 52%; RR 0.84) and less hypertension at 2 years (32% vs 41%; RR 0.78). Intraventricular hemorrhage did not differ (RR 1.09; p=0.72). Long-term risks and benefits by gestational age at birth (Ninan 2022: 30 studies, >1.25 million children) Group Outcome Measure Extremely preterm ↓ neurodevelopmental impairment aOR 0.69 (0.57-0.84) — ~31% lower Extremely preterm ↓ cerebral palsy aOR 0.60 (0.43-0.83) — ~40% lower Late preterm ↑ neurocognitive disorders aHR 1.12 (1.05-1.20) — ~12% higher Term (≥37 weeks) ↑ mental/behavioral disorders aHR 1.47 (1.36-1.60) — ~47% more Term (≥37 weeks) ↑ neurocognitive disorders aHR 1.16 (1.10-1.21) — ~16% more CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Crowther CA et al. ASTEROID, Lancet Child Adolesc Health 2019;3(11):769-780 · Ninan K et al. JAMA Pediatr 2022;176(6):e220483. Supports the rule against routine use of corticosteroids in late preterm/term infants or repeating courses. Räikkönen et al., JAMA 2020 (670,097 children): HR 1.33 (1.26-1.41) for any mental/behavioral disorder.

Survival and cerebral palsy in low birthweight infants: implications for perinatal care. Paediatr Perinat Epidemiol 1992;6:298-310 · Moster D et al. NEJM 2008;359(3):262-273. grupos.bajada: Differential diagnosis, PUQE scale, stepwise pharmacologic treatment, and safe rehydration. This module is also available in Calculator Mode with interactive PUQE.
grupos.html:
1Diagnosis and differentiation

NVP (Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy): physiological/mild, affecting up to 80% of pregnant patients, onset at weeks 4-9, resolution at weeks 16-20.

HG (Hyperemesis Gravidarum): severe and intractable form, 0.3-2% of pregnancies. Classic triad:

  • Intractable vomiting.
  • Weight loss >5% of prepregnancy weight.
  • Ketonuria/ketonemia + electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis).

2PUQE Scale (assesses the previous 24h — 3 questions, 1-5 points each, total range 3-15)

Question1 point5 points
P1 — Duration of nauseaNone>6 hours
P2 — Episodes of retching without vomitingNone≥7
P3 — Episodes of vomitingNone≥7
Total scoreClassificationManagement
≤6Mild NVPOutpatient / dietary
7-12Moderate NVPOutpatient pharmacologic treatment
≥13Severe HGHospital care / parenteral hydration

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Koren G et al. 2002 y 2005 (PUQE scale) · ACOG PB 189 (2018).

3Stepwise pharmacologic treatment

LineScenarioMedications and doses
1st lineMild to moderate, outpatientPyridoxine (B6) 10-25mg orally q6-8h; preferred combination: Doxylamine 10mg + Pyridoxine 10mg (2 tablets at bedtime, up to 4 tablets/day).
2nd linePersistent / moderate to severeDimenhydrinate 50-100mg orally or rectally q4-6h; Metoclopramide 10mg IV/orally q8h (avoid >5 days, risk of extrapyramidal effects); Promethazine 12.5-25mg orally/IV/rectally q4-6h.
3rd lineSevere HG / hospitalizedOndansetron 4-8mg IV/orally q8h (preferably from week 10 because of debate about cleft palate); Methylprednisolone 16mg IV/orally q8h x3 days, then taper (restricted to >10 weeks, risk of orofacial cleft).

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG PB 189 (2018, reaffirmed 2021) · RCOG GTG 69 (2016).

4Rehydration and hospital safety

0.9% Normal Saline or Lactated Ringer’s solution.

🚫 Golden safety rule: Thiamine (B1) 100mg IV BEFORE or WITH the first infusion of glucose-containing fluids — never administer dextrose alone to a malnourished patient without prior thiamine (prevents Wernicke encephalopathy/osmotic demyelination).

KCl replacement according to the electrolyte panel.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 189 (2018, reaffirmed 2021) · Koren G. et al. (2002, 2005) — validation of the PUQE scale · RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69 (2016).

grupos.titulo: Labor Progress — Preventing the First Cesarean Delivery
grupos.bajada: Three partograph models (Ministry CLAP, WHO 2020, ACOG 2024) with usage flowcharts, arrest criteria, and prevention of the first cesarean delivery.
grupos.html:
1Active-phase onset — three sources, not combined

SourceActive-phase onsetExpected progression
Ministry CLAP — MSPBS partograph (PAHO/WHO-CLAP)4 cmAlert line (1 cm/h) and action line 4 h later
WHO 2020 — Labour Care Guide5 cmMaximum time per centimeter; no 1 cm/h rule if mother and fetus are well
ACOG 2024 — CPG 8 (ratifies the ACOG/SMFM 2014 consensus)6 cmHours without cervical change, no fixed cm/h

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS · WHO · CLAP · FIGO · Labour Care Guide 2018 · ACOG.

The three sources are shown separately, without merging. The Calculator’s dynamic partograph (Childbirth tab) lets you choose the model: Ministry CLAP (default), WHO 2020 or ACOG 2024. How to use each: cards 9 to 12.

2Key ACOG/SMFM recommendations 2014 (Grade 1B — strong recommendation)

  • Prolonged latent phase (>20h nulliparous, >14h multiparous in the 2014 consensus; ACOG 2024: >16 h in nulliparous patients) should NOT be an indication for cesarean delivery on its own.
  • Slow but progressive active phase (not arrested) should not be an indication for cesarean delivery.
  • Operative vaginal delivery (forceps/vacuum) in the 2nd stage by trained personnel: a reasonable alternative to cesarean delivery — training should be encouraged.
  • Fetal monitoring: appropriate use of CTG categories (ACOG/NICHD classification) to reduce unnecessary cesarean deliveries for suspected fetal compromise, including intrauterine resuscitation measures before cesarean delivery.
  • External cephalic version for breech presentation from 36 0/7 weeks, when there is no contraindication.
  • Elective induction only with a favorable cervix, or after considering the risk of failure if the cervix is unfavorable.
  • Fetal macrosomia: elective cesarean delivery for suspected macrosomia should be limited to an estimated fetal weight ≥ 5000g (or ≥ 4500g if diabetes is present) — do not perform routine cesarean delivery for suspected macrosomia without reaching that threshold (weak recommendation, lower-quality evidence).

3Active-phase arrest (1st stage) — ACOG 2024

Diagnose only if:

  • Dilation ≥ 6 cm, AND
  • Ruptured membranes, AND
  • No cervical progress despite ≥ 4 h of adequate uterine activity (more than 200 MVUs with an intrauterine pressure catheter), or ≥ 6 h of inadequate activity with oxytocin

Source: ACOG CPG 8 (2024). Detail and flowchart in sheet 11.

4Prolonged second stage (pushing) — ACOG 2024

ParityACOG 2024 (current)Traditional definition (no longer current)
NulliparousMore than 3 h of pushing3 h with an epidural · 2 h without an epidural
MultiparousMore than 2 h of pushing2 h with epidural · 1 h without epidural

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG CPG 8 (2024) · ACOG/SMFM Obstetric Care Consensus No. 1 (2014).

Beyond these time limits, ACOG recommends an individualized approach (progress of descent, epidural, occiput posterior position, patient preference) before diagnosing arrest. The traditional definition is shown for historical reference only.

5Ministry CLAP Partograph — MSPBS Paraguay model

ParameterOfficial MSPBS value
Latent phase<4 cm
Active phase / start of the partograph≥4 cm
Expected dilatation≥1 cm/hour
RecordingAbove the alert line from 4 cm; normal progress on or to its left
Alert line → action line4 hours (time to refer, reassess and correct causes)
Upon reaching the action lineFinal assessment and decision on the safest mode of delivery

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS — Standards for Preconception, Prenatal, Labor, Birth and Postpartum Care · WHO partograph, Lancet 1994;343:1399-404 · CLAP/SMR 1577 (2011).

Recording frequency: FHR, contractions and maternal pulse every 30 min · temperature every 2 h · BP every 4 h · at each vaginal examination: dilatation, descent and molding. Amniotomy: not routine; only for abnormal progress.

The manual does not name Friedman: it is cited as the WHO/CLAP partograph (alert/action line, 1994). Sources: MSPBS — Standards for Preconception, Prenatal, Labor, Birth and Postpartum Care · WHO partograph, Lancet 1994;343:1399-404 · CLAP/SMR 1577 (2011).

6WHO 2020 Labour Care Guide

  • Active phase from 5 cm; do not apply the 1 cm/h rule to justify interventions if the mother and fetus are stable.
  • Companion of choice and freedom of position.
  • Vaginal examination every 4 h in uncomplicated active labor.
  • Intermittent auscultation (Pinard/Doppler): every 15-30 min during dilatation, every 5 min or after each contraction during the second stage.
  • Second stage: non-supine positions, spontaneous pushing, perineal protection or warm compresses, restrictive episiotomy.
  • Third stage: oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV, controlled cord traction, cord clamping at 1-3 min.
  • Newborn: skin-to-skin contact for 60-90 min, breastfeeding in the first hour; defer anthropometric measurements, eye prophylaxis and vitamin K; bathing after 24 h.

Practices NOT routinely recommended: enema, pubic shaving, admission pelvimetry, prophylactic IV access in low-risk patients, early amniotomy, oxytocin to shorten labor, routine episiotomy, Kristeller maneuver (prohibited).

Sources: WHO Intrapartum care for a positive childbirth experience (2018) · WHO Labour Care Guide (2020) · FIGO 2019 (third stage, IJGO 145:256-8) · Lalonde A. IJGO 2012;119:84-7.

7Birth positions

RecommendationBenefit
Semi-sitting / obstetric chairLess blood loss and PPH; comfortable for the clinician
Upright / standing with supportMore effective contractions, improved fetal oxygenation
Classic lithotomyFewer perineal lacerations (according to the source)
Seated on a birth stoolMore effective contractions, pain relief
All foursLess perineal trauma, facilitates descent
Supported squattingIncreases pelvic diameters

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Lugones Botell M, Ramírez Bermúdez M. El parto en diferentes posiciones a través de la ciencia, la historia y la cultura. Rev Cubana Obstet Ginecol 2012;38(1):134-45 (cited in the UdeA/UNFPA workshop).

WHO recommends free choice of position, not one mandatory position. Source: Lugones MB. Rev Cubana Obstet Ginecol 2012;38(1) (UdeA workshop).

8Labor pain, analgesia, cord clamping, and bonding

  • Labor pain is physiological; nonpharmacological pain relief: warm water, movement, breathing, massage, and continuous support.
  • In the absence of contraindications, maternal request alone is a sufficient indication for an epidural.
  • Delayed cord clamping (1-3 min): less neonatal anemia and fewer transfusions, improved transition, and placental blood transfer (Edmonds 2013).
  • Skin-to-skin contact: warmth, bonding and attachment, greater breastfeeding success; requires continuous support from the team.

Sources: WHO 2018 · Edmonds P. Midwifery Today 2013;(108):58-62 · UdeA workshop.

9How to use the Ministry CLAP Partograph — flowchart

Admission in labor: vaginal examination, FHR, contractions, vital signs
▼
Cervical dilation of 4 cm or more?
▼
NO — latent phase (2-3 cm)
Do not open the partograph. Ambulation, oral hydration, monitoring of FHR and contractions; reassess according to progress.
YES — open the partograph
Mark the first point (X for dilation) on the alert line; the action line is 4 h to the right.
▼
Record: Every 30 min: FHR, contractions (number and duration in 10 min) and pulse · temperature every 2 h · BP every 4 h · at each vaginal examination: membranes and fluid, molding, dilation (X) and descent (O) · urine at each void.
▼
Where is the dilation curve?
▼
On or to the left of the alert line
Normal progress: continue the plan (ambulation, oral hydration, light meals, position changes).
To the right of the alert line
Assess causes (uterine activity, fetal position, possible cephalopelvic disproportion) and correct them. The 4 h until the action line are for timely referral if birth is not imminent.
On the action line
Final assessment and decision on the safest mode of delivery.
▼
Full dilation → second stage: duration up to 2 h according to the MSPBS guideline.

Admission: cervical dilation of 5 cm or more (active phase)?
▼
NO — latent phase

YES — open the guide
One column per assessment: supportive care, baby, woman, labor, medication, plan.
▼

NO

Cervical dilation of 6 cm or more?
▼
NO — latent phase
Do not apply active-phase criteria. Prolonged latent phase: >16 h (nulliparous women). There is no definition of latent-phase arrest: avoid cesarean delivery for this reason if the mother and fetus are well.
YES — active phase
▼
Are the membranes ruptured?
▼
No: arrest is not diagnosed; consider amniotomy if there is no progress.
Yes: count the time without cervical change.
▼
Adequate contractions

Inadequate contractions with oxytocin
No cervical change for ≥6 h → active-phase arrest.
Inadequate contractions without oxytocin
Consider augmentation before measuring.

ItemWhat ACOG says

fichas.texto: Prolonged latent phase (>20h nulliparous, >14h multiparous in the 2014 consensus; ACOG 2024: >16 h in nulliparous patients) should NOT be an indication for cesarean delivery on its own. Slow but progressive active phase (not arrested) should not be an indication for cesarean delivery. Operative vaginal delivery (forceps/vacuum) in the 2nd stage by trained personnel: a reasonable alternative to cesarean delivery — training should be encouraged. Fetal monitoring: appropriate use of CTG categories (ACOG/NICHD classification) to reduce unnecessary cesarean deliveries for suspected fetal compromise, including intrauterine resuscitation measures before cesarean delivery. External cephalic version for breech presentation from 36 0/7 weeks, when there is no contraindication. Elective induction only with a favorable cervix, or after considering the risk of failure if the cervix is unfavorable. Fetal macrosomia: elective cesarean delivery for suspected macrosomia should be limited to an estimated fetal weight ≥ 5000g (or ≥ 4500g if diabetes is present) — do not perform routine cesarean delivery for suspected macrosomia without reaching that threshold (weak recommendation, lower-quality evidence).

fichas.texto: Active phase from 5 cm; do not apply the 1 cm/h rule to justify interventions if the mother and fetus are stable. Companion of choice and freedom of position. Vaginal examination every 4 h in uncomplicated active labor. Intermittent auscultation (Pinard/Doppler): every 15-30 min during dilatation, every 5 min or after each contraction during the second stage. Second stage: non-supine positions, spontaneous pushing, perineal protection or warm compresses, restrictive episiotomy. Third stage: oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV, controlled cord traction, cord clamping at 1-3 min. Newborn: skin-to-skin contact for 60-90 min, breastfeeding in the first hour; defer anthropometric measurements, eye prophylaxis and vitamin K; bathing after 24 h. Practices NOT routinely recommended: enema, pubic shaving, admission pelvimetry, prophylactic IV access in low-risk patients, early amniotomy, oxytocin to shorten labor, routine episiotomy, Kristeller maneuver (prohibited). Sources: WHO Intrapartum care for a positive childbirth experience (2018) · WHO Labour Care Guide (2020) · FIGO 2019 (third stage, IJGO 145:256-8) · Lalonde A. IJGO 2012;119:84-7.

grupos.nombre: First-Half Pregnancy Hemorrhage — Miscarriage, Ectopic Pregnancy, Cervical Insufficiency/Cerclage
grupos.titulo: First-Half Bleeding — Miscarriage, Ectopic Pregnancy, Cervical Insufficiency/Cerclage
grupos.bajada: Differential diagnosis <20-22 weeks, luteal support, anti-D prophylaxis, and cervical insufficiency with cerclage.
grupos.html:
1Differential diagnosis (<20-22 weeks)

First-half bleeding — conditions and key findings
ConditionBleedingPain / uterine activityInternal osKey findings
Threatened miscarriageScant/moderateMild crampingCLOSEDViability confirmed by ultrasound
Miscarriage in progress/inevitableHeavyProgressive contractionsOPEN ± protruding tissue/PROM—
Incomplete miscarriagePersistent activePartial expulsionPatentUltrasound: heterogeneous endometrial thickness >15mm
Complete miscarriageBleeding stopsPain resolves, complete expulsionClosedHomogeneous endometrial stripe <10-15mm
Missed miscarriageNo active bleedingNo cervical changesClosedRetained embryonic/fetal demise
Ectopic pregnancyDark, scantAdnexal pelvic pain + amenorrhea (triad)—β-hCG above the discriminatory zone >1500-2000 IU/L without an intrauterine gestational sac
Gestational trophoblastic disease / hydatidiform moleWith "bunch of grapes" vesicles——Uterus larger than expected for gestational age, β-hCG >100.000 IU/L, "snowstorm" appearance on ultrasound

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG PB 200 (2018) · NICE NG126 (2019/2023).

2Management of threatened miscarriage

General measures: relative rest, sexual abstinence, avoid repeated vaginal examinations.

Progesterone — CaVeSal recommends: micronized progesterone 400 mg vaginally every 12 h until week 16, even without a history of miscarriage.

Variants: MSPBS 2018 not routinely indicated · NICE NG126 only with ≥1 prior miscarriage (PRISM trial) · in favor: RANZCOG, FOGSI 2024, Cochrane 2018 y Cochrane 2021.

  • Micronized progesterone 400mg vaginally every 12h until week 16.
  • Alternative: Dydrogesterone 40mg orally initially, then 10mg every 8h.

Anti-D prophylaxis: if Rh-negative, unsensitized, with clinically significant bleeding → anti-D immunoglobulin 120-300mcg IM within the first 72h.

3Cervical insufficiency (CI) and cerclage

Definition: inability of the cervix to retain the pregnancy in the absence of contractions/clinical abruption, with painless dilation/effacement in the 2nd trimester (16-24 weeks) → recurrent fetal loss or extreme preterm birth.

Types:

  • History-indicated (prophylactic/elective): ≥2-3 prior unexplained painless 2nd-trimester losses or preterm births. Timing: week 12⁺⁰-14⁺⁶ (after confirming viability and ruling out aneuploidy).
  • Ultrasound-indicated (therapeutic): prior spontaneous preterm birth <34 weeks + cervical length <25mm on transvaginal ultrasound surveillance before week 24.
  • Emergency/rescue: painless dilation with membranes protruding into the vagina/external cervical os between weeks 16-24, without active labor, chorioamnionitis, or placental abruption.

Classification: primary (congenital, malformations, collagen disorders) or secondary (conization, dilations, lacerations). Prophylactic cerclage (based on history), therapeutic cerclage (based on ultrasound), or emergency cerclage (based on physical examination) (Ginecol Obstet Méx 2020).

By history — variants: RCOG GTG 75: ≥3 losses or preterm births in the 2nd trimester; with 1-2, serial ultrasound at 16-24 weeks and cerclage if ≤25 mm. ACOG: may be offered after 1 typical loss.

Short cervix without prior history (≤20 mm): vaginal progesterone; cerclage is not indicated.

Cerclage techniques
TechniqueParticularity
McDonaldSubmucosal purse-string without dissection, nonabsorbable suture (Mersilene); most commonly used
ShirodkarVesicocervical dissection, higher suture placement
Espinosa Flores (Mexico, 1966)Simple transcardinal ligature without mucosal dissection; short procedure and easy removal
Abdominal (Benson-Durfee)By laparotomy or laparoscopy, preconceptionally or at 10-14 weeks, after failed vaginal cerclage or with a very short cervix; delivery by cesarean

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: GPC IMSS 539 · UNAM (Espinosa Flores) · FASGO 2021 · ACOG PB 142.

Contraindications: active labor, intra-amniotic infection, active bleeding, PROM, placental abruption, lethal fetal anomaly, or fetal demise.

Fetal fibronectin: does not diagnose cervical insufficiency; predicts preterm birth in preterm labor (high negative predictive value).

Cerclage removal: scheduled electively at 36-37 weeks (or immediately if active labor/chorioamnionitis).

4Abortion: classification and evacuation

Management according to abortion type
Type<13 weeks13-22 weeks
Threatened miscarriage (incipient)Expectant ± progesterone (see card 2); anti-D if Rh(-)
In progress: imminent (dilated cervix) or inevitable (PROM)MVAExpulsion (oxytocin/misoprostol) + D&C
IncompleteMVA, or misoprostol 600 µg PO / 400 µg SL (WHO); MSPBS: 400-800 µg vaginallyD&C after cervical preparation
CompleteNo evacuation; clinical follow-up
Missed (fetal demise confirmed on ultrasound)Misoprostol 800 µg vaginally every 3 h ×2 or 600 µg SL every 3 h ×2 → MVAMisoprostol 200 µg every 4-6 h up to 5 doses (every 6 h with uterine scar); oxytocin 16-22 wk → D&C

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS 2018 (p. 63) · WHO 2022 · NICE NG126.

Evacuation: WHO recommends aspiration and advises against sharp curettage before 14 weeks; MSPBS uses MVA before 13 and D&C from 13 to 22. The calculator ends at 13 weeks.

5Infected and septic abortion

  • With sepsis or septic shock: IV antibiotics within the 1st hour + immediate evacuation for source control (Code Yellow — Sepsis, Rule 4-5-3; SSC 2021).
  • Without sepsis: IV antibiotics and evacuation 6-8 h after initiation (Clinical Practice Guideline IMSS-088, Ecuador Clinical Practice Guideline). Other guidelines: 12 h or 24-48 h.
  • MSPBS regimens (72 h): ampicillin + metronidazole · cefazolin + metronidazole · ceftriaxone + metronidazole · gentamicin + metronidazole · gentamicin + clindamycin · ampicillin/sulbactam + clindamycin · ampicillin 2 g + gentamicin 5 mg/kg + metronidazole.

6Recurrent pregnancy loss

  • WHO / RCOG GTG 17: 3 consecutive losses.
  • ESHRE 2022 / ASRM: ≥2, not necessarily consecutive.
  • National literature (Acosta, Paraguay): 3 consecutive or 5 nonconsecutive losses.

Management: genetic counseling and gynecologic-obstetric and reproductive evaluation.

7Pregnancy of unknown location and ectopic pregnancy

PUL: do not treat without ultrasound confirmation; βhCG at 48 h with a minimum rise of 49 % (<1500), 40 % (1500-3000) or 33 % (>3000) (AAFP 2020).

Complicated (free fluid, severe pain, instability): emergency surgery + Code Red; salpingectomy is preferred.

Methotrexate follow-up: β-hCG on days 4 and 7; decline ≥15 % → weekly until negative; otherwise, second dose or surgery. Anti-D if Rh(-).

8Hydatidiform mole

Diagnosis: complete (snowstorm appearance, enlarged uterus, very high β-hCG, diploid) vs. partial (fetus, placenta with cysts, triploid). Chest X-ray in all cases.

Treatment: suction evacuation with oxytocin started at the time of aspiration; histopathology in all cases; contraception.

fichas.texto: General measures: relative rest, sexual abstinence, avoid repeated vaginal examinations. Progesterone — CaVeSal recommends: micronized progesterone 400 mg vaginally every 12 h until week 16, even without a history of miscarriage. Variants: MSPBS 2018 not routinely indicated · NICE NG126 only with ≥1 prior miscarriage (PRISM trial) · in favor: RANZCOG, FOGSI 2024, Cochrane 2018 y Cochrane 2021. Micronized progesterone 400mg vaginally every 12h until week 16. Alternative: Dydrogesterone 40mg orally initially, then 10mg every 8h. Anti-D prophylaxis: if Rh-negative, unsensitized, with clinically significant bleeding → anti-D immunoglobulin 120-300mcg IM within the first 72h.

fichas.texto: Definition: inability of the cervix to retain the pregnancy in the absence of contractions/clinical abruption, with painless dilation/effacement in the 2nd trimester (16-24 weeks) → recurrent fetal loss or extreme preterm birth. Types: History-indicated (prophylactic/elective): ≥2-3 prior unexplained painless 2nd-trimester losses or preterm births. Timing: week 12⁺⁰-14⁺⁶ (after confirming viability and ruling out aneuploidy). Ultrasound-indicated (therapeutic): prior spontaneous preterm birth <34 weeks + cervical length <25mm on transvaginal ultrasound surveillance before week 24. Emergency/rescue: painless dilation with membranes protruding into the vagina/external cervical os between weeks 16-24, without active labor, chorioamnionitis, or placental abruption. Classification: primary (congenital, malformations, collagen disorders) or secondary (conization, dilations, lacerations). Prophylactic cerclage (based on history), therapeutic cerclage (based on ultrasound), or emergency cerclage (based on physical examination) (Ginecol Obstet Méx 2020). By history — variants: RCOG GTG 75: ≥3 losses or preterm births in the 2nd trimester; with 1-2, serial ultrasound at 16-24 weeks and cerclage if ≤25 mm. ACOG: may be offered after 1 typical loss. Short cervix without prior history (≤20 mm): vaginal progesterone; cerclage is not indicated. Cerclage techniques Technique Particularity McDonald Submucosal purse-string without dissection, nonabsorbable suture (Mersilene); most commonly used Shirodkar Vesicocervical dissection, higher suture placement Espinosa Flores (Mexico, 1966) Simple transcardinal ligature without mucosal dissection; short procedure and easy removal Abdominal (Benson-Durfee) By laparotomy or laparoscopy, preconceptionally or at 10-14 weeks, after failed vaginal cerclage or with a very short cervix; delivery by cesarean CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: GPC IMSS 539 · UNAM (Espinosa Flores) · FASGO 2021 · ACOG PB 142. Contraindications: active labor, intra-amniotic infection, active bleeding, PROM, placental abruption, lethal fetal anomaly, or fetal demise. Fetal fibronectin: does not diagnose cervical insufficiency; predicts preterm birth in preterm labor (high negative predictive value). Cerclage removal: scheduled electively at 36-37 weeks (or immediately if active labor/chorioamnionitis).

fichas.texto: Management according to abortion type Type <13 weeks 13-22 weeks Threatened miscarriage (incipient) Expectant ± progesterone (see card 2); anti-D if Rh(-) In progress: imminent (dilated cervix) or inevitable (PROM) MVA Expulsion (oxytocin/misoprostol) + D&C Incomplete MVA, or misoprostol 600 µg PO / 400 µg SL (WHO); MSPBS: 400-800 µg vaginally D&C after cervical preparation Complete No evacuation; clinical follow-up Missed (fetal demise confirmed on ultrasound) Misoprostol 800 µg vaginally every 3 h ×2 or 600 µg SL every 3 h ×2 → MVA Misoprostol 200 µg every 4-6 h up to 5 doses (every 6 h with uterine scar); oxytocin 16-22 wk → D&C CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS 2018 (p. 63) · WHO 2022 · NICE NG126. Evacuation: WHO recommends aspiration and advises against sharp curettage before 14 weeks; MSPBS uses MVA before 13 and D&C from 13 to 22. The calculator ends at 13 weeks.

fichas.texto: With sepsis or septic shock: IV antibiotics within the 1st hour + immediate evacuation for source control (Code Yellow — Sepsis, Rule 4-5-3; SSC 2021). MSPBS regimens (72 h): ampicillin + metronidazole · cefazolin + metronidazole · ceftriaxone + metronidazole · gentamicin + metronidazole · gentamicin + clindamycin · ampicillin/sulbactam + clindamycin · ampicillin 2 g + gentamicin 5 mg/kg + metronidazole.
