grupos.nombre: Second-Half Pregnancy Hemorrhage — Placental Abruption, Placenta Previa, Uterine Rupture, Vasa Previa
grupos.titulo: Second-half hemorrhage — placental abruption, placenta previa, uterine rupture, vasa previa
grupos.bajada: Differential diagnosis of the 4 main causes, ACOG/RCOG management, MSPBS/SPGO variant + 2021 Code Red, and emergency protocols.
grupos.html:
1Differential diagnosis of the 4 main causes

CauseBleedingPain / uterine toneFetal statusContext
Placental abruptionDarkSudden, severe abdominal pain, uterine hypertonia/boardlike uterusRapid onset of acute fetal distressCommon with preeclampsia/trauma
Placenta previaBright red, painlessNormal uterine tone (soft uterus)Fetal heart rate initially normalInsidious onset
Uterine ruptureVariableAcute, lacerating intrapartum pain, abrupt cessation of uterine contractionsMaternal shock + extreme fetal bradycardiaHistory of cesarean delivery/myomectomy common; loss of fetal station
Vasa previaImmediately after rupture of membranes, 100% of fetal origin—Bradycardia/severe decelerationsHigh immediate fetal mortality
🚫 DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION IS PROHIBITED if placenta previa is suspected — it may precipitate massive hemorrhage.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG PB 183 (2017) · RCOG GTG 63 · MSPBS/SPGO 2018 · MSPBS Code Red 2022.

2Management of Placenta Previa and Placental Abruption (ACOG/RCOG)

Placenta previa: Diagnosis by transvaginal ultrasound — placenta previa if it covers the internal os; low-lying placenta if <20mm from the internal os.

  • Stable/no active bleeding: fetal lung maturation at 34-36⁺⁶ weeks; elective cesarean delivery at 36⁺⁰-37⁺⁶.
  • Severe active hemorrhage: stabilization + immediate emergency cesarean delivery, regardless of gestational age.

Placental abruption: immediate delivery.

  • Emergency cesarean delivery: general rule if the fetus is alive with compromise or the mother is unstable.
  • Fetal demise: MSPBS recommends cesarean delivery for grades II and III; RCOG GTG 63 and the 2013 Colombian CPG accept vaginal delivery with a stable mother, early amniotomy, and oxytocin (see card 9).

3Paraguayan variant: MSPBS/SPGO + Code Red 2021 (additional variant)

Timing definition: bleeding in the second half of pregnancy = vaginal bleeding from 22.0 weeks until before birth.

Initial stabilization protocol:

  • O2 via non-rebreather mask at 10 L/min, target SpO2 >95%.
  • 2 large-bore peripheral IV lines (14G or 16G).
  • Tube color code: blue (coagulation: PT/aPTT/fibrinogen), red/brown (chemistry), lavender (CBC + crossmatch/blood bank).
  • Warm crystalloids at 37-39°C in 250-500 mL boluses, target SBP ≥90 mmHg while avoiding fluid overload.
  • Check vital signs every 15 min with EAPO + Foley catheter, target urine output ≥30 mL/h.

Expectant management (placenta previa only) — eligibility: GA <34 weeks + scant/self-limited bleeding + stable mother + normal fetal well-being.

  • Strict bed rest in the left lateral position.
  • Lung maturation: Betamethasone 12mg IM every 24h ×2 doses or dexamethasone 6mg IM every 12h ×4 doses (if <34 weeks).
  • Neuroprotection with MgSO4 if preterm labor is threatened at <32 weeks.
  • Serial CBCs + strict monitoring of blood loss.

Indications for emergency cesarean delivery (regardless of GA): active moderate-to-severe bleeding unresponsive to conservative measures; hemodynamic instability/shock; acute fetal distress; confirmed placental abruption or uterine rupture/strong suspicion; complete placenta previa at term ≥37.0 weeks.

ACOG/RCOG vs. MSPyBS/SPGO comparison
PointACOG/RCOGMSPyBS/SPGO
Elective cesarean delivery for stable placenta previa36⁺⁰-37⁺⁶ weeks≥37.0 weeks (at term)
Temporal definition of the condition>20-22 weeks≥22.0 exact weeks

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS/SPGO · Code Red 2021 · ACOG · RCOG · SPGO.

4Uterine rupture: immediate management

  1. Activate the obstetric emergency team + notify the obstetrician on call.
  2. Left lateral position + supplemental oxygen by face mask; stop oxytocin infusion if running.
  3. 2 large-bore IV lines (16G), samples for CBC + coagulation studies + crossmatch for 6 units.
  4. Crystalloids/blood products as needed; continuous monitoring of vital signs + CTG.
  5. Prepare the operating room for emergency cesarean delivery — birth within 30 minutes of the decision (Category 1), anticipating neonatal resuscitation.
  6. In hemodynamic instability: fluid resuscitation/transfusion in parallel with surgical preparation, without waiting for complete stabilization before operating.

5Uterine rupture: intraoperative surgical management

Incision: Pfannenstiel incision provides good exposure of the lower uterine segment/pelvis; a vertical midline incision provides better exposure for exploring the entire abdominal cavity (including the uterine fundus)—preferred when fetal distress and maternal instability coexist.

Repair vs. hysterectomy: depends on the extent of the injury, patient stability, desire for future fertility, and surgeon experience — if adequate closure and hemostasis cannot be achieved → hysterectomy (usually subtotal).

Complications to manage: concomitant uterine atony (uterotonics + hemostatic sutures + intrauterine balloon); bladder injury if the laceration extends to the bladder, or suspected ureteral injury → consult urology.

Hemorrhage control after delivery if bleeding persists: abdominal packing, uterine artery ligation, internal iliac artery ligation, topical hemostatic agents, cesarean hysterectomy as a last resort.

General anesthesia is usual; regional/spinal anesthesia is contraindicated in cases of severe bleeding diathesis.

6Vasa previa: management

Antenatal diagnosis by ultrasound (color Doppler along the cervical route) allows elective cesarean delivery to be scheduled before the onset of labor — fetal survival >95% with antenatal diagnosis + planned cesarean delivery, vs. fetal mortality ≥60% when diagnosed intrapartum.

  • Timing of elective cesarean delivery: SMFM Consult Series #37 recommends scheduled cesarean delivery between 34⁺⁰ and 37⁺⁶ weeks (GRADE 2C).
  • Antenatal corticosteroids: consider between 28-32 weeks if there is a risk of urgent preterm delivery (GRADE 2C), not routinely in asymptomatic patients; a 2023 review suggests administering them within the 7 days before scheduled delivery.
  • Antenatal hospitalization: proposed from 30-34 weeks in some series (GRADE 2C), but evidence is insufficient to make it a mandatory standard — individualized decision.
🚫 Undiagnosed vasa previa: high risk of rupture when membranes rupture — immediate emergency cesarean delivery in the event of bleeding + bradycardia/acute deceleration after amniotomy.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: SMFM.

7Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS)

FIGO 2019 clinical classification
GradeIntraoperative finding
1Adherent placenta (creta): no myometrial invasion
2Increta: myometrial invasion, without reaching the serosa
3aPercreta limited to the uterine serosa
3bPercreta with bladder invasion
3cPercreta with invasion of other pelvic tissues or organs
Risk of placenta accreta spectrum with placenta previa according to number of cesarean deliveries (Silver 2006)
Cesarean delivery1ª2ª3ª4ª≥5ª
Risk of PAS3%11%40%61%67%

Without placenta previa, risk ranges from 0.24% to 6.74% according to the number of cesarean deliveries.

Ultrasound signs (ISUOG 2016): loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, myometrial thinning <1 mm, disruption of the bladder line, placental bulge, focal exophytic mass; Doppler: uterovesical or subplacental hypervascularity and bridging vessels.

Timing of scheduled cesarean delivery
SourceWindow
ACOG/SMFM Obstetric Care Consensus No. 7 (2018)34+0 to 35+6 weeks
RCOG Green-top 27b (2018)35+0 to 36+6 weeks

Management: level III-IV center with a multidisciplinary team and blood bank; corticosteroids if <37 weeks; tranexamic acid at onset; uterine incision away from the placenta and cesarean hysterectomy with the placenta in situ (do not attempt placental separation). Activate Code Red in the event of bleeding.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Jauniaux E et al. FIGO classification, Int J Gynaecol Obstet 2019 · FIGO — Classification of PAS disorders · Silver RM et al. Obstet Gynecol 2006;107:1226-32 · ACOG/SMFM OCC No. 7 · RCOG GTG 27b · ISUOG/EW-AIP 2016.

8Placenta previa — MSPBS details

  • Classification: complete, partial, marginal, lateral (>2 cm from the internal os). Definitive diagnosis from 32 weeks.
  • Expectant management <34+0 weeks with mild bleeding; from 34+0, cesarean delivery with recurrent bleeding. MSPBS mentions 35 weeks in one chapter; CaVeSal uses 34+0 for consistency.
  • Asymptomatic complete previa: admission at 36 and cesarean at 37 (ACOG/SMFM: 36+0-37+6).
  • Marginal previa in labor: amniotomy and trial of vaginal birth with the operating room ready; lateral previa: vaginal delivery may be possible.
  • Tocolysis (hybrid): nifedipine only with preterm labor, light bleeding, and stability; avoid with heavy bleeding, instability, or fetal compromise (RCOG GTG 63).
  • Prior cesarean: rule out placenta accreta (calculation in the CaVeSal prenatal calculator).

9Placental abruption — grades and management

Grades (MSPBS) and management
GradeFindingsManagement
I<11 %, normal FHR<34 weeks: monitored expectant management + antenatal corticosteroids; ≥34: delivery
II~50 %, uterine hypertonus, fetal compromiseEmergency cesarean delivery
III>50 %, tetany, fetal death, shock, DICCesarean delivery (MSPBS) + correction of coagulopathy

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS 2018 (p. 83).

  • Fetal death — expectant management: RCOG GTG 63, Colombia CPG 2013 y Universidad Nacional de Colombia: vaginal delivery if the mother is stable, with early amniotomy and oxytocin.
  • Tocolysis: optional in mild abruption <34 weeks with a stable mother and no fetal compromise, at the discretion of the senior obstetrician, to complete fetal maturation (observational studies).
  • ≥34 weeks in advanced labor: vaginal delivery may be possible with amniotomy and continuous monitoring (NHS Worcestershire).

10Impending uterine rupture

Signs of impending rupture
SignDescription
BandlPathological retraction ring rising toward the umbilicus (hourglass uterus)
FrommelTaut round ligaments, palpable like cords
PinardScant, dark vaginal bleeding (Paraguayan and classical literature); some sources describe it as cervical edema
OtherUterine hyperactivity (oxytocin/misoprostol), hematuria, abnormal FHR

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Clínica Universidad de Navarra · Medway.

Impending: discontinue uterotonics, initiate acute uterine inhibition, and perform urgent cesarean delivery. Established: laparotomy; uterine repair if the rupture is not extensive and the patient is stable, hysterectomy if irreparable; evaluate the bladder if hematuria occurred.

11PAS and vasa previa — timing and conservative management

Timing of delivery
TableMSPBSACOG/SMFMFIGO/RCOG
SBPHospitalization at 32 weeks; delivery at 36-3734+0-35+635+0-36+6
Vasa previa—34+0-37+0; hospitalization at 30-34 individualized—

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS 2018 · ACOG/SMFM · SMFM CS 44 · FIGO 2018.

  • Planned PAS: TXA 1 g, incision away from the placenta, no traction or uterotonics, cesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ.
  • Conservative (focal, in centers with experience): placenta in situ, one-stage resection, arterial embolization (FIGO 2018 conservative management). MSPBS includes methotrexate; FIGO does not recommend it. Prophylactic iliac balloons: not routinely.
  • Vasa previa with bleeding after PROM or a sinusoidal pattern: immediate cesarean delivery.

(2021) · Queenan, Spong, Lockwood — Protocols for High-Risk Pregnancies, 7th ed. (2021) · RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 27b — Vasa Praevia · SMFM Consult Series #37 (Sinkey, Odibo, Dashe, Am J Obstet Gynecol 2015;213:615-619).

Repair vs. hysterectomy: depends on the extent of the injury, patient stability, desire for future fertility, and surgeon experience — if adequate closure and hemostasis cannot be achieved → hysterectomy (usually subtotal). Complications to manage: concomitant uterine atony (uterotonics + hemostatic sutures + intrauterine balloon); bladder injury if the laceration extends to the bladder, or suspected ureteral injury → consult urology. Hemorrhage control after delivery if bleeding persists: abdominal packing, uterine artery ligation, internal iliac artery ligation, topical hemostatic agents, cesarean hysterectomy as a last resort. General anesthesia is usual; regional/spinal anesthesia is contraindicated in cases of severe bleeding diathesis.

fichas.texto: Antenatal diagnosis by ultrasound (color Doppler along the cervical route) allows elective cesarean delivery to be scheduled before the onset of labor — fetal survival >95% with antenatal diagnosis + planned cesarean delivery, vs. fetal mortality ≥60% when diagnosed intrapartum. Timing of elective cesarean delivery: SMFM Consult Series #37 recommends scheduled cesarean delivery between 34⁺⁰ and 37⁺⁶ weeks (GRADE 2C). Antenatal corticosteroids: consider between 28-32 weeks if there is a risk of urgent preterm delivery (GRADE 2C), not routinely in asymptomatic patients; a 2023 review suggests administering them within the 7 days before scheduled delivery. Antenatal hospitalization: proposed from 30-34 weeks in some series (GRADE 2C), but evidence is insufficient to make it a mandatory standard — individualized decision. 🚫 Undiagnosed vasa previa: high risk of rupture when membranes rupture — immediate emergency cesarean delivery in the event of bleeding + bradycardia/acute deceleration after amniotomy. fichas.texto: Classification: complete, partial, marginal, lateral (>2 cm from the internal os). Definitive diagnosis from 32 weeks. Expectant management <34+0 weeks with mild bleeding; from 34+0, cesarean delivery with recurrent bleeding. MSPBS mentions 35 weeks in one chapter; CaVeSal uses 34+0 for consistency. Asymptomatic complete previa: admission at 36 and cesarean at 37 (ACOG/SMFM: 36+0-37+6). Marginal previa in labor: amniotomy and trial of vaginal birth with the operating room ready; lateral previa: vaginal delivery may be possible. Tocolysis (hybrid): nifedipine only with preterm labor, light bleeding, and stability; avoid with heavy bleeding, instability, or fetal compromise (RCOG GTG 63). Prior cesarean: rule out placenta accreta (calculation in the CaVeSal prenatal calculator).

Fetal death — expectant management: RCOG GTG 63, Colombia CPG 2013 y Universidad Nacional de Colombia: vaginal delivery if the mother is stable, with early amniotomy and oxytocin. Tocolysis: optional in mild abruption <34 weeks with a stable mother and no fetal compromise, at the discretion of the senior obstetrician, to complete fetal maturation (observational studies). ≥34 weeks in advanced labor: vaginal delivery may be possible with amniotomy and continuous monitoring (NHS Worcestershire).

Impending: discontinue uterotonics, initiate acute uterine inhibition, and perform urgent cesarean delivery. Established: laparotomy; uterine repair if the rupture is not extensive and the patient is stable, hysterectomy if irreparable; evaluate the bladder if hematuria occurred.

grupos.bajada: Chronological classification, third stage of labor (Schultze and Duncan, timing), monitoring during the first 2 hours, uterine involution, lochia, and maternal supplementation.
grupos.html:
1Chronological classification

  • Immediate (first 24h): highest risk of PPH/4Ts — monitor vital signs, uterine tone (Pinard’s safety globe) and bleeding every 15 min for the first 2 h (MSPBS), then every 6 h — see flowchart in sheet 5.
  • Early (day 2 to 7-10): onset of lactogenesis II, progressive intra-pelvic uterine involution (~1cm/day), red/serous lochia.
  • Late (day 11 to 42/6 weeks): return of the genital organs to the pre-pregnancy state, resolution of lochia (alba), resumption of ovulation if not exclusively breastfeeding.

2Clinical checks and care

Uterine involution: the uterine fundus should not be palpable above the pubic symphysis from postpartum day 10-12.

Lochia — chronological progression
TypeDaysCharacteristics
Red / bloody1-3/4Blood + decidual remnants
Serous4-10Pink/brown, exudate + leukocytes
White / alba10-28/42Whitish/yellowish, mucus + epithelial cells
⚠️ Warning sign: foul odor (suspected puerperal endometritis) or persistent heavy bloody lochia after day 14 (suspected retained placental tissue/subinvolution).

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: WHO 2022 (postnatal care) · ACOG CO 736 (2018).

Perineal/surgical wound care: wash with water and mild soap, pat dry, monitor for infection/dehiscence of episiotomy repair or cesarean incision.

4Third stage of labor — placental delivery

Definition (MSPBS): from the birth of the newborn until expulsion of the placenta. A period with potential risk of hemorrhage.

Phases (third-stage ultrasound)
PhaseWhat happensMedian duration
LatentFrom birth until the onset of placental separation; myometrial-placental blood flow ceases. This phase determines the total duration~2 min (5 s – 13 min)
SeparationThe placenta separates from the myometrium~50 s
ExpulsionFrom complete separation to passage through the vagina~80 s

Signs of placental separation: lengthening of the cord · sudden gush of blood · the uterus rises and becomes globular (Schröder) · the cord does not retract with suprapubic pressure (Küstner). Both signs were positive in 98 % of placentas with ultrasound-confirmed separation.

Mechanisms of placental expulsion
MechanismHow it is expelledFrequency and implications
SchultzeCentral separation, expelled like an inverted umbrella: fetal surface first; the clot remains within the membranes~80 % · less visible bleeding before expulsion
DuncanSeparation from the edge, expelled sideways: maternal surface first~20 % · more bleeding and risk of retained membranes: inspect carefully

Ultrasound shows that separation usually begins at the lower pole; the observed mechanism is determined as the placenta exits through the vulva.

Birth — oxytocin 10 IU IM within the first minute (after ruling out a second fetus)
▼
Controlled cord traction with a contraction and suprapubic counterpressure, only with signs of placental separation
▼
Placenta delivered at 15 min and no PPH?
▼
YES
Check placental and membrane integrity · uterine massage · checks every 15 min for 2 h
NO
Controlled cord traction, mobilize or squat, empty the bladder. Monitor bleeding
▼
30 min without delivery → prepare for manual removal with analgesia and antibiotic prophylaxis · with PPH at any time → uterotonic + manual removal without waiting, Code Red
Third-stage duration — variations
SourceCriterionStatus
WHO/FIGO/ICM 2025 (rec. 30)Without PPH: intervene at 15 min; at 30 min, prepare for manual removal. With PPH: uterotonic and removalUsed by the calculator
NICE NG235 (1.10.20)Prolonged: >30 min with active management; >60 min with physiological managementVariant
MSPBS 2022Active management: oxytocin 10 IU IM <1 min, controlled cord traction, massage; no routine intrauterine examinationNational guideline

CaVeSal® original table · Based on: MSPBS, Normas de Cuidados 2022, p. 69 · WHO/FIGO/ICM 2025, rec. 16, 30 and 31 · NICE NG235 (2023) · Herman et al., ultrasound and clinical findings in the third stage · El-Mowafi, GFMER — Schultze 80 % / Duncan 20 %. Third-stage timer in the calculator →

5Immediate postpartum period — first 2 hours and beyond

Placenta delivered — uterine massage, examination of the birth canal, and repair of lacerations
▼
First 2 h, in the delivery room or recovery area — every 15 min: contracted uterus and Pinard safety globe (massage if needed) · measured blood loss · HR and BP · EAPO
▼
Blood loss ≥300 mL with HR >100, shock index >1, SBP <100 or DBP <60, or ≥500 mL, or EAPO alert?
▼
YES
Postpartum hemorrhage: MOTIVE and Code Red. Do not transfer until stabilized
NO at 2 h
Mother and newborn to the inpatient ward (no bleeding, no infection, normal vital signs, nonhemorrhagic, non-foul-smelling lochia)
▼
Then every 6 h: vital signs · Pinard safety globe · lochia · vulvoperineal abnormalities (hematomas, urinary retention) · lower extremities · bodily functions (urination, bowel movements) · emotional status (Edinburgh)
▼
Discharge from 48 h no hemorrhage, no infection, and normal vital signs · follow-up at 8 days
Postpartum monitoring — variations
SourceFrequency and parametersLength of stay
MSPBS 2022Every 15 min for 2 h (uterus, Pinard, EAPO); then every 6 hDischarge from 48 h onward
WHO 2018 (rec. 52 and 55)Uterine tone in all women; routine assessment of bleeding, uterine contraction, fundal height, temperature, and pulse during the first 24 h, starting in the first hour; BP shortly after birth and, if normal, again within 6 h; documented urination within 6 hMinimum 24 h after uncomplicated vaginal birth (rec. 56)
WHO/FIGO/ICM 2025 (rec. 22)PPH criterion within 24 h, with special monitoring during the first 2 h—

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS, Normas de Cuidados 2022, pp. 69-71 · WHO 2018, intrapartum care, rec. 52, 55 and 56 · WHO/FIGO/ICM 2025, rec. 22. Dynamic 2 h monitoring in the calculator →

6Maternal supplementation during the postpartum period/lactation

SupplementDoseNotes
Elemental iron60-100mg/day POAt least 3 months postpartum — especially in cases of peripartum blood loss or Hb<11g/dL
Folic acid400mcg/day POTogether with iron
Calcium1000-1200mg/dayDiet or supplement if dairy intake is inadequate
Iodine150-200mcg/day—
Vitamin D600-1000 IU/dayMaternal

grupos.bajada: Physiology, diagnosis, and stepwise decision tree for mastitis, breast abscess, and drainage techniques.
grupos.html:
1Physiology and basic technique

Hormonal axis: prolactin (production through suckling) + oxytocin (milk ejection through myoepithelial contraction).

Correct latch: mouth wide open, lower lip everted, covering most of the lower areola, chin against the breast, nose unobstructed.

Physiological breast engorgement: manually express a few drops beforehand to soften the areola, frequent on-demand feeds, brief warm compresses before feeding + local cold after feeding.

2Diagnosis of postpartum mastitis

Etiology: milk stasis + bacterial superinfection; most common pathogen Staphylococcus aureus (and S. epidermidis).

Clinical presentation: severe unilateral breast pain, wedge-shaped/well-demarcated erythema, local warmth, induration, fever ≥38.5°C, flu-like symptoms.

3Management decision tree

  1. Initial management (ALL cases):
    • NEVER stop breastfeeding — frequent and effective emptying of the affected breast is the mainstay; breast milk poses no infectious risk to a term infant.
    • Warm compresses before feeding + cold after feeding.
    • Analgesia: Ibuprofen 400-600mg orally every 8h or acetaminophen 500-1000mg orally every 6-8h.
    • Maternal hydration and rest.
  2. Reassess at 12-24h — start antibiotics ONLY IF there are systemic symptoms (fever >38.5°C, chills, myalgia) OR there is no clinical improvement after 12-24h of optimized nonpharmacological management.
  3. Antibiotic regimen (10-14 days) if the above criterion is met:
    ScenarioMedications and doses
    1st line (methicillin-susceptible, outpatient)Cephalexin 500mg orally every 6h; Cloxacillin/Dicloxacillin 500mg orally every 6h; Amoxicillin + Clavulanic acid 875/125mg orally every 8-12h
    Penicillin/beta-lactam allergyClindamycin 300mg orally every 6h; Erythromycin 500mg orally every 6h
    Suspected MRSATrimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800mg orally every 12h (avoid if infant is <1 month old with jaundice) or IV vancomycin if hospitalization is required

    CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ABM Clinical Protocol #36 (2022) · WHO — Mastitis.

4Breast abscess: suspicion and ultrasound diagnosis

Clinical suspicion: persistent painful fluctuant mass with erythema that does not resolve after 48-72h of antibiotics.

Criteria for referral to the emergency department/surgery:

  • Treatment failure (persistence/worsening after 48-72h of appropriate antibiotics + effective milk drainage).
  • Signs of a collection (fluctuant mass, induration, overlying skin thinned/shiny).
  • Severe systemic involvement (refractory fever >38.5°C, tachycardia, hypotension, marked leukocytosis, suspected sepsis/SIRS).
  • Local complications (ischemia, skin necrosis, rapid spread of erythema, suspected granulomatous mastitis/inflammatory breast cancer — oncologic red flag).
  • Technical difficulty (image-guided percutaneous drainage not feasible at the facility).

Ultrasound diagnosis (gold standard): hypoechoic/anechoic collection, irregular/microlobulated margins, thickened wall with Doppler hypervascularity; heterogeneous contents with mobile internal echoes, septa, sometimes fluid-fluid levels or gas bubbles; posterior acoustic enhancement; color Doppler shows no flow in the center with increased peripheral vascularity (inflammatory halo); perilesional edema.

5Stepwise drainage techniques

  1. Ultrasound-guided fine-/large-bore needle aspiration (first line): collections <3-5cm, intact skin without necrosis. 16G-18G needle + 10-20mL syringe under ultrasound guidance, complete aspiration + saline irrigation. May be repeated every 48-72h if recurrence (success rate >85-90%). Always send for culture (aerobes, anaerobes, susceptibility testing).
  2. Percutaneous catheter drainage: abscesses ≥3-5cm or rapid recurrence after simple aspiration. Ultrasound-guided 8-12Fr pigtail catheter, daily irrigation, removal when output is <10-15mL/24h and the cavity has collapsed.
  3. Open surgical incision and drainage: failure of percutaneous drainage/repeated aspiration, extensive multiloculated abscesses, or skin compromise with necrosis/ischemia. Curvilinear incision respecting Langer’s lines (or periareolar), gentle digital debridement, irrigation + passive drainage (Penrose drain or iodoform gauze) for healing by secondary intention.

6Breastfeeding during abscess treatment

Do not stop breastfeeding; continue emptying the affected breast.

  • If the infant’s mouth does NOT come into direct contact with the wound/drain/infected area → direct breastfeeding is safe.
  • If the incision/drainage involves the areola or nipple → express milk mechanically/by hand; breastfeed from the unaffected breast while visible pus contamination persists.

Sources: Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine (ABM) Clinical Protocol #36 — The Mastitis Spectrum (revised 2022) · WHO — Mastitis: Causes and Management · ABM Clinical Protocol #4 (PMC 2014).

fichas.titulo: Breast abscess: suspicion and ultrasound diagnosis
fichas.texto: Clinical suspicion: persistent painful fluctuant mass with erythema that does not resolve after 48-72h of antibiotics. Criteria for referral to the emergency department/surgery: Treatment failure (persistence/worsening after 48-72h of appropriate antibiotics + effective milk drainage). Signs of a collection (fluctuant mass, induration, overlying skin thinned/shiny). Severe systemic involvement (refractory fever >38.5°C, tachycardia, hypotension, marked leukocytosis, suspected sepsis/SIRS). Local complications (ischemia, skin necrosis, rapid spread of erythema, suspected granulomatous mastitis/inflammatory breast cancer — oncologic red flag). Technical difficulty (image-guided percutaneous drainage not feasible at the facility). Ultrasound diagnosis (gold standard): hypoechoic/anechoic collection, irregular/microlobulated margins, thickened wall with Doppler hypervascularity; heterogeneous contents with mobile internal echoes, septa, sometimes fluid-fluid levels or gas bubbles; posterior acoustic enhancement; color Doppler shows no flow in the center with increased peripheral vascularity (inflammatory halo); perilesional edema.
fichas.fuentes: Sources: Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine (ABM) Clinical Protocol #36 — The Mastitis Spectrum (revised 2022) · WHO — Mastitis: Causes and Management · ABM Clinical Protocol #4 (PMC 2014).

fichas.texto: Ultrasound-guided fine-/large-bore needle aspiration (first line): collections <3-5cm, intact skin without necrosis. 16G-18G needle + 10-20mL syringe under ultrasound guidance, complete aspiration + saline irrigation. May be repeated every 48-72h if recurrence (success rate >85-90%). Always send for culture (aerobes, anaerobes, susceptibility testing). Percutaneous catheter drainage: abscesses ≥3-5cm or rapid recurrence after simple aspiration. Ultrasound-guided 8-12Fr pigtail catheter, daily irrigation, removal when output is <10-15mL/24h and the cavity has collapsed. Open surgical incision and drainage: failure of percutaneous drainage/repeated aspiration, extensive multiloculated abscesses, or skin compromise with necrosis/ischemia. Curvilinear incision respecting Langer’s lines (or periareolar), gentle digital debridement, irrigation + passive drainage (Penrose drain or iodoform gauze) for healing by secondary intention.
fichas.fuentes: Sources: Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine (ABM) Clinical Protocol #36 — The Mastitis Spectrum (revised 2022) · WHO — Mastitis: Causes and Management · ABM Clinical Protocol #4 (PMC 2014).

fichas.texto: Do not stop breastfeeding; continue emptying the affected breast. If the infant’s mouth does NOT come into direct contact with the wound/drain/infected area → direct breastfeeding is safe. If the incision/drainage involves the areola or nipple → express milk mechanically/by hand; breastfeed from the unaffected breast while visible pus contamination persists.
fichas.fuentes: Sources: Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine (ABM) Clinical Protocol #36 — The Mastitis Spectrum (revised 2022) · WHO — Mastitis: Causes and Management · ABM Clinical Protocol #4 (PMC 2014).

1Quick access: 3 basic steps by code

MSPBS/DGPS operational summary — details for each code are in its tab
Root causeStep 1Step 2Step 3Step 4
Severe hemorrhage / hypovolemic shockFluid resuscitationControl the hemorrhageEtiologic treatment—
Severe hypertensive disordersFluid resuscitationAnticonvulsantAntihypertensive—
Severe obstetric infectionsFluid resuscitationAntibioticAntipyreticRemove the septic focus

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS/DGPS Paraguay, “Time is life” (ICT model, training material) · MSPBS Maternal and Neonatal Code Red Guide, 2nd ed. (2021).

2“Time is life”: survival curve and 3 delays

Survival by time to treatment
TimingSurvival
Time zero (identify)100%
1-20 min (stabilize)~60%
20-60 min (treat/transfer)<15%
>60 min<10%

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Cresswell et al., Lancet Glob Health 2025 · WHO, Trends in Maternal Mortality 2000-2023

  • Delay 1: in seeking help.
  • Delay 2: in reaching care.
  • Delay 3: in receiving appropriate treatment.
  • They correspond to delays in identifying, stabilizing and treating/transferring, each associated with declining survival.
  • Pathophysiology: hypovolemic shock with DIC and peripheral redistribution (cardiothoracic due to sympathetic activity; peripheral due to parasympathetic activity).

Global context: causes of maternal death — hemorrhage ~27%, hypertensive disorders ~14%, sepsis ~11% (Cresswell et al., Lancet Glob Health 2025). In 2023, there were ~260,000 maternal deaths (≈1 every 2 minutes), global MMR 197/100,000 live births, 40% lower than in 2000 (WHO, Trends in Maternal Mortality 2000-2023).

Three-delays model: Thaddeus & Maine 1994. Official graphic version, MSPBS/DGPS Paraguay.

3ICT — Stage 1: Identify

  • Apply the Early Obstetric Warning Score (EAPO) and start the timer.
  • Look for signs of MODS (multiple organ dysfunction syndrome): severe, acquired functional abnormality of at least 2 organ systems; an early detection criterion for extreme maternal morbidity/near-miss.
  • Determine the cause: hemorrhage (4 Ts), severe hypertensive disorder, or infection.

Definition of MODS adopted from the Latin American obstetric literature (Rev Méd IMSS).

4ICT — Stage 2: Stabilize (basic care)

5 basic steps: call for help · 2 peripheral IV lines · oxygen therapy · urinary catheterization · prevent hypothermia.

Detailed version (8 steps):

  1. Call for help.
  2. Ensure airway patency.
  3. Administer oxygen.
  4. Insert 2 intravenous catheters, No. 14, 16, or 18 gauge.
  5. Parenteral hydration with normal saline: maintain systolic BP >90 mmHg and urine output >30 mL/h (or >0.5 mL/kg/h); in hypertension, maintain diastolic BP >90 mmHg.
  6. Urinary catheter and urine output monitoring.
  7. Cover with a blanket to prevent hypothermia.
  8. Monitor vital signs using the Code Red Alert Scale every 5-10 min.

Urine output target: >0.5 mL/kg/h (international clinical standard, WHO/StatPearls) or >30 mL/h (MSPBS/DGPS); both are shown with their source.

5Response to the initial crystalloid bolus (500 mL boluses)

ATLS classification adapted to obstetrics (Plaat)
ResponseClinical findings% blood loss / volumeTransfusion requirement
RapidReturns to normal10-25% or 500-1500 mL (compensated/mild shock)Transfusion unlikely; type-compatible blood with crossmatch testing (45-60 min)
TransientRecurrent hypotension (SBP <90), impaired mental status, weak radial pulse, tachycardia26-40% or 1500-2000 mL (moderate shock)Likely: emergency packed red blood cell package, 2 units PRBCs, or emergency transfusion package, 4 units PRBCs / 6 units FFP / 6 units platelets, ABO-compatible
No responseAbnormal parameters or targets not achieved at any time>40% or >2000 mL (severe shock)Immediate: group-specific packed red blood cells without crossmatch (15 min), or O-/O+ if unavailable; O-/O+ FFP; O Rh-compatible platelets

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ATLS · Plaat F (classification adapted to obstetrics) · WHO 2025.

Intervention according to response: sustained improvement → no further intervention; partial improvement → fluid challenges; no improvement → blood products + surgery; no response → immediate surgical control.

Do not administer predetermined 1-2 L fluid loads or use replacement formulas. IV isotonic crystalloid boluses of 500 mL at 39 °C; assess radial pulse and mental status. Isotonic crystalloids over colloids (WHO 2025, Rec. 28).

6ICT — Stage 3: Treat/Transfer. Control bleeding by Tone (sequence 1-5)

  1. Continuous external uterine massage throughout management, until bleeding stops.
  2. Bimanual massage for ≥20 min or until bleeding stops if external massage is ineffective; additional uterotonics, Pinard safety balloon, and tranexamic acid.
  3. Continue bimanual compression until bleeding stops (no bleeding when compression is released and uterus is contracted).
  4. Abdominal aortic compression: closed fist (thumb out), pressing downward just above the umbilicus and slightly to the left.
  5. Immediate surgical intervention if uterine tone is not restored: B-Lynch compression suture or obstetric hysterectomy.

Technique consistent with WHO, Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth, 2nd ed. 2017.

7Oxytocin for atony (microdrip) and ergometrine as second-line treatment

  • Oxytocin IM: 10 IU if no IV line is in place.
  • Oxytocin IV: 5 IU slowly over 5 min; may be repeated after 5 min up to a maximum of 10 IU.
  • IV maintenance: 20 IU in 500 cc of normal saline over 4 h (80 mIU/min = 42 drops/min = 126 cc/h by pump).
  • Misoprostol 800 µg SL as a 3rd option if oxytocin or ergonovine is unavailable.
Ergometrine / methylergonovine 0.2 mg: three evidence-based variants
VariantInterval to 2nd doseContinuationMaximum
WHO (2012 / MCPC 2017) — IM or slow IV15 min0.2 mg every 4 h5 doses (1 mg) in 24 h
FIGO 2022 / ACOG / FDA — IM or slow IVNo intermediate dose0.2 mg every 2-4 h5 doses (1 mg) in 24 h
Regional adaptation for Latin America (Colombia/Peru/Panama) — IM20 min (one additional dose only)0.2 mg every 4-6 h5 ampoules in 24 h

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: WHO · FIGO 2022 · ACOG.

Contraindicated in hypertension, preeclampsia/eclampsia, and heart disease. Indicated if oxytocin is unavailable or the response is insufficient after 30 min.

8Uterine inversion and surgical hierarchy

Antibiotic prophylaxis after correction (single dose, together with oxytocin to prevent recurrence):

  • Ampicillin 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV, or
  • Cefazolin 1 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV (penicillin allergy).

Vascular ligation: bilateral uterine artery ligation (O'Leary) is the first-choice conservative surgical option (simpler, faster, immediate efficacy ~80-90%); internal iliac artery ligation is more complex (ureteral/venous risk, efficacy ~65-70%) and is reserved for failure of the former. Variants: Posadas technique (posterior selective devascularization of the uterine and internal tubal arteries, Series of 750 cases) and Tsirulnikov (triple ligation of the round ligaments, utero-ovarian and uterine arteries). Vaginal bridge: Zea technique (INPer — Zea technique).

The hierarchy reflects technical ease and risk profile, not absolute superiority in efficacy (FIGO/WHO).

9Hemostatic resuscitation

  • 1:1:1 ratio — RBCs 6 U : FFP 6 U : 1 apheresis unit (or 6 U) of platelets.
  • Cryoprecipitate 10-20 units.
  • Fibrinogen concentrate 2 g.
  • Tranexamic acid 1 g.
  • Fibrinogen <2 g/L: independent risk factor for massive PPH, OR 12.0 (95% CI 2.6-56.1) (Cortet et al., Br J Anaesth 2012); between 2 and 3 g/L, OR 1.90 (1.16-3.09).

Supporting reviews: Butwick, Int J Obstet Anesth 2013;22:87-91 · Pacheco et al., AJOG 2011;205(6):526-532.

Expected tasks per 30-minute block
BlockObstetricianAnesthesiologist
0-30 minDiagnosis using the 4 Ts, uterine massage, medical managementMonitoring, labs, 2 IV lines, fluid boluses
30-60 minBalloon tamponade, non-pneumatic antishock garment, hemostatic suturesInvasive monitoring, transfusion, vasopressors
60-90 minHysterectomy, damage controlMassive transfusion, coagulation factors

11Primary xABCDE survey adapted for the pregnant patient

Assess and treat in order; if the patient deteriorates, return to “x”. Tasks are carried out simultaneously by team members.

xABCDE (ATLS 11th ed., 2025) with pregnancy-specific adjustments
StepWhat to assess/doAdjustment in the pregnant patient
x Exsanguinating hemorrhageMassive, compressible external bleeding: direct pressure, packing, tourniquet if involving an extremity (record the time)For obstetric bleeding: activate Code Red and follow the sequence for control by Tone (card 6)
A AirwayPatency; cervical spine protection if trauma occurredConsider earlier intubation: the pregnant patient desaturates faster. Higher risk of failed intubation: it should be performed by the most experienced operator
B BreathingRR, SpO₂, symmetry, auscultationO₂ for SpO₂ 94-98 %. If a chest drain is placed, 1-2 spaces higher (3rd-4th intercostal space) because of diaphragm elevation
C CirculationPulse, BP, capillary refill, 2 large-bore IV lines, labs, bleeding controlFrom 20 weeks: manual left uterine displacement (preferred in the unstable patient) or 15-30° left lateral tilt. The pregnant patient may show no signs until losing around 30% of blood volume; tachycardia with normal BP = early sign
D Disability (neurologic deficit)Glasgow or AVPU, pupils, blood glucoseRule out a metabolic cause (blood glucose) before attributing the presentation to trauma
E ExposureUndress and examine the entire bodyPrevent hypothermia: warmed fluids, warm environment, temperature >36.5 °C
Acronym variants
VariantDifferenceSource
ABCDEClassic scheme, without an initial “x”ATLS through the 10th ed.; maternal collapse guidelines
<C>ABCDE“C” for catastrophic hemorrhage before AVictorian State Trauma System; NICE NG39
xABCDE“x” for exsanguinating hemorrhage before AATLS 11th ed. (ACS, 2025)
XABCDE-FAdds “F”: fetal assessment after stabilizing the motherObstetric emergency checklist (Heras). The “F” is supported by: fetal monitoring from 24 weeks, once the mother is stable; “the best treatment for the fetus is to resuscitate the mother well” (StatPearls; Victoria obstetric guideline)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: StatPearls — Trauma Assessment (xABCDE, ATLS 11th ed.) · ACS — ATLS 11 launch · Victorian State Trauma System — Obstetric Trauma Guideline v2.0, pp. 7-9 and 11 · Krywko DM et al. StatPearls — Pregnancy Trauma · Frimley Health — Maternal Collapse in Pregnancy and the Puerperium (ABCDE) · Heras A. — Preeclampsia Checklist.

12FAST / eFAST in pregnant and postpartum patients

Views and findings
WindowSearch
SubxiphoidPericardial effusion / tamponade
Hepatorenal (Morrison)Free fluid. In preeclampsia/HELLP with epigastric or right upper quadrant pain: subcapsular hepatic hematoma (hypoechoic crescent beneath the capsule)
PerisplenicFree fluid
Suprapubic / pelvisFree fluid; uterus: fetal heartbeat, placenta, amniotic fluid
Pulmonary (eFAST)Pneumothorax, pleural effusion. B-pattern (≥3 B-lines per field) = pulmonary edema
  • Positive FAST in an unstable pregnant patient = significant finding. If stable, it can be performed during the secondary survey, ideally by a second operator.
  • Performance for free fluid: sensitivity 61 % and specificity 94 % in pregnant patients (compared with 71 % and 97 % in nonpregnant patients). A negative FAST does not rule out bleeding.
  • Ultrasound has low sensitivity for placental abruption: it cannot be used to rule it out.
  • Severe preeclampsia: B-pattern was associated with elevated filling pressures. Restrict fluids (pilot study, n = 20).
  • Subcapsular hematoma: bedside ultrasound in the unstable patient; CT if stable.

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Victorian Obstetric Trauma Guideline v2.0, pp. 8 and 15 · OpenAnesthesia — Obstetric Trauma · Zieleskiewicz L et al. Anesthesiology 2014;120(4):906-914 · Hepatic rupture in HELLP, case report (PMC) · Subcapsular hepatic hematoma in HELLP (PMC).

What to monitor and how often
ParameterTarget / frequency
Vital signs (EAPO)Every 5-10 min during the Compensate and Treat stages. Communicate to the team using colors (red / yellow / green)
Urine output (urinary catheter with collection bag)Normal: 50 cc/h or 0.5 cc/kg/h. Compensated hemorrhage: SBP >90 mmHg + urine output >30 cc/h. Sepsis: >0.5 cc/kg/h. Also assess urine characteristics
Lactate / base deficitInitial level and its clearance: identifies incomplete resuscitation even if BP has normalized
TemperatureAvoid hypothermia (lethal triad: hypoperfusion/acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy)
Fetus (trauma, ≥24 weeks)CTG for at least 4 h after trauma, once the mother is stabilized
Magnesium sulfate: criteria for stopping or not repeating a dose (variants)
MonitoringMSPBS 2022WHO (product information)
Respiratory rate<12/min<16/min
Patellar reflexDecreased or absentAbsent
Urine output<30 cc/h<30 mL/h in the previous 4 h
Antidote10% calcium gluconate, 1 g (10 cc) IV over 3 min (MSPBS)

fichas.titulo: Primary xABCDE survey adapted for the pregnant patient
fichas.texto: Assess and treat in order; if the patient deteriorates, return to “x”. Tasks are carried out simultaneously by team members. xABCDE (ATLS 11th ed., 2025) with pregnancy-specific adjustments Step What to assess/do Adjustment in the pregnant patient x Exsanguinating hemorrhage Massive, compressible external bleeding: direct pressure, packing, tourniquet if involving an extremity (record the time) For obstetric bleeding: activate Code Red and follow the sequence for control by Tone (card 6) A Airway Patency; cervical spine protection if trauma occurred Consider earlier intubation: the pregnant patient desaturates faster. Higher risk of failed intubation: it should be performed by the most experienced operator B Breathing RR, SpO₂, symmetry, auscultation O₂ for SpO₂ 94-98 %. If a chest drain is placed, 1-2 spaces higher (3rd-4th intercostal space) because of diaphragm elevation C Circulation Pulse, BP, capillary refill, 2 large-bore IV lines, labs, bleeding control From 20 weeks: manual left uterine displacement (preferred in the unstable patient) or 15-30° left lateral tilt. The pregnant patient may show no signs until losing around 30% of blood volume; tachycardia with normal BP = early sign D Disability (neurologic deficit) Glasgow or AVPU, pupils, blood glucose Rule out a metabolic cause (blood glucose) before attributing the presentation to trauma E Exposure Undress and examine the entire body Prevent hypothermia: warmed fluids, warm environment, temperature >36.5 °C Acronym variants Variant Difference Source ABCDE Classic scheme, without an initial “x” ATLS through the 10th ed.; maternal collapse guidelines <C>ABCDE “C” for catastrophic hemorrhage before A Victorian State Trauma System; NICE NG39 xABCDE “x” for exsanguinating hemorrhage before A ATLS 11th ed. (ACS, 2025) XABCDE-F Adds “F”: fetal assessment after stabilizing the mother Obstetric emergency checklist (Heras). The “F” is supported by: fetal monitoring from 24 weeks, once the mother is stable; “the best treatment for the fetus is to resuscitate the mother well” (StatPearls; Victoria obstetric guideline) CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: StatPearls — Trauma Assessment (xABCDE, ATLS 11th ed.) · ACS — ATLS 11 launch · Victorian State Trauma System — Obstetric Trauma Guideline v2.0, pp. 7-9 and 11 · Krywko DM et al. StatPearls — Pregnancy Trauma · Frimley Health — Maternal Collapse in Pregnancy and the Puerperium (ABCDE) · Heras A. — Preeclampsia Checklist.

fichas.titulo: FAST / eFAST in pregnant and postpartum patients
fichas.texto: Views and findings Window Search Subxiphoid Pericardial effusion / tamponade Hepatorenal (Morrison) Free fluid. In preeclampsia/HELLP with epigastric or right upper quadrant pain: subcapsular hepatic hematoma (hypoechoic crescent beneath the capsule) Perisplenic Free fluid Suprapubic / pelvis Free fluid; uterus: fetal heartbeat, placenta, amniotic fluid Pulmonary (eFAST) Pneumothorax, pleural effusion. B-pattern (≥3 B-lines per field) = pulmonary edema Positive FAST in an unstable pregnant patient = significant finding. If stable, it can be performed during the secondary survey, ideally by a second operator. Performance for free fluid: sensitivity 61 % and specificity 94 % in pregnant patients (compared with 71 % and 97 % in nonpregnant patients). A negative FAST does not rule out bleeding. Ultrasound has low sensitivity for placental abruption: it cannot be used to rule it out. Severe preeclampsia: B-pattern was associated with elevated filling pressures. Restrict fluids (pilot study, n = 20). Subcapsular hematoma: bedside ultrasound in the unstable patient; CT if stable. grupos.nombre: Mode of Delivery — Robson, Bishop, Biometry
grupos.titulo: Mode of Delivery — Robson Classification, Bishop Score, and Maternal-Fetal Biometry
grupos.bajada: Robson classification at admission with management by group, cesarean audit (WHO/PAHO), cervical ripening, and cesarean alert criteria for macrosomia, SGA/FGR, and maternal height.
grupos.html:
1Robson Classification — 10 groups (WHO 2015, FIGO 2016)

GroupDefinition
1Nulliparous, singleton, cephalic, ≥37 weeks, spontaneous labor
2Nulliparous, singleton, cephalic, ≥37 weeks, induced labor (2a) or cesarean before labor (2b)
3Multiparous with no previous cesarean, singleton, cephalic, ≥37 weeks, spontaneous labor
4Multiparous with no previous cesarean, singleton, cephalic, ≥37 weeks, induced labor (4a) or cesarean before labor (4b)
5At least one previous cesarean, singleton, cephalic, ≥37 weeks (5.1: one cesarean; 5.2: two or more)
6All nulliparous women with a singleton breech fetus
7All multiparous women with a singleton breech fetus (including previous cesarean)
8All multiple pregnancies (including previous cesarean)
9Singleton fetus in transverse or oblique lie (including previous cesarean)
10Singleton cephalic fetus <37 weeks (including previous cesarean)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: PAHO/WHO — Robson Classification: application manual (2018).

It is classified using 6 variables: parity, prior cesarean delivery, onset of labor, number of fetuses, presentation/lie, and GA. Groups are mutually exclusive. Groups 1, 2 and 5 usually account for most cesarean deliveries and are the target of reduction strategies. Source: PAHO/WHO — Robson Classification: application manual (2018).

The 6 variables
VariableOptionsNote
ParityNulliparous · MultiparousMultiparous: at least one previous birth, vaginal or cesarean
Previous cesareanNo · 1 · 2 or moreDefines subgroups 5.1 and 5.2
Onset of laborSpontaneous · Induced · Cesarean before laborAs found at admission, regardless of what was planned. An emergency cesarean before labor starts counts as «before labor»
Number of fetusesSingleton · Multiple
Presentation / lieCephalic · Breech · Transverse or oblique
Gestational ageWeeksCut-off at 37+0

CaVeSal® proprietary table · Based on: PAHO/WHO — Robson Classification: application manual (2018).

Classification at admission and real-time use

  • It is applied to every woman admitted for birth, prospectively: each woman is assigned a group at admission and followed to the outcome (WHO — Robson Platform; WHO implementation manual).
  • Real-time use is institutional: each birth is recorded as it happens to track the cesarean rate by group and plan actions (quality improvement experience). WHO provides a platform where hospitals upload these data (WHO Bulletin).
  • Standard report by group: number of cesareans, number of women, group size, group cesarean rate, absolute and relative contribution to the overall rate (Robson report table).
  • Robson does not assess whether a cesarean was appropriately indicated: that requires an audit of indications.
  • In CaVeSal®: the Prenatal Calculator shows the probable group (prognosis); the Emergency calculator assigns the group at admission with intrapartum management (Labor tab).

2Robson — intrapartum management by group

GroupManagementSources
1Prolonged latent phase and slow but progressive labor are not indications for cesarean. Partograph according to the chosen model (Ministry CLAP from 4 cm, WHO 2020 from 5 cm, ACOG from 6 cm). Active-phase arrest: ≥6 cm with ruptured membranes and no change with ≥4 h of adequate contractions or ≥6 h of oxytocin with inadequate contractions. Second stage: ≥3 h of pushing before diagnosing arrest (longer with epidural, individualized). Continuous support.WHO — Labour Care Guide 2020 · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014)
2a / 4aInduce only with a clear indication; from 41+0 weeks induction is recommended. Bishop ≤6: cervical ripening (oral misoprostol 25 µg q2h or vaginal 25 µg q6h, balloon, or balloon + oxytocin). Do not diagnose failed induction in the latent phase before ≥24 h of induction and ≥12-18 h of oxytocin after membrane rupture. Never unsupervised; induce where an operating room is available.WHO — Induction of labour at or beyond term (2022) · WHO — Induction of labour (2011) · WHO — Mechanical methods (2022) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014)
2b / 4bVerify and document the indication. Without a medical indication, do not schedule before 39 weeks.ACOG CO 765 (2019) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014)
3Same criteria as Group 1 with multiparous standards. Second stage: ≥2 h of pushing. Lowest cesarean rate group: a cesarean here deserves review of the indication.WHO — Labour Care Guide 2020 · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014)
5.1VBAC if: low transverse (or low vertical) incision, no previous rupture and no contraindication to vaginal birth. Contraindicated: classical cesarean, T or J incision, previous rupture. Only with 24-h emergency cesarean, blood bank and NICU. Continuous fetal monitoring and one-to-one care (abnormal FHR is the most common sign of rupture). Induction with mechanical methods; misoprostol contraindicated; oxytocin with caution. Epidural not contraindicated. Interval under 18 months: higher risk. EFW >4500 g: cesarean (FIGO).FIGO — VBAC (2025) · ACOG PB 205 (2019) · RCOG GTG 45 · WHO — Induction of labour (2011)
5.2Two cesareans: FIGO generally does not recommend VBAC (only with a previous vaginal birth, senior obstetrician counseling and a high-complexity center); RCOG and ACOG allow it with counseling. Three or more: cesarean. With placenta previa or low anterior placenta, rule out accreta.FIGO — VBAC (2025) · ACOG PB 205 (2019) · RCOG GTG 45
6Offer external cephalic version (ECV) from 36 weeks. Without ECV: planned cesarean from 39 weeks, or vaginal breech birth only with an institutional protocol, trained operator and written consent. In labor: ultrasound (type of breech, head flexion, EFW) and continuous monitoring; inadequate progress → cesarean. Imminent delivery: hands-off assistance.ACOG CO 745 (2018, reaf. 2023) · RCOG GTG 20b
7Same as Group 6, with ECV from 37 weeks. With one previous low transverse cesarean, ECV may be attempted if she is a good VBAC candidate.ACOG CO 745 (2018, reaf. 2023) · RCOG GTG 20b · FIGO — VBAC (2025)
8Uncomplicated dichorionic or monochorionic diamniotic twins, >32 weeks, first twin cephalic, no significant discordance: vaginal birth and cesarean are equally safe. First twin non-cephalic: cesarean. Monoamniotic: cesarean (32+0-33+6). Triplets: cesarean. One previous low transverse cesarean does not contraindicate VBAC. Active third stage due to higher hemorrhage risk.NICE NG137 (2019) · ACOG PB 231 (2021) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) · FIGO — VBAC (2025)
9In labor or with ruptured membranes: cesarean (cord prolapse, uterine rupture). Before labor and without contraindications: ECV from 37 weeks. Ultrasound to rule out a mechanical cause (placenta previa, fibroids, anomalies). With back down, consider a vertical uterine incision.GLOWM · StatPearls — ECV
10Lung maturation, neuroprotection, tocolysis and PROM according to the preterm labor and PROM cards in this guide. Notify neonatology. Prematurity alone does not determine the mode of birth; it is decided by obstetric conditions.ACOG CO 831 (2021)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: sources listed for each group · PAHO/WHO — Robson Classification (2018).

Fetal lung maturation, magnesium sulfate neuroprotection, tocolysis and PROM follow the management already set in their cards in this guide and in the calculator. Does not replace clinical judgment.

Variant: the modified Bishop score (Calder) replaces effacement with cervical length (cm). Unfavorable cervix → cervical ripening (misoprostol, Foley balloon) before oxytocin. Source: StatPearls — Bishop Score.

4SGA vs FGR (Delphi consensus)

CategoryCriterion
SGAEFW and/or AC p3-p10, normal anatomy and normal Doppler; follow-up every 2 weeks
FGREFW/AC <p3 (with any Doppler finding), or <p10 with abnormal Doppler (UA PI >p95, mean uterine artery PI >p95, CPR/MCA <p5), or a drop of >2 quartiles over ≥2 weeks (late-onset FGR)

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Gordijn SJ et al. Consensus definition of fetal growth restriction: a Delphi procedure. Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol 2016;48(3):333-9 · Hospital Universitario Virgen de las Nieves — FGR Protocol (2025) · Valenti EA et al. 2017 FASGO Consensus Update: FGR · Sardá Maternity Hospital — Clinical Practice Guideline for Fetal Growth Restriction.

It is subdivided into early-onset (<32 weeks) and late-onset (≥32 weeks). Sources: Delphi consensus (Gordijn 2016) · HUVN FGR protocol · FASGO 2017 · SARDA.

5Macrosomia and cesarean delivery alert (ACOG PB 216)

Glycemic statusEFWManagement
No diabetes≥5000 gPlanned cesarean delivery justified
No diabetes4000-4999 gTrial of labor with monitoring of the second stage; avoid midpelvic instrumental delivery
Gestational or pregestational diabetes≥4500 gPlanned cesarean delivery justified
Diabetes4000-4499 gTrial of labor with monitoring

CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG PB 216 (2020) · RCOG GTG 42 (2018, shoulder dystocia).

Macrosomia: ≥4000 g (some guidelines reserve the term for ≥4500 g); LGA: EFW ≥p90. In our setting, consider a history of birth weight ≥4000 g. Sources: ACOG PB 216 (2020) · RCOG GTG 42 (2018, shoulder dystocia).

6Short maternal stature and cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)

  • Height <145-150 cm is not an indication for cesarean delivery (WHO 2018, FIGO, ACOG): it is a biomechanical risk factor; allow a trial of labor with a strict partograph and, if available, intrapartum ultrasound.
  • MSPBS: height <145 cm → referral to orthopedics and genetics (possible skeletal dysplasia), not a criterion for mode of delivery.
  • CPD is diagnosed intrapartum: adequate uterine activity (3-5/10 min, >2-4 h), dilation ≥5-6 cm, and lack of progress in dilation or descent. Signs: cervical edema, marked caput with overlapping sutures, persistent asynclitism. Once confirmed → cesarean delivery.
  • Estimated fetal weight ≥4000 g + short stature → heightened alert for surveillance of CPD, not automatic cesarean delivery.

Sources: WHO Intrapartum care 2018 · MSPBS Manual Nacional Prenatal · ACOG PB 216 · Williams Obstetrics 26.ª ed. (2022) · Caldwell-Moloy 1933 (tipos de pelvis).

fichas.titulo: Short maternal stature and cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)
fichas.texto: Height <145-150 cm is not an indication for cesarean delivery (WHO 2018, FIGO, ACOG): it is a biomechanical risk factor; allow a trial of labor with a strict partograph and, if available, intrapartum ultrasound. MSPBS: height <145 cm → referral to orthopedics and genetics (possible skeletal dysplasia), not a criterion for mode of delivery. CPD is diagnosed intrapartum: adequate uterine activity (3-5/10 min, >2-4 h), dilation ≥5-6 cm, and lack of progress in dilation or descent. Signs: cervical edema, marked caput with overlapping sutures, persistent asynclitism. Once confirmed → cesarean delivery. Estimated fetal weight ≥4000 g + short stature → heightened alert for surveillance of CPD, not automatic cesarean delivery. Sources: WHO Intrapartum care 2018 · MSPBS Manual Nacional Prenatal · ACOG PB 216 · Williams Obstetrics 26.ª ed. (2022) · Caldwell-Moloy 1933 (tipos de pelvis).
